Smallest immediate dependency/build change, but every new S3 compatibility issue remains owned work. Keep only if SDK adapter/behavior costs outweigh retirement of the fork.



Prototype acceptance checklist:

Path-style custom endpoints, signing/credentials, escaped keys, range and conditional reads, correct origin not-found/precondition classification.
If-Match / If-None-Match upload and multipart completion, copy conditions, retry/re-upload behavior, cancellation, and operation timeout ownership.
Seekable spooled bodies; no hidden whole-object memory upload/download.
Exact Content-Type, Content-Encoding, user metadata, ETag, Last-Modified, object/part checksum round-tripping required by the current server.
Known checksum defaults: AWS SDK S3 v1.74.1 introduced automatic CRC32 upload checksums; download validation is also configurable. Decide intentionally rather than accepting a wire/performance change accidentally. AWS SDK
Error-injected and cross-gateway write-back tests, then the benchmark matrix below. A self-hosted origin is useful but not sufficient proof of real AWS interoperability.

Keep the existing small net/http origin implementation unless a replacement preserves validators, range handling, redirects, and its read-only/no-listing contract. filesystem/inmem remain development origins; current filesystem user metadata is process-local, not production-persistent metadata.

title: Capability-by-capability modernization review
text:
internal/objcache/read.go resolves parent object metadata before looking up aligned range blocks. When only range blocks are cached and the parent body row is absent, it calls origin.Attributes again. Thus an apparently warm range workload can still pay an origin HEAD RTT.
Recommendation: a small logged PostgreSQL parent-metadata record, shared by all gateways, containing size, validator/generation, response metadata, and validation time. Resolve ranges against it and bind every range block to that generation. Preserve TTL revalidation, tombstones, write-back shadowing, and stale-fill fences. Read-only workers must be able to use the replicated record without trying to renew or mutate it.
This potentially removes a network round trip on the workload that matters most, rather than optimizing a few Go allocations. It adds state and therefore needs a clear benefit in request counts and latency. It is not an in-process metadata cache.
An explicit immutable-prefix mode is another avenue for immutable DuckLake data files: reduce repeated validation and simplify state transitions for those keys. Do not silently infer immutability from .parquet, and do not apply it to arbitrary mutable objects or delete/recreate keys.




NGINX slice caching: well-established ranged HTTP caching, but introduces another cache/process and does not provide PostgreSQL-replicated cache hits, transactional write-back, or shared RESP data. Useful for a read-only edge variant, not an equivalent internal replacement. Its documentation also warns about slice/background-update interaction. NGINX
DuckDB’s external file cache: already caches remote bytes in memory and is enabled by default in the inspected DuckDB 2.0 configuration. It complements pgvs3 but is local to the client, not a cross-gateway cache. Benchmark with client caching both enabled and disabled to avoid attributing client hits to the server. Do not use old enable_object_cache advice: that pragma is a deprecated no-op in DuckDB 2.0. DuckDB cache
Local LRU/Ristretto/filesystem cache: could be a valid different design, but violates the current zero-local-object/metadata-cache invariant and does not make shared PostgreSQL state unnecessary.
UNLOGGED read fills: excluded by the requested design and replica-sharing requirement; not a proposed optimization.

title: Capability-by-capability modernization review
text:
At this commit, internal/objcache/tier.go sets a 2-minute fill lease and 45-second waiter budget; a whole-object fill may run for 10 minutes. internal/store/filllease.go has acquire/release/cleanup but no renewal path. Slow origins can therefore outlive ownership, and waiters can fall back to duplicate origin traffic before the owner finishes.
Plan one cohesive improvement:

Renew using the database clock and owner token while work is alive.
Fence final publication by the live lease owner/generation as well as the expected origin version. Release ownership conditionally.
Cancel/discard a fill on ownership loss; do not let renewal become local authority or a reason to hold a DB connection during download.
Make waiting/fallback policy explicit and size-aware. More waiting reduces duplicate traffic but can worsen tail latency; measure both.
Test a fill exceeding 2 minutes, owner crash, cancelled waiter, lost renewal, overwrite/delete/recreate, and several gateways requesting the same range.

Local singleflight remains useful but cannot coordinate separate gateways. Session advisory locks during the entire download would be shorter to write but consume a database session per slow origin request, undoing current isolation.



internal/objcache/writeback.go detaches the database body into a spool before uploading, but retains the session key-lock connection through the origin upload. That is intentional ordering protection, not merely an accidental connection leak.
Do not replace it with a token check after upload and call it safe. A token can reject stale local publication after an old upload has already overwritten the remote object. A lock-free alternative needs demonstrated remote ordering: conditional origin mutations with the correct base version, or immutable generation objects plus a conditional authoritative pointer. The latter changes origin key/layout semantics and is not a transparent refactor.
River/PGMQ/generic workers can supply claim/retry machinery, but do not remove the atomic body-plus-outbox commit, supersession, public ETag, merged listings, delete coordination, pending-row flush guards, or remote side-effect ordering. CDC/Debezium would add a service and delivery semantics, not simplify this bounded in-process worker by default.
Retain logged bodies until they are safely committed at the origin under the existing policy. Scratch files are disposable; acknowledged pending bodies are not. Processing and remote side effects must be treated as at least once, with idempotency/preconditions where required, not end-to-end exactly once.

title: Capability-by-capability modernization review
Capability-by-capability modernization review
text:
Redcon is a compact server dependency, not an obvious source of excess owned code. RESP3 has a different type/handshake surface and is a compatibility expansion, not a necessary modernization. gnet is an event-loop transport; PostgreSQL’s blocking work still needs dispatch/backpressure and all command semantics remain owned. External Valkey changes the one-database authority and backup model. RESP sources
Better avenues within scope:

Measure SET batching independently: current README records that 4 KiB redcon read batches can fragment the old pipelined write coalescing. Tune/prototype batching only against latency and throughput together.
Keep SQL-native atomic operations, TTL, numeric mutation, NX/XX, GETDEL, APPEND/SETRANGE, and shared-cache visibility; do not replace them with read/modify/write in Go.
internal/store/cache_mset.go falls back to sequential single-key writes when any value exceeds the inline ceiling. That path is not atomic across keys. Review a staged-body/one-publication-transaction implementation, or an explicit documented/rejected unsupported case; do not imply full Redis MSET semantics for the existing fallback.
Cross-namespace FLUSHALL is also sequential. State that boundary explicitly rather than adding a broad transaction/locking framework by default.
Continue explicitly rejecting MULTI/EXEC/WATCH; a pipeline is not a transaction. Keep HELLO 3 rejection and RESP2 client instructions unless RESP3 becomes an explicit requirement.

title: Capability-by-capability modernization review
text:
The official OJS Go SDK is a client/worker SDK, not a server binding. The reference PostgreSQL backend is a broader server with features deliberately excluded from pgvs3. Its inspected module also uses a sibling-directory module replacement; packaging/release maturity needs verification before embedding. Its actual LICENSE is Apache-2.0, despite an inconsistent changelog statement. Validate lease-token fencing against any upstream implementation. OJS sources
For the current bounded API:

Standard http.ServeMux method/wildcard routes may remove dispatch plumbing in internal/ojs. Preserve exact error envelopes, HEAD behavior, trailing slash handling, methods, and /ojs/manifest routing. ServeMux
Go 1.27 already backs encoding/json with the v2 implementation. Changing the import is not an automatic speed upgrade. Stable v2 offers MarshalWrite/UnmarshalRead and stricter defaults, but duplicate-name, invalid-UTF-8, nil collection, case matching, and omission behavior can change the wire contract. Use golden fixtures and compatible options where needed. Do not rely on old experimental format tags: the released API removed them. Go27 JSON migration
Broad OpenAPI/server generation is only attractive if an authoritative spec exactly captures pgvs3’s implemented subset and token extension. Generating a larger server and then maintaining exceptions is not an established saving.







Candidate
Fit




Existing atomic claim SQL
Already consolidated to candidate/update/return with SKIP LOCKED, including due/expired eligibility. Highest confidence for retaining current priorities, leases, retention, and namespace behavior.


River
Strong PostgreSQL job framework and a sensible choice for applications wanting its worker ecosystem. An OJS server would still need lifecycle/state/token/namespace adapters; some advanced features are Pro. Do not replace working claim SQL solely to recreate the current server on top. River


PGMQ
Lightweight visibility-timeout queue, with SQL-only installation as well as an extension. Managed hosting is therefore not categorically disqualifying, but OJS states, priority/retry policy, token fencing, stream batches, and namespace lifecycle remain to be mapped. A visibility window is not end-to-end exactly-once processing. PGMQ


Reference OJS PostgreSQL backend
Closest wire-family alternative, but much broader scope, deployment surface, and dependencies. Most relevant if full OJS becomes a goal, not as a proven small dependency replacement. OJS sources



Do not unify jobs and streams into one delivery algorithm just because both carry JSON. Mutable competing-worker jobs and replayable fan-out streams have different row ownership, retention, and acknowledgment semantics.



PgQue’s snapshot batches and rotating log are directly relevant to the existing three-segment stream model. Replacing current code with an upstream package still requires checking member cooperation, batch leases/acks, nack retries, DLQ, payload/quota limits, schema ownership, and managed-PostgreSQL operation. Keep the design; use upstream as a comparison and potential future extraction target rather than assuming method names establish equivalence. PgQue
Consider debounced LISTEN/NOTIFY as a lossy wakeup hint for job/stream long polls and outbox workers only if polling load is significant. One dedicated session can wake eligible local waiters; reconnect and periodic polling must recover missed notifications. Notifications must not become queue authority or cache invalidation correctness, and one notification per item can introduce global-lock/contention costs. River documents batching/throttling concerns. This is not a default replacement for the already-small polling path. Notify

title: Capability-by-capability modernization review
text:
Keep schema-per-namespace while the supported limit is 100. It preserves a clear physical/drop/export boundary. A single shared table makes SQL generation easier but complicates fast bucket disk reclamation and isolation; partitioning can restore some benefits while adding DDL and maintenance. No evidence in this review justifies that trade yet.
Keep SQL-native same-bucket shared-file copies and cross-bucket INSERT ... SELECT. Global content-addressed bytes/dedup could save storage, but require cross-namespace reference tracking and undermine independent drop, clone, and schema exports. Generic S3 copy helpers must not silently replace these paths with gateway byte streaming.
Keep bounded GC and the existing advisory-lock leader. pg_cron or pg_partman would add installation/version requirements and would not eliminate reference safety, snapshot lifetime, or cooperative stream retention.
Sequence review item: clone_namespace copies already-issued IDs, then calls setval(GREATEST(last_value, max_id)); adoption has a related pattern. The read/max/set sequence is not itself a concurrency-safe monotonic update relative to concurrent allocation. PostgreSQL documents that setval changes are immediately visible and not rolled back. Audit with a deterministic clone/adopt-versus-allocation test before changing it; do not claim a reproduced collision from source inspection alone. An ordinary in-database clone should not need to readjust an already-ahead sequence; imported schema adoption needs its own safe allocation/reconciliation design. Sequences
The existing Go block of 64 file IDs is a cache of values already allocated by PostgreSQL, not a locally authoritative ID generator. Replacing it with UUIDs merely because Go 1.27/PostgreSQL 18 supply new UUID facilities would add key/index costs without an established need.

title: Capability-by-capability modernization review
text:
The chart provides 10 GiB of scratch. Default fill and pending-worker budgets can each allow eight spools; sixteen 1 GiB bodies already exceed that, before foreground write spools, other temporary usage, and logs. Count-only limits do not bound bytes. GOMEMLIMIT does not bound scratch storage or all process/cgroup memory.
Use one process-wide scratch-byte budget across fills, pending uploads, and foreground spooling, in addition to operation counts. x/sync/semaphore.Weighted is already available through the existing dependency. Weighted K8s resources

Reserve known sizes before creating large spools; reject or use an explicit pass-through policy when a request cannot fit.
Define a hard bound for unknown-length inputs. Naively blocking all partial spools while each waits for more bytes can deadlock the budget; reserve a bounded maximum or use nonblocking growth with a clean abort/fallback policy.
Release on every error/cancel/close path and account for simultaneous spool copies rather than just logical object size.
Align chart ephemeral-storage requests/limits, emptyDir.sizeLimit, spool configuration, and metrics. emptyDir.sizeLimit is not a scheduler reservation.
Preserve disk, not tmpfs, for large scratch bodies. A scratch file is not a reason to move acknowledged bodies out of PostgreSQL.




Current quota and --max-db-bytes checks are documented sampled, per-worker guardrails. They are not hard cross-worker storage quotas. PostgreSQL roles and tablespaces alone do not create a general per-namespace byte-quota mechanism; the operational wording should not suggest that they do.
Audit unknown-length multipart admission and overwrite accounting separately. A hard logical quota would need transactional reservations, commit/release, crash cleanup, and unknown-size policy; a single shared counter can become a write hotspot. Sharded reservation blocks trade exactness for throughput. Do not add that machinery without a hard-quota requirement. Physical disk/WAL headroom still needs monitoring regardless of logical reservations.

title: Capability-by-capability modernization review
text:
DuckLake 1.1, released 2026-10-21 with DuckDB 2.0, improves catalog/pruning and stores row-group counts in metadata. Small insertion/deletion inlining already places changes directly in the PostgreSQL catalog instead of creating a Parquet file for every change. Prefer configuring existing inlining and compaction over adding another pgvs3 small-file staging layer. DuckLake
Pin exact client/catalog versions in compatibility and performance runs. Existing DuckLake catalogs do not automatically become 1.1. The inspected stable inlining page still conflicts with the 1.1 release description on PostgreSQL VARIANT support; use versioned release behavior and a contract test, not an unqualified support claim.
pg_ducklake is a potentially simpler analytics deployment for people wanting SQL analytics inside PostgreSQL. It is not an S3 server, RESP cache, or OJS replacement, and its extension availability on Aurora has not been verified. Keep it in the scope-changing alternatives list. Direct DuckLake-on-cloud-S3 is likewise simpler if storing all file bytes in PostgreSQL ceases to be a requirement. pg_ducklake

title: Capability-by-capability modernization review
text:
internal/telemetry/telemetry.go owns HTTP tracing, a ResponseWriter wrapper, and basic query spans; S3/OJS/RESP/store metrics have separate exposition code.

otelhttp can own standard server/client spans and response-body lifetime handling. Preserve X-Trace-Id, filter probes/metrics if desired, use bounded route names, and test streaming/Flush/ResponseController behavior. Disable per-read/write events for large bodies unless explicitly wanted. OTel HTTP
otelpgx covers queries, batches, connect/acquire, prepare, high-level COPY, and pool statistics. Direct PgConn calls and custom streaming spans still need explicit coverage; a new tracer does not magically observe every low-level operation. Do not include query parameters or object keys in metric labels, and decide whether SQL text should be exported. OTel pgx
Prometheus client collectors can replace manual text formatting while retaining current cheap atomic observations: use a custom collector at scrape time, not necessarily a dynamic CounterVec lookup on every request. Preserve metric names/labels and test cardinality plus histogram correctness. Native histograms or a full OTel metrics pipeline are optional scope, not prerequisites to removing duplicate exposition. Prometheus
Keep standard slog and pprof. Go 1.27’s goroutine-leak profile helps diagnose some unreachable blocked goroutines, but is not a complete leak or shutdown detector. Go27

The current tracing module is small enough that dependency/version cost might outweigh deletion. Benchmark export disabled, sampled tracing, and export enabled under collector failure. Do not accidentally turn disabled telemetry into a hot-path allocation or network requirement.

title: Capability-by-capability modernization review
text:
The README says pending write-back bodies survive crash/failover without qualifying replication policy. Logged storage and synchronous_commit=on guarantee local WAL durability, but do not by themselves guarantee lossless promotion of an asynchronous standby. Synchronous-standby configuration and promotion policy determine remote durability; immediate visibility on arbitrary standbys additionally depends on replay. Aurora uses a different storage/HA model and needs service-specific validation. WAL
Clarify this operationally rather than silently enabling synchronous replication and changing latency/availability. Benchmark the intended production durability mode, not an async mode while claiming RPO=0. Keep all current data logged.
pgx already supports target_session_attrs=read-write and related host-role validation. This is a useful optional writer-connection guard alongside managed writer endpoints, plus role reporting in doctor/readiness. It does not replace endpoint failover, retries, or fencing. Read-only gateways may intentionally connect to the primary, so do not require a physical standby in that mode. PGX




Keep managed PITR or a standard tool such as pgBackRest for physical base backup/WAL retention. pgBackRest supports parallelism, standby backup, bundled files, and block-incremental repositories; choose using restore and archive throughput measurements, not a new backup implementation in pgvs3. pgBackRest
If self-managing PostgreSQL on Kubernetes, an established operator such as CloudNativePG can own database HA and backup orchestration. Prefer its plugin-based Barman Cloud path for new configurations; old native backup examples are version-sensitive/deprecated. This is an operator choice, not another dependency in the gateway. CNPG
A schema pg_dump is an export boundary, not a complete standalone system restore: restore into an initialized matching layout, reconcile global catalog/IDs, and verify functions/config/outbox dependencies. Large-object backing would weaken this simple boundary further.
Whole-cluster PITR preserves PostgreSQL transactional state, but it cannot rewind external origin writes or worker side effects. Test restoration with pending uploads and reconcile remote versions before restarting retry workers.
Keep backups/WAL archives outside the pgvs3 database being protected. Using the same gateway as its only backup object store creates a circular recovery dependency.
Drill recovery of DuckLake catalog plus files, RESP TTL data, jobs, stream consumer positions, tombstones, and acknowledged pending bodies. A reachable database or a successful dump alone is not the acceptance test.




Keep ko, static distroless images, Helm, stateless Deployments, network policy, and external PostgreSQL. Replacing this with a gateway operator would add an API/controller without simplifying the current resource set. Pin release images or digests for repeatable rollout instead of relying on latest.
Budget connections across main + chunk pools, maintenance/key-lock sessions, other applications, HPA maximums, and rollout surge. The chart’s three workers at pool 64 can have a much larger database connection footprint than the apparent poolMax value. HPA cannot make PostgreSQL capacity infinite.
Match termination grace to actual transfer/drain policy: the chart’s 60 seconds does not guarantee completion of requests whose HTTP deadlines permit 30 minutes. Keep bounded cancellation/retry behavior rather than claiming arbitrary-size transfers always finish on rollout.
Trusted private networking remains the security boundary. No proposal here adds gateway auth, signature validation, or TLS termination. Preserve default-deny ingress, loopback/private exposure, and existing external mesh options.

title: Capability-by-capability modernization review
text:
The refactor already consolidated environment parsing. Keep standard flag unless command growth makes declarative Kong schemas cheaper: Kong supports subcommands, env/default tags, validation, and help generation. Compare a complete small command group, including parsing precedence, global flag placement, explicit false/zero values, exit codes, and existing scripts. Cobra/Viper would be more machinery than demonstrated need here. Kong
A shared option definition used for help/config documentation may yield more benefit than changing parsers. Go 1.27 generic methods can improve selected helper ergonomics, but a broad generics rewrite is not a capability improvement.
Keep the single version-pinned baseline and drift doctor. Goose/Atlas-style migration histories solve in-place upgrades, which are not currently required. New third-party schemas must not accidentally introduce an unplanned migration policy.



Use stable testing/synctest for retry/backoff, timer, long-poll, cancellation, and waiter unit tests. Go 1.27’s fake-network httptest.NewTestServer can make HTTP timing tests deterministic without real sockets. Real PostgreSQL/network I/O is not durably blocked inside synctest; keep database and failover integration tests. Synctest Go27
Keep one harness per layer as CONTRIBUTING requires:

Unit/model/fuzz tests for state transitions, range/key/XML/JSON/RESP parsing.
PostgreSQL integration for locks, MVCC, sequence allocation, quotas, leases, GC, and concurrent mutation; do not validate replacement SQL only against mocks.
The existing pinned Go s3t allow-list, not a reintroduced Python Ceph suite.
Existing real-client contract/interop tests for boto3, DuckDB/DuckLake, rclone/restic, OJS workers, and RESP2 clients.
Differential/golden fixtures for adapter and wire-format changes, plus race, crash, shutdown, read-only replica, and origin-error cases.

PG19/Go experimental SIMD/event-loop rewrites are not default modernization targets. Stable features already in the project’s baseline offer better near-term risk/reward.

title: Capability-by-capability modernization review
text:
This is an implementation order for approval, not work already performed.









Order
Change
Expected payoff
Risk / proof required




1
Shared parent metadata for range-only cache hits
Remove avoidable origin RTTs on Parquet range workloads
New shared state; prove TTL/generation/delete/write-back and read-only semantics; count origin HEADs


2
One byte-weighted scratch budget + matching chart resources
Predictable 1 GiB concurrency; avoid scratch exhaustion and cascading retries
Unknown-length policy, fairness, clean abort, no budget leaks/deadlock; measure loaded throughput


3
Renewable, owner-fenced fill leases and explicit wait policy
Reduce duplicate slow-origin traffic across gateways
Renewal/owner loss/crash tests; tail latency and duplicate-byte measurements


4
PostgreSQL 18 old/new publication SQL
Less duplicated state/GC/CAS code without a new dependency
Full absent-key/CAS/TTL/copy/multipart/outbox tests; new layout if structural changes


5
AWS SDK origin adapter versus existing fork
Retire substantial owned S3-client behavior
Conditional multipart, checksums, cancellation, buffering, errors, binary size; no claim of benefit before comparison


6
synctest timer tests, then bounded OJS routing/envelope cleanup
Less flaky timing and smaller protocol plumbing
Wire goldens and real integration retained; JSON v2 semantic changes opt-in


7
Standard tracing/Prometheus exposition pilots
Less instrumentation maintenance; better boundary coverage
Disabled/enabled overhead, metric compatibility, streaming, dependency growth


8
Explicit cache state columns; optional debounced wakeups
Clearer lifecycle model; possibly lower idle polling
Only after state table and workload evidence; do not merge namespaces or require NOTIFY



Small operational/documentation work can proceed independently: qualify failover durability, clarify PgBouncer restrictions, distinguish guardrails from hard quotas, document oversized MSET behavior, and align connection/scratch/drain budgets. Reproduce the clone/adopt sequence hazard before selecting its remedy.
Not recommended now: whole S3-server replacement, River/PGMQ rewrite, job/stream algorithm unification, RESP3/gnet rewrite, one-bytea storage, large-object storage, global dedup, a migration framework, another cache service, or merging logged cache/write-back namespaces without a semantic proof.

title: Capability-by-capability modernization review
text:
Use the current binary as the control and change one major variable at a time. Record exact tool/library/database versions, hardware, origin bandwidth/latency, concurrency, warm/cold state, durability settings, repetitions, and variance.







Area
Required comparison




Large objects
10 MiB, 64 MiB, 256 MiB, 1 GiB Parquet and incompressible fixtures; single-client and saturated GET/PUT


Ranges
Footer/tiny ranges, aligned 1 MiB/8 MiB spans, multipart boundaries; cold fill, warm body, warm range-only, post-TTL; origin HEAD/GET counts


Write-back
ACK latency and origin drain rate, pending oldest age/bytes, retry amplification, conditional completion, concurrent overwrite/delete


Small values
4 KiB HEAD/GET/SET, pipeline depth 1/16, MGET/MSET inline and oversized, mutation/TTL races


Jobs/streams
Enqueue/claim/ack and receive/ack p50/p95/p99, idle poll query rate, contention/vacuum, fan-out and stalled consumer retention


Resources
CPU, allocations/RSS/cgroup memory, spool peak bytes, WAL bytes, DB pool wait/connections, origin requests/bytes, build/image size


Failure/replication
Owner expiry/crash, origin disconnect/timeout/conflict, mid-COPY cancel/restart, stale worker, primary promotion, replica lag, restored pending outbox



For latency/time metrics require candidate <= 1.20 × baseline on each relevant path. For throughput, define the gate explicitly rather than using an inverse accidentally: no more than 20% throughput loss means candidate >= 0.80 × baseline; also report elapsed-time ratios for fixed work. Resource growth and correctness/compatibility requirements remain independent acceptance conditions. Improvements must not merely shift cost from ACK time to an unbounded background backlog.
Existing refactoring measurements met the prior 20% budget; they are not evidence that any replacement above will meet it. At the time of the original review no candidate had been implemented or benchmarked; see the implementation status at the top for the subsequent work. Real AWS/Aurora and real promotion remain separate validation requirements. A constrained local origin is useful for repeatable comparisons, not proof of those environments.

title: Capability-by-capability modernization review
text:
Primary documentation/source inspected during this review; links can evolve. Version-specific statements above identify inspected versions where material.
Additional source details:

VersityGW backend contract

pgx COPY implementation and reader cancellation caveat

title: Hardening and compatibility options
text:
Historical analysis, not the active backlog. Priorities and status labels below describe the reviewed snapshots and may be superseded. Use the current architecture, ranked roadmap and implementation evidence.

Source paths and line numbers in this historical note refer to the reviewed snapshots. See the current file map.

Implementation note (2026-10-24): thanos-io/objstore has been replaced by a small internal S3/filesystem origin adapter. References to objstore below are historical research notes, not the current implementation.
Implementation note (2026-10-24): the SQS protocol was removed and replaced by the OJS v1 core HTTP binding. SQS/FIFO/redrive sections below describe the previous implementation and are kept as historical design notes.
Implementation note (2026-10-26): the PostgreSQL origin listing index was removed in layout v18. Listings now walk the origin directly; listing-index sections below are historical.

Status: decisions recorded 2026-10-23; implemented 2026-10-24. The trust-model wording, presigned-URL rejection, decoder hardening, SSE/ACL policy, per-key deletes, pending/outbox multipart write-through, origin ETags, FIFO queues, the listing index, read-only SQS metadata, and the database budget guard are implemented. The origin tier now validates checksums before mutation, enforces conditional PUT/COPY, preserves origin metadata, leases outbox rows and fences stale flushes with the captured origin version, normalizes configured listing prefixes, derives listing entries from list responses, and discards refreshes raced by writes.









Section
Decision




1. aws-chunked
A+D — strict 8 MiB cap, 128-byte header, reject unknown streaming algorithms, enforce decoded length when present, rolling buffer with no declared-size allocation


2. cache listing
B — PostgreSQL listing index


3. write-through
C+outbox — pending sentinel plus s3p.pending_uploads


4. DeleteObjects
A — HTTP 200 with per-key Deleted/Error, Quiet honored


5. origin ETag/Content-Type
B — origin ETag plus real Content-Type


6. SQS FIFO
B — full FIFO (dedup, per-group ordering, sequence numbers; high-throughput deferred)


7. SSE/Object Lock/ACL/tags
B — compatibility tier


8. read-only SQS
B — metadata-only operations allowed


9. quotas
A+D — best-effort gauge plus write-admission disk guard


10. verification
B+C+D — integration, fuzzers, SDK matrix



Each section states the problem, what the relevant AWS/objstore behavior is, several implementation options with trade-offs, and a recommendation. Pick one option per section (or defer) before code changes begin.
Priority is about risk to data or availability, not effort:



Priority
Meaning




P0
remote crash / unbounded work / silent data-visible divergence


P1
protocol lie that a normal client can rely on


P2
scalability or operator ergonomics









internal/s3/chunked.go trusts the declared chunk size:
data := make([]byte, size)   // line 86
size is parsed from an attacker-supplied hex line. A PUT with x-amz-content-sha256: STREAMING-... and a line such as ffffffffff asks Go to allocate ~1 TiB. A failed large allocation is a fatal runtime OOM, not a recoverable panic, so one small request can kill the gateway. Separately, a body made of blank lines recurses once per line (return c.Read(p), line 58) and grows the goroutine stack without bound.
There is also no total-size or chunk-count limit, and no consistency check against x-amz-decoded-content-length.




The wire format is <hex-size>[;chunk-signature=<sig>]\r\n<data>\r\n, terminated by a zero-size chunk and optional trailers (AWS chunked upload, trailers).
AWS requires chunks of at least 8 KiB (except the last) and recommends at least 64 KiB. The official Rust SDK defaults to 64 KiB (aws-runtime).
Other gateways cap the declared size: Supabase’s SigV4 stream parser defaults maxChunkSize to 8 MB and maxHeaderLength to 128 bytes (source).
The values pgvs3 must accept are STREAMING-UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD-TRAILER, STREAMING-AWS4-HMAC-SHA256-PAYLOAD[-TRAILER], and STREAMING-AWS4-ECDSA-P256-SHA256-PAYLOAD[-TRAILER] (AWS auth overview).














Approach
Behavior
Cost / risk




A
Strict AWS-shaped limits
Header line ≤ 128 B; chunk size ≤ 8 MiB; reject unknown STREAMING-* values; enforce x-amz-decoded-content-length when present; iterative parser
Safest. A client using > 8 MiB chunks fails (rare; SDKs use 64 KiB).


B
Compatibility-first
Cap at 64 MiB, allow any STREAMING-*, no decoded-length check, iterative parser
Preserves unusual clients; a single 64 MiB allocation per connection is still a memory-amplification vector.


C
Configurable
--max-chunk-size (default 8 MiB), --max-upload-bytes (default 0 = unlimited), strict parsing otherwise
Flexible; two more knobs and a way to misconfigure production.


D
Stream without buffering
Keep a rolling buffer, never allocate the declared size
Removes the allocation bug entirely, but the decoder must handle a chunk spanning many Read calls and is more code.






A + D. Parse iteratively with a fixed 128-byte header buffer and a bounded chunk buffer; never allocate from the declared size. Enforce the decoded length when the header is present. Reject unknown streaming algorithms with 400 InvalidRequest instead of attempting to parse them.
Add --max-upload-bytes as a separate, optional disk-protection control (not a substitute for the chunk cap).




Is any known client (rclone, restic, DuckDB, SlateDB) using chunks above 8 MiB? If yes, use 64 MiB.
Should a missing x-amz-decoded-content-length be rejected for signed streaming (AWS requires it) but allowed for unsigned trailer streaming?








Tier.List (internal/objcache/objcache.go:535) recursively walks the entire origin prefix, sorts everything, then truncates to limit. listObjectsV2 calls it once per page, so listing a bucket is O(N²). For each key not fresh in the PostgreSQL cache it then calls origin.Attributes, i.e. one origin HEAD per key — up to 1,000 HEADs for a single page.




S3 ListObjectsV2 is already paginated: up to 1,000 keys per request, with ContinuationToken / NextContinuationToken, KeyCount, MaxKeys, and StartAfter (AWS API).
thanos objstore exposes IterWithAttributes and WithUpdatedAt, and the S3 provider supports both, but IterObjectAttributes only carries Name and LastModified; it does not expose Size or ETag (objstore.go, s3 provider). So IterWithAttributes removes the mtime HEAD but not the size/ETag HEAD.
minio-go/v7 is already an indirect dependency (go.mod:48), so a native S3 lister does not add a new module.














Approach
Behavior
Cost / risk




A
IterWithAttributes only
Avoid HEAD for LastModified; still one HEAD per key for size/ETag
Small change, does not fix the actual cost. Not sufficient alone.


B
PostgreSQL listing index
s3c_<ns>.listing(prefix, key, size, etag, mtime, updated_at); list with LIMIT; fill on read/write; TTL refresh
O(page) when warm, O(N) on cold start; new table + DDL + invalidation semantics; stale within TTL.


C
Provider-aware lister
New Lister interface: S3 uses minio-go ListObjectsV2; filesystem uses WalkDir + Stat; inmem uses its map
O(page) always, exact metadata, no HEADs; provider-specific code and config duplication; bypasses objstore for list only.


D
Bound the origin listing
Require a prefix or cap at N keys, return 501/InvalidArgument beyond
Simple and honest; breaks large-bucket listing.


E
Hybrid
C for s3; current Iter for filesystem/inmem (local stat is cheap)
Best practical behavior; two listing paths to test.






E. Keep objstore for GET/PUT/DELETE, add a narrow Lister for S3 origins, and keep the current path for local providers with a hard key cap and context timeout. If a native lister is too much, B is the fallback, but it only helps after the first listing and adds cache-invalidation work.
Implemented: B, with the internal adapter’s Iter returning page metadata directly. The index avoids per-key HEADs, refreshes are generation checked, and oversized refreshes return an explicit error instead of an unbounded walk.




Should the continuation token stay the raw last key (current) or become an opaque base64 {prefix, lastKey}? S3 says tokens are obfuscated; clients must treat them as opaque either way.
Does the cache tier need delimiter support from the origin, or is client-side roll-up after a bounded page acceptable?
Is listing an origin bucket a supported use case, or should it be documented as best-effort with a key cap?








The two write paths order their effects differently:

Tier.Upload writes the origin first, then PostgreSQL.
Multipart completion must assemble part rows into one object. Publishing the cache first exposes bytes the origin does not have; uploading first holds a PostgreSQL transaction and connection open across the origin network call.

The implemented design uses a pending sentinel (origin_etag = 'pending:<upload-id>') plus an s3p.pending_uploads outbox row, published in the same transaction. Readers treat the sentinel as a miss, so pending bytes are never served. CompleteMultipartUpload then spools the pending object, releases the PostgreSQL connection, uploads it to the origin, and atomically swaps the sentinel for the origin version while deleting the outbox row. If the first flush fails, the request returns an error but the outbox row remains for a background worker to retry with bounded exponential backoff. Database leases serialize normal retries across gateways; the origin version captured at completion is passed as an If-Match (or If-None-Match: *) precondition so a stale flush cannot overwrite a newer PUT, DELETE, or multipart completion even after its lease expires.
Tier.Copy goes through Upload, so it inherits the origin-first order. DeleteMany uses per-key results (section 4) and evicts each cache key and outbox row immediately after its origin delete succeeds.













Approach
Behavior
Cost / risk




A
Origin-first everywhere
PUT stays as-is; multipart completion streams the assembled object from PostgreSQL to the origin, then publishes the cache
Origin is authoritative; no phantom; one extra PostgreSQL read per completed multipart; client waits for the origin upload either way.


B
Pending state column
Add state (pending/committed) to cache objects; readers treat pending as a miss; mark committed after the origin upload
No double read; crash leaves pending rows for GC; schema + read-path changes.


C
Sentinel + outbox
Publish with origin_etag = 'pending:<uuid>' plus an s3p.pending_uploads row; readers miss on the sentinel; replace with the real version after the origin upload; retry failures in the background
No per-object schema change; small read-path checks; one additive table; crash recovery and retries.


D
Keep current + delete on failure
Smallest change; the phantom window and partial-batch behavior remain
Does not meet the “explicit rejection over silent approximation” principle.






C + outbox (implemented). A successful CompleteMultipartUpload still waits for the first origin upload, but the PostgreSQL transaction and connection are released before the network call; crash recovery and retries are durable in s3p.pending_uploads. Make cache population best-effort on PUT: if the origin succeeds and the cache write fails, return success and log; the next read is a miss.
DeleteMany uses per-key results (section 4) and evicts each cache key and outbox row immediately after its origin delete succeeds.




Is the cache tier expected to survive an origin outage for reads (current TTL behavior), or is the origin always authoritative?
Should a failed cache write fail the client request when the origin succeeded? (Recommendation: no, except for read-after-write within the TTL.)








deleteObjects (internal/s3/server.go:580) returns one 500 if any delete fails, and otherwise marks every key deleted. S3 returns 200 OK with a <Deleted> or <Error> element per key, and Quiet mode returns only errors. For an origin bucket, a mid-batch failure can leave earlier keys deleted while the client sees a single failure.




AWS DeleteObjects returns per-key Deleted/Error entries in a 200 response; Quiet suppresses successful entries (AWS API).
General-purpose buckets require Content-MD5 for multi-object delete; directory buckets also accept a checksum header.














Approach
Behavior
Cost / risk




A
Per-key results
PG: one transaction, but report each key; origin: sequential deletes, collect per-key errors; always 200 unless the request itself is invalid
Matches S3; PG batch remains atomic even if individual keys “fail” only for not-found (which is success).


B
All-or-nothing
Current behavior; 500 on any failure
Not S3-compatible; cannot be made atomic for origin deletes.


C
Hybrid with savepoints
PG: savepoint per key, so a key-level failure does not roll back the batch; origin: per-key
Closest to S3; more SQL and more round trips.






A with C only if PG key-level failures can actually occur (they currently cannot for a normal delete; missing keys are success). Add the <Error> XML type and honor Quiet. Decide separately whether to require Content-MD5 (strict AWS behavior) or keep it optional for client compatibility.




Should a malformed key in a 1,000-key batch fail the whole request or produce one <Error> entry? AWS fails the request for malformed XML/keys.
Do we need VersionId fields in the response for wire compatibility even though versioning is out of scope? (Probably omit; clients tolerate absence.)








etagFor(version) returns md5("<size>-<mtime-ns>"), and Head derives Content-Type from the file extension (objcache.go:624). Origin ETags and stored content types are not authoritative. Conditional requests and client caches therefore cannot use the origin’s version identity.




S3 ListObjectsV2 returns ETag, Size, LastModified, and StorageClass; HeadObject returns Content-Type (ListObjectsV2).
objstore’s ObjectAttributes exposes Size, LastModified, and Version (ETag/generation), but not ContentType (objstore.go). Content-Type requires a provider-specific StatObject/Stat.














Approach
Behavior
Cost / risk




A
Keep synthetic
Cache ETags are cache-local; document it
No work; clients cannot correlate with origin.


B
Return origin ETag
Use the origin’s ETag for origin objects and store it in origin_etag; cache-filled objects keep the content MD5 or adopt the origin ETag
Better compatibility; one-time client cache invalidation; needs provider metadata.


C
Dual headers
ETag = origin ETag, X-Pgvs3-Content-MD5 = local content hash
Preserves both identities; non-standard header.


D
Extend objstore upstream
Add ContentType/ETag to ObjectAttributes and implement in providers
Best long-term; dependency/PR cycle.






B for ETag, plus a provider-specific stat for Content-Type on S3 origins; C if local content MD5 must remain observable. D is the clean upstream fix if the project is willing to carry a fork/PR.




Is an ETag change acceptable in the current alpha, or should it be gated behind a flag for one release?
Should write-through uploads return the origin ETag or the pgvs3 content MD5? (Origin ETag is more useful for read-after-write.)








CreateQueue accepts FifoQueue=true and .fifo names, and SendMessage accepts MessageGroupId / MessageDeduplicationId, but SendMessages ignores GroupID/DedupID. A client that asks for FIFO gets a standard queue with no ordering or deduplication guarantee. That is a silent correctness downgrade.




FIFO queue names must end in .fifo; MessageGroupId is required; deduplication uses MessageDeduplicationId or content hashing over a 5-minute interval; messages in a group are delivered in order; per-message DelaySeconds is not supported (AWS FIFO identifiers, CreateQueue, SendMessage).
Throughput is 300 API calls/s per method without batching, up to 3,000 messages/s with batches; high-throughput mode raises this further (queue types).














Approach
Behavior
Cost / risk




A
Reject FIFO
.fifo names or FifoQueue=true → 400 InvalidParameterValue; MessageGroupId on standard queues is accepted (AWS fair queues)
Honest; small change; no FIFO users.


B
Full FIFO
Dedup table with a 5-minute window, per-group sequence/order, SequenceNumber, visibility, batch dedup; no high-throughput mode initially
Correct; new schema, ordering query, more tests.


C
Minimal FIFO
Dedup + per-group ordering, reject unsupported attributes (ContentBasedDeduplication optional), no sequence numbers
Smaller than B; still a schema and receive-path change.


D
Status quo
Accept and treat as standard
Dangerous; violates the explicit-rejection principle.






A now. Add FIFO only if a real consumer needs it; then B, not C, because partial FIFO is another silent approximation. Regardless of choice, validate FifoQueue and .fifo consistency at CreateQueue.
Implemented: B (full FIFO without high-throughput mode).




Is any target workload (DuckLake, SlateDB, restic) using FIFO queues?
Should MessageGroupId on a standard queue be stored and returned as an attribute for fair-queue compatibility, or ignored?









x-amz-server-side-encryption: AES256 and aws:kms are accepted (now in internal/s3/request.go) but no encryption is performed.
Object Lock, ACL, and tagging headers are ignored; x-amz-tagging is not persisted.
x-amz-storage-class is ignored and listings always report STANDARD.

A client that sets Object Lock or SSE-KMS reasonably believes a guarantee exists. Object Lock is the dangerous one: it is a WORM/retention promise.




S3 stores the SSE algorithm and returns it on PUT/GET/HEAD; since January 5, 2023, new objects are encrypted by default with SSE-S3 (AWS SSE-S3).
Object Lock provides retention/legal hold and requires versioning; ACLs and tagging are separate authorization/metadata features. All are documented as out of scope for pgvs3.














Approach
Behavior
Cost / risk




A
Strict reject
Any SSE header → 501 NotImplemented; Object Lock → 501; ACL other than private → 501; tagging → 501; storage class other than STANDARD → 501
Honest; may break clients that send defaults.


B
Compatibility tier
Accept AES256 and x-amz-acl: private as documented no-ops (at-rest encryption delegated to PostgreSQL); reject aws:kms, public ACLs, Object Lock, tagging, non-STANDARD classes
Keeps common clients working; still no encryption guarantee for AES256.


C
Store and echo
Persist SSE/ACL/tagging metadata and echo it, without enforcement
Better wire fidelity; misleading for Object Lock and security-sensitive headers.


D
Full support
Implement encryption (pgcrypto/KMS), Object Lock enforcement, ACL model
Large; ACL/authorization contradicts the trust model.






B for SSE/ACL, with an explicit log line and docs stating that AES256 is satisfied only if the PostgreSQL volume is encrypted. A for Object Lock, tagging, and non-STANDARD storage classes. Never accept aws:kms as a no-op. If the project wants zero ambiguity, choose A across the board.




Do rclone/restic/boto3 send x-amz-acl: private or AES256 by default in the supported test matrix? (If yes, A breaks them.)
Is x-amz-tagging used by any target workload? If not, reject it.








--read-only rejects every SQS request (internal/sqs/sqs.go:97), including ListQueues, GetQueueUrl, and GetQueueAttributes. The docs say read-only gateways serve local-AZ reads; queue consumers cannot even inspect queues.
ReceiveMessage is genuinely a write: it sets visible_at, increments receive_count, and stores a receipt. On a PostgreSQL hot standby, SELECT ... FOR UPDATE is rejected anyway, so a read-only SQS consumer cannot work without changing semantics.













Approach
Behavior
Cost / risk




A
Keep blanket 403
Current behavior; document that SQS is primary-only
Simple; metadata inspection unavailable.


B
Allow metadata-only ops
ListQueues, GetQueueUrl, GetQueueAttributes work; Send/Receive/Delete/Purge return 403
Useful introspection; per-op read-only checks; works on standbys.


C
Peek mode
ReceiveMessage returns messages without leasing
Not SQS semantics; two consumers could process the same message; not recommended.






B, with a clear 403 AccessDenied message for ReceiveMessage explaining that leasing requires a writable primary. Document that SQS consumers need a primary gateway.




Does GetQueueAttributes need ApproximateNumberOfMessages on a standby (a SELECT over messages), or are static attributes enough?
Should ListQueues be exposed when the gateway is read-only but the database is a primary? (It is a read, so yes.)








checkQuota (internal/store/namespace.go:412) keeps an in-process gauge refreshed at most once per second from pg_total_relation_size. Each pod has its own gauge, and only the maintenance leader calls refreshQuotas. With multiple pods, a namespace can overshoot its quota by roughly one second of writes per pod, plus concurrent writers.













Approach
Behavior
Cost / risk




A
Document best-effort
Keep current; call it a soft limit
No work; quotas are not a billing boundary.


B
Shared counter
namespace_usage(kind,name,used,quota) with UPDATE ... WHERE used + $delta <= quota; rollback on failure
Near-hard across pods; one hot row per namespace; must reconcile with actual relation size.


C
Advisory lock + recalc
Lock the namespace, compute pg_total_relation_size, then write
Exact; serializes writes per namespace and adds a size query.


D
PostgreSQL disk guard
Reject writes when free space is below a threshold, independent of quota
Protects the database, not tenant fairness; useful as a complement.






A for now, B if quotas become a contract. Add D as an operational safety net regardless (e.g. --min-free-bytes checked on write admission).




Is quota a hard tenant boundary or just a guardrail?
Should refreshQuotas run on every gateway instead of only the leader?








The repository has ~12k lines of Go and 22 unit tests; internal/s3/server.go (~1k lines), the cache tier, and the SQS receive/redrive path have little unit coverage. text:

Each section states the problem, what the relevant AWS/objstore behavior is, several implementation options with trade-offs, and a recommendation. Pick one option per section (or defer) before code changes begin.
Priority is about risk to data or availability, not effort:



Priority
Meaning




P0
remote crash / unbounded work / silent data-visible divergence


P1
protocol lie that a normal client can rely on


P2
scalability or operator ergonomics

title: Hardening and compatibility options
text:
internal/s3/chunked.go trusts the declared chunk size:
data := make([]byte, size)   // line 86
size is parsed from an attacker-supplied hex line. A PUT with x-amz-content-sha256: STREAMING-... and a line such as ffffffffff asks Go to allocate ~1 TiB. A failed large allocation is a fatal runtime OOM, not a recoverable panic, so one small request can kill the gateway. Separately, a body made of blank lines recurses once per line (return c.Read(p), line 58) and grows the goroutine stack without bound.
There is also no total-size or chunk-count limit, and no consistency check against x-amz-decoded-content-length.




The wire format is <hex-size>[;chunk-signature=<sig>]\r\n<data>\r\n, terminated by a zero-size chunk and optional trailers (AWS chunked upload, trailers).
AWS requires chunks of at least 8 KiB (except the last) and recommends at least 64 KiB. The official Rust SDK defaults to 64 KiB (aws-runtime).
Other gateways cap the declared size: Supabase’s SigV4 stream parser defaults maxChunkSize to 8 MB and maxHeaderLength to 128 bytes (source).
The values pgvs3 must accept are STREAMING-UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD-TRAILER, STREAMING-AWS4-HMAC-SHA256-PAYLOAD[-TRAILER], and STREAMING-AWS4-ECDSA-P256-SHA256-PAYLOAD[-TRAILER] (AWS auth overview).














Approach
Behavior
Cost / risk




A
Strict AWS-shaped limits
Header line ≤ 128 B; chunk size ≤ 8 MiB; reject unknown STREAMING-* values; enforce x-amz-decoded-content-length when present; iterative parser
Safest. A client using > 8 MiB chunks fails (rare; SDKs use 64 KiB).


B
Compatibility-first
Cap at 64 MiB, allow any STREAMING-*, no decoded-length check, iterative parser
Preserves unusual clients; a single 64 MiB allocation per connection is still a memory-amplification vector.


C
Configurable
--max-chunk-size (default 8 MiB), --max-upload-bytes (default 0 = unlimited), strict parsing otherwise
Flexible; two more knobs and a way to misconfigure production.


D
Stream without buffering
Keep a rolling buffer, never allocate the declared size
Removes the allocation bug entirely, but the decoder must handle a chunk spanning many Read calls and is more code.






A + D. Parse iteratively with a fixed 128-byte header buffer and a bounded chunk buffer; never allocate from the declared size. Enforce the decoded length when the header is present. Reject unknown streaming algorithms with 400 InvalidRequest instead of attempting to parse them.
Add --max-upload-bytes as a separate, optional disk-protection control (not a substitute for the chunk cap).




Is any known client (rclone, restic, DuckDB, SlateDB) using chunks above 8 MiB? If yes, use 64 MiB.
Should a missing x-amz-decoded-content-length be rejected for signed streaming (AWS requires it) but allowed for unsigned trailer streaming?

title: Hardening and compatibility options
text:
Tier.List (internal/objcache/objcache.go:535) recursively walks the entire origin prefix, sorts everything, then truncates to limit. listObjectsV2 calls it once per page, so listing a bucket is O(N²). For each key not fresh in the PostgreSQL cache it then calls origin.Attributes, i.e. one origin HEAD per key — up to 1,000 HEADs for a single page.




S3 ListObjectsV2 is already paginated: up to 1,000 keys per request, with ContinuationToken / NextContinuationToken, KeyCount, MaxKeys, and StartAfter (AWS API).
thanos objstore exposes IterWithAttributes and WithUpdatedAt, and the S3 provider supports both, but IterObjectAttributes only carries Name and LastModified; it does not expose Size or ETag (objstore.go, s3 provider). So IterWithAttributes removes the mtime HEAD but not the size/ETag HEAD.
minio-go/v7 is already an indirect dependency (go.mod:48), so a native S3 lister does not add a new module.














Approach
Behavior
Cost / risk




A
IterWithAttributes only
Avoid HEAD for LastModified; still one HEAD per key for size/ETag
Small change, does not fix the actual cost. Not sufficient alone.


B
PostgreSQL listing index
s3c_<ns>.listing(prefix, key, size, etag, mtime, updated_at); list with LIMIT; fill on read/write; TTL refresh
O(page) when warm, O(N) on cold start; new table + DDL + invalidation semantics; stale within TTL.


C
Provider-aware lister
New Lister interface: S3 uses minio-go ListObjectsV2; filesystem uses WalkDir + Stat; inmem uses its map
O(page) always, exact metadata, no HEADs; provider-specific code and config duplication; bypasses objstore for list only.


D
Bound the origin listing
Require a prefix or cap at N keys, return 501/InvalidArgument beyond
Simple and honest; breaks large-bucket listing.


E
Hybrid
C for s3; current Iter for filesystem/inmem (local stat is cheap)
Best practical behavior; two listing paths to test.






E. Keep objstore for GET/PUT/DELETE, add a narrow Lister for S3 origins, and keep the current path for local providers with a hard key cap and context timeout. If a native lister is too much, B is the fallback, but it only helps after the first listing and adds cache-invalidation work.
Implemented: B, with the internal adapter’s Iter returning page metadata directly. The index avoids per-key HEADs, refreshes are generation checked, and oversized refreshes return an explicit error instead of an unbounded walk.




Should the continuation token stay the raw last key (current) or become an opaque base64 {prefix, lastKey}? S3 says tokens are obfuscated; clients must treat them as opaque either way.
Does the cache tier need delimiter support from the origin, or is client-side roll-up after a bounded page acceptable?
Is listing an origin bucket a supported use case, or should it be documented as best-effort with a key cap?

title: Hardening and compatibility options
text:
The two write paths order their effects differently:

Tier.Upload writes the origin first, then PostgreSQL.
Multipart completion must assemble part rows into one object. Publishing the cache first exposes bytes the origin does not have; uploading first holds a PostgreSQL transaction and connection open across the origin network call.

The implemented design uses a pending sentinel (origin_etag = 'pending:<upload-id>') plus an s3p.pending_uploads outbox row, published in the same transaction. Readers treat the sentinel as a miss, so pending bytes are never served. CompleteMultipartUpload then spools the pending object, releases the PostgreSQL connection, uploads it to the origin, and atomically swaps the sentinel for the origin version while deleting the outbox row. If the first flush fails, the request returns an error but the outbox row remains for a background worker to retry with bounded exponential backoff. Database leases serialize normal retries across gateways; the origin version captured at completion is passed as an If-Match (or If-None-Match: *) precondition so a stale flush cannot overwrite a newer PUT, DELETE, or multipart completion even after its lease expires.
Tier.Copy goes through Upload, so it inherits the origin-first order. DeleteMany uses per-key results (section 4) and evicts each cache key and outbox row immediately after its origin delete succeeds.













Approach
Behavior
Cost / risk




A
Origin-first everywhere
PUT stays as-is; multipart completion streams the assembled object from PostgreSQL to the origin, then publishes the cache
Origin is authoritative; no phantom; one extra PostgreSQL read per completed multipart; client waits for the origin upload either way.


B
Pending state column
Add state (pending/committed) to cache objects; readers treat pending as a miss; mark committed after the origin upload
No double read; crash leaves pending rows for GC; schema + read-path changes.


C
Sentinel + outbox
Publish with origin_etag = 'pending:<uuid>' plus an s3p.pending_uploads row; readers miss on the sentinel; replace with the real version after the origin upload; retry failures in the background
No per-object schema change; small read-path checks; one additive table; crash recovery and retries.


D
Keep current + delete on failure
Smallest change; the phantom window and partial-batch behavior remain
Does not meet the “explicit rejection over silent approximation” principle.






C + outbox (implemented). A successful CompleteMultipartUpload still waits for the first origin upload, but the PostgreSQL transaction and connection are released before the network call; crash recovery and retries are durable in s3p.pending_uploads. Make cache population best-effort on PUT: if the origin succeeds and the cache write fails, return success and log; the next read is a miss.
DeleteMany uses per-key results (section 4) and evicts each cache key and outbox row immediately after its origin delete succeeds.




Is the cache tier expected to survive an origin outage for reads (current TTL behavior), or is the origin always authoritative?
Should a failed cache write fail the client request when the origin succeeded? (Recommendation: no, except for read-after-write within the TTL.)

title: Hardening and compatibility options
text:
deleteObjects (internal/s3/server.go:580) returns one 500 if any delete fails, and otherwise marks every key deleted. S3 returns 200 OK with a <Deleted> or <Error> element per key, and Quiet mode returns only errors. For an origin bucket, a mid-batch failure can leave earlier keys deleted while the client sees a single failure.




AWS DeleteObjects returns per-key Deleted/Error entries in a 200 response; Quiet suppresses successful entries (AWS API).
General-purpose buckets require Content-MD5 for multi-object delete; directory buckets also accept a checksum header.














Approach
Behavior
Cost / risk




A
Per-key results
PG: one transaction, but report each key; origin: sequential deletes, collect per-key errors; always 200 unless the request itself is invalid
Matches S3; PG batch remains atomic even if individual keys “fail” only for not-found (which is success).


B
All-or-nothing
Current behavior; 500 on any failure
Not S3-compatible; cannot be made atomic for origin deletes.


C
Hybrid with savepoints
PG: savepoint per key, so a key-level failure does not roll back the batch; origin: per-key
Closest to S3; more SQL and more round trips.






A with C only if PG key-level failures can actually occur (they currently cannot for a normal delete; missing keys are success). Add the <Error> XML type and honor Quiet. Decide separately whether to require Content-MD5 (strict AWS behavior) or keep it optional for client compatibility.




Should a malformed key in a 1,000-key batch fail the whole request or produce one <Error> entry? AWS fails the request for malformed XML/keys.
Do we need VersionId fields in the response for wire compatibility even though versioning is out of scope? (Probably omit; clients tolerate absence.)

title: Hardening and compatibility options
text:
etagFor(version) returns md5("<size>-<mtime-ns>"), and Head derives Content-Type from the file extension (objcache.go:624). Origin ETags and stored content types are not authoritative. Conditional requests and client caches therefore cannot use the origin’s version identity.




S3 ListObjectsV2 returns ETag, Size, LastModified, and StorageClass; HeadObject returns Content-Type (ListObjectsV2).
objstore’s ObjectAttributes exposes Size, LastModified, and Version (ETag/generation), but not ContentType (objstore.go). Content-Type requires a provider-specific StatObject/Stat.














Approach
Behavior
Cost / risk




A
Keep synthetic
Cache ETags are cache-local; document it
No work; clients cannot correlate with origin.


B
Return origin ETag
Use the origin’s ETag for origin objects and store it in origin_etag; cache-filled objects keep the content MD5 or adopt the origin ETag
Better compatibility; one-time client cache invalidation; needs provider metadata.


C
Dual headers
ETag = origin ETag, X-Pgvs3-Content-MD5 = local content hash
Preserves both identities; non-standard header.


D
Extend objstore upstream
Add ContentType/ETag to ObjectAttributes and implement in providers
Best long-term; dependency/PR cycle.






B for ETag, plus a provider-specific stat for Content-Type on S3 origins; C if local content MD5 must remain observable. D is the clean upstream fix if the project is willing to carry a fork/PR.




Is an ETag change acceptable in the current alpha, or should it be gated behind a flag for one release?
Should write-through uploads return the origin ETag or the pgvs3 content MD5? (Origin ETag is more useful for read-after-write.)

title: Hardening and compatibility options
text:
CreateQueue accepts FifoQueue=true and .fifo names, and SendMessage accepts MessageGroupId / MessageDeduplicationId, but SendMessages ignores GroupID/DedupID. A client that asks for FIFO gets a standard queue with no ordering or deduplication guarantee. That is a silent correctness downgrade.




FIFO queue names must end in .fifo; MessageGroupId is required; deduplication uses MessageDeduplicationId or content hashing over a 5-minute interval; messages in a group are delivered in order; per-message DelaySeconds is not supported (AWS FIFO identifiers, CreateQueue, SendMessage).
Throughput is 300 API calls/s per method without batching, up to 3,000 messages/s with batches; high-throughput mode raises this further (queue types).














Approach
Behavior
Cost / risk




A
Reject FIFO
.fifo names or FifoQueue=true → 400 InvalidParameterValue; MessageGroupId on standard queues is accepted (AWS fair queues)
Honest; small change; no FIFO users.


B
Full FIFO
Dedup table with a 5-minute window, per-group sequence/order, SequenceNumber, visibility, batch dedup; no high-throughput mode initially
Correct; new schema, ordering query, more tests.


C
Minimal FIFO
Dedup + per-group ordering, reject unsupported attributes (ContentBasedDeduplication optional), no sequence numbers
Smaller than B; still a schema and receive-path change.


D
Status quo
Accept and treat as standard
Dangerous; violates the explicit-rejection principle.






A now. Add FIFO only if a real consumer needs it; then B, not C, because partial FIFO is another silent approximation. Regardless of choice, validate FifoQueue and .fifo consistency at CreateQueue.
Implemented: B (full FIFO without high-throughput mode).




Is any target workload (DuckLake, SlateDB, restic) using FIFO queues?
Should MessageGroupId on a standard queue be stored and returned as an attribute for fair-queue compatibility, or ignored?

title: Hardening and compatibility options
text:
x-amz-server-side-encryption: AES256 and aws:kms are accepted (now in internal/s3/request.go) but no encryption is performed.
Object Lock, ACL, and tagging headers are ignored; x-amz-tagging is not persisted.
x-amz-storage-class is ignored and listings always report STANDARD.

A client that sets Object Lock or SSE-KMS reasonably believes a guarantee exists. Object Lock is the dangerous one: it is a WORM/retention promise.




S3 stores the SSE algorithm and returns it on PUT/GET/HEAD; since January 5, 2023, new objects are encrypted by default with SSE-S3 (AWS SSE-S3).
Object Lock provides retention/legal hold and requires versioning; ACLs and tagging are separate authorization/metadata features. All are documented as out of scope for pgvs3.














Approach
Behavior
Cost / risk




A
Strict reject
Any SSE header → 501 NotImplemented; Object Lock → 501; ACL other than private → 501; tagging → 501; storage class other than STANDARD → 501
Honest; may break clients that send defaults.


B
Compatibility tier
Accept AES256 and x-amz-acl: private as documented no-ops (at-rest encryption delegated to PostgreSQL); reject aws:kms, public ACLs, Object Lock, tagging, non-STANDARD classes
Keeps common clients working; still no encryption guarantee for AES256.


C
Store and echo
Persist SSE/ACL/tagging metadata and echo it, without enforcement
Better wire fidelity; misleading for Object Lock and security-sensitive headers.


D
Full support
Implement encryption (pgcrypto/KMS), Object Lock enforcement, ACL model
Large; ACL/authorization contradicts the trust model.






B for SSE/ACL, with an explicit log line and docs stating that AES256 is satisfied only if the PostgreSQL volume is encrypted. A for Object Lock, tagging, and non-STANDARD storage classes. Never accept aws:kms as a no-op. If the project wants zero ambiguity, choose A across the board.




Do rclone/restic/boto3 send x-amz-acl: private or AES256 by default in the supported test matrix? (If yes, A breaks them.)
Is x-amz-tagging used by any target workload? If not, reject it.

title: Hardening and compatibility options
text:
--read-only rejects every SQS request (internal/sqs/sqs.go:97), including ListQueues, GetQueueUrl, and GetQueueAttributes. The docs say read-only gateways serve local-AZ reads; queue consumers cannot even inspect queues.
ReceiveMessage is genuinely a write: it sets visible_at, increments receive_count, and stores a receipt. On a PostgreSQL hot standby, SELECT ... FOR UPDATE is rejected anyway, so a read-only SQS consumer cannot work without changing semantics.













Approach
Behavior
Cost / risk




A
Keep blanket 403
Current behavior; document that SQS is primary-only
Simple; metadata inspection unavailable.


B
Allow metadata-only ops
ListQueues, GetQueueUrl, GetQueueAttributes work; Send/Receive/Delete/Purge return 403
Useful introspection; per-op read-only checks; works on standbys.


C
Peek mode
ReceiveMessage returns messages without leasing
Not SQS semantics; two consumers could process the same message; not recommended.






B, with a clear 403 AccessDenied message for ReceiveMessage explaining that leasing requires a writable primary. Document that SQS consumers need a primary gateway.




Does GetQueueAttributes need ApproximateNumberOfMessages on a standby (a SELECT over messages), or are static attributes enough?
Should ListQueues be exposed when the gateway is read-only but the database is a primary? (It is a read, so yes.)

title: Hardening and compatibility options
text:
checkQuota (internal/store/namespace.go:412) keeps an in-process gauge refreshed at most once per second from pg_total_relation_size. Each pod has its own gauge, and only the maintenance leader calls refreshQuotas. With multiple pods, a namespace can overshoot its quota by roughly one second of writes per pod, plus concurrent writers.













Approach
Behavior
Cost / risk




A
Document best-effort
Keep current; call it a soft limit
No work; quotas are not a billing boundary.


B
Shared counter
namespace_usage(kind,name,used,quota) with UPDATE ... WHERE used + $delta <= quota; rollback on failure
Near-hard across pods; one hot row per namespace; must reconcile with actual relation size.


C
Advisory lock + recalc
Lock the namespace, compute pg_total_relation_size, then write
Exact; serializes writes per namespace and adds a size query.


D
PostgreSQL disk guard
Reject writes when free space is below a threshold, independent of quota
Protects the database, not tenant fairness; useful as a complement.






A for now, B if quotas become a contract. Add D as an operational safety net regardless (e.g. --min-free-bytes checked on write admission).




Is quota a hard tenant boundary or just a guardrail?
Should refreshQuotas run on every gateway instead of only the leader?

title: Why Each Bucket’s chunks Table Is Unpartitioned
text:
Every chunk read in pgvs3 is a range scan on one file:
WHERE file_id = $1 AND no BETWEEN $2 AND $3
To keep point reads to a single partition (so PostgreSQL’s planner can prune everything else), the partition key must start with file_id:

no or hash(no): spreads a file’s chunks across partitions, but forces every point read to scan all partitions.
hash(file_id, no): breaks file_id partition pruning, so reads again hit every partition.
bucket: requires denormalizing bucket onto every chunk row and puts an entire lake into one partition anyway.

The only partitioning scheme that both prunes point reads and spreads large files is a two-level HASH(file_id) → RANGE(no) layout:
PARTITION BY HASH (file_id)   -- 8 hash partitions
  PARTITION BY RANGE (no)     -- 8 ranges of 1,024 rows (~8 MiB each)
Measured on the 6-vCPU benchmark host against a single unpartitioned table:



Workload
1 table (default)
16 hash
64 hash
8×8 hash/range




4 KiB GET, 1 worker
1,104/s
888/s
945/s
868/s


4 KiB GET, 16 workers
3,852/s
2,784/s
3,227/s
2,628/s


4 KiB PUT, 16 workers
1,051/s
908/s
981/s
941/s


64 MiB GET, 1 worker
441 MiB/s
—
—
556 MiB/s


64 MiB GET, 16 workers
985 MiB/s
—
—
1,002 MiB/s





Partitioning adds planner and catalog overhead on every query, hurting small reads by 15–32% and writes by ~10%, while DuckLake’s single-writer model has no insert contention to spread across tables.
Each bucket’s chunks table therefore remains a single unpartitioned relation (up to PostgreSQL’s 32 TiB single-relation limit), while ≤64 KiB objects live inline in that schema’s objects table and large reads scale via 8 MiB parallel snapshot queries.

title: SlateDB ObjFS on pgvs3
text:
duckdb_object_storage is an optional native DuckDB filesystem backed by SlateDB/OpenDAL. It uses pgvs3’s existing S3 interface; it does not replace the gateway’s logged PostgreSQL layout, shared caching or other clients. Physical objects are SlateDB WAL/SST/manifest data, not interoperable Parquet files. See the measured results and accepted optimization before choosing a configuration.


just object-storage-setup
just object-storage --object-storage-mib 10,100 --passes 3
just object-storage --object-storage-mib 1024 --passes 3
just bench object-storage ... is equivalent. The default includes all three sizes; use a smaller functional smoke when changing tooling:
just object-storage --object-storage-mib 1 --passes 1 \
  --object-storage-ddl-iterations 1 --object-storage-small-commits 2
Provisioning pins ObjFS 0.2.0 / DuckDB 2.0.0, upstream commit 56d9c7b928836cfaffa6790c77b7640d50102fe3. The qualified Linux amd64 community binary SHA-256 is dfd7040b4a0204aaa9aff142932ae7b5d2ec78634541d2c9f6e3bc0f329b4e12. DuckDB’s installer handles the community signing key; the benchmark verifies the binary before loading it from its private .tmp/deps/duckdb-object-storage/ installation directory. It does not change global DuckDB configuration or enable unsigned extensions for normal community-artifact runs.
The community endpoint is mutable, and its version-qualified 0.2.0 URL was not available during this evaluation. Keep a verified cache. A changed binary fails the pin rather than silently becoming the new baseline.
