It reuses the same deterministic Parquet generation, row-hash validation, S3 counters and PostgreSQL capacity observations as the Differential comparison, rather than another load engine.

Identical approximately 10/100/1,024 MiB inputs, actual sizes and hashes; three repetitions with rotated profile order. DuckLake data inlining is disabled.
Empty/loaded-table DDL, bulk loading, 32-row commits, a 1% string update, half deletion and a full data-table drop. Each completed mutation’s statement latency is the remote-sync acknowledgement, not a locally buffered return.
Fresh processes through gateway B, without the writer’s buffers or local authoritative files; full and selective scans each get a separate reader. External file and Parquet metadata caches are off, while native DuckDB buffers and explicitly budgeted SlateDB caches remain visible in same-client repeats.
Attachment, schema discovery, first query and repeated query are separate. Their fresh-read sum excludes process/extension setup, which is also recorded.
OpenDAL/cache statistics plus actual gateway request/response-byte deltas. DuckDB’s httpfs log alone misses OpenDAL traffic. Successful timing samples reject retried 5xx responses instead of crediting backoff as an engine difference.
Object bytes, allocated PostgreSQL bucket/catalog relations, WAL positions, client files and process RSS. These are point inventories, not a hard total memory/scratch admission budget or a cloud cost model.

All input/key/string/hash aggregates, schema defaults, updates/deletes and post-cleanup sentinel reads must match. Reports retain per-path medians/budget results; a gain in one query cannot hide a regression in another.



SlateDB can retain recently committed data in its object WAL/memtables. Opening a new reader may replay substantial WAL data during ATTACH, even when a query alone looks cheap. Small probes can show zero SST-cache hits because they never exercise SSTs, not because cache settings were ineffective.
For each profile the benchmark measures both:

Fresh readers while the writer remains open.
A clean writer close, then new readers over the same data.

Closing the filesystem flushes its remaining state and can greatly reduce fresh reader bootstrap. The closing cost is measured, and a break-even reader count is reported when it saves time. All profiles, including DuckLake, go through the same close/read/reopen workflow. The old writer is closed before the new writer starts; this is not concurrent writing or a relaxed durability mode.
This is useful for explicitly quiescent/read-mostly delivery. It is not a transparent optimization for a continuously active writer. Long-lived readers can also reuse buffers/caches, but those private caches are not pgvs3 shared hits.



The extension routes the native database and recovery WAL files through SlateDB. The contract/probe terminates the writer with os._exit, without an explicit checkpoint/detach/shutdown, then verifies it using a different process/gateway and resumes writing. That is process-death evidence, not power-loss or arbitrary partition qualification.
SQL read-only does not mean read-only object access. The pinned extension opens SlateDB readers in managed-checkpoint mode, which writes a retention checkpoint to the object store. A SQL READ_ONLY attachment issued a PUT in the probe. Through pgvs3’s read-only gateway that PUT is correctly rejected; the client then failed to complete within the bounded negative-probe deadline. Neither the gateway’s role restriction nor PostgreSQL standby safety is weakened to accommodate it. Route these SQL read-only clients to a writable object endpoint; this evaluation does not establish ObjFS on physical read-only replicas.
Existing readonly clients may follow the writer manifest on roughly a 10-second poll interval, and detach/reattach can reuse the cached reader. Fresh-process readers and same-process readers are therefore different consistency cases. The benchmark does not claim instant refresh or certify follower behavior.
Use one externally coordinated writer. Upstream documents manifest-epoch takeover as a delayed fencing backstop, not a fail-fast file lock. Concurrent writers, automatic failover coordination and arbitrary network partitions are outside this evaluation; do not infer them from a successful single-writer probe.



Native CHECKPOINT is not a request to compact/expire all SlateDB objects. ObjFS 0.2.0 exposes cache/I/O statistics but no SQL override for SlateDB compaction or object-retention policy. The benchmark records checkpoint, a bounded background observation, writer close, pgvs3 reaping and ordinary PostgreSQL vacuum separately. It does not delete SSTs/WAL/manifests manually or shorten their retention by editing stored metadata. Objects retained by normal backend policy remain a cost.
Ordinary PostgreSQL vacuum may make dead pages reusable without shrinking relation files. Deleting the disposable namespace happens only after measurements and is not credited as table-level reclamation. Local/kernel/server cache state, encoded file layout and extra memory all affect results; no default storage/client choice changes merely because one native query is fast.
Raw jobs, results, profiles and failed probes remain in the unique printed .tmp/verify/bench.*/ directory. --out must be fresh. Standard-library tooling tests run in CI; the large opt-in matrix is not a replacement for the existing gateway performance acceptance or required client contract.

title: Modernization implementation and performance comparison
text:
This is completed implementation/evidence history across v24/v25, not the active backlog. See design.md for the current contracts and roadmap.md for ranked next work.
Date: 2026-10-28. Control: a879472 (layout v23). Candidate: layout v24.
This implements the highest-value bounded changes from the capability review, retaining PostgreSQL 18+, logged shared state, the one-port trusted-network model, and specialized object streaming. Fresh databases are required; there is no layout migration.



Shared parent metadata for range-only caching. Logged, schema-local records cache size, origin validator and headers, but never represent a body. Validation uses the database clock and excludes time spent waiting for HEAD. TTL/retention, mutation fences, flush/drop and read-only consumption are covered.
One-round-trip cache shadow resolution. Write-back ownership/tombstones take precedence over shared read cache in one PostgreSQL query. Missing or partially initialized cache namespaces retain independent-lookup fallback.
Renewable, publication-fenced fill ownership. Owner-token renewal uses the database clock. Publication locks/checks live ownership and the origin version; an expired, cancelled or superseded owner cannot publish. Waiters do not cancel the owner and have explicit, fetch-budget-aware fallback limits.
Shared disk spool byte admission. Fills, foreground writes and pending uploads share a configurable 8 GiB payload budget. Unknown-length growth is nonblocking to avoid partial-reservation deadlock. Cleanup is idempotent; known-size copies retain file-copy fast paths. Exhaustion is retryable before acknowledgment; acknowledged pending bodies remain logged in PostgreSQL.
Outbox wake hints. Successful durable publication wakes a local worker instead of always waiting for the idle poll. The buffered hint is lossy and carries no job authority; database claims and one-second cross-gateway/crash fallback polling remain unchanged.
PostgreSQL 18 publication SQL. Inline and chunked entry points share one mutation. RETURNING old.file_id, old.parts supplies garbage ownership without an unconditional pre-read. TTL, CAS, multipart metadata cleanup, origin fences and body/outbox atomicity remain transactional.
Cache retirement safety. External origin changes retire only the observed write-cache generation. Old fill ownership and read-cache fences are removed atomically, preventing stale-fill resurrection without hiding the new origin. Newer publications and authoritative delete tombstones remain protected.
Compatibility and diagnostics. Missing keys are distinct from missing buckets, restoring static-index fallback. Namespace stats have the correct result shape. Partial payloads do not advertise whole-object checksums. Warm range hits are reported accurately. Helm scratch resources and spool metrics are aligned, and durability/pooling/quota documentation is qualified.

Preserved: unconditional multipart write-back, including small multipart bodies. The end-to-end test now waits for asynchronous origin persistence rather than incorrectly requiring the origin file to exist before acknowledgment. Session key locks remain around remote writes; a local token check alone cannot stop a stale remote upload.

The isolated experiment used a loopback HTTP origin with no storage backend, checksum validation or signature verification. Clients still signed requests; implicit retries, payload hashing and additional checksum work were disabled where appropriate to match the existing client. MinIO used its low-level Core single-PUT API rather than silently switching to multipart at smaller sizes. Five repetitions used 250 ms benchmark windows; table values are medians.

Same PostgreSQL 18 instance for both disposable databases, 1 GiB shared_buffers, synchronous_commit=on, and worker AIO. No UNLOGGED storage.
Separate control/candidate processes and databases; identical client and fixture bytes. Request order alternates before/after across five repetitions.
Actual Snappy Parquet fixtures generated with DuckDB 2.0, with 122,880-row groups: 10,490,851; 67,128,878; 268,489,564; and 1,073,940,706 bytes. The largest is approximately 1 GiB, 0.019% above that exact byte boundary.
HEAD, GET, footer ranges and PUT at concurrency 1 and 4. S3 signing is omitted in the gateway load generator because signatures are intentionally ignored; both binaries use that same client. Transport experiments above still sign.
Relevant per-case gates: candidate median p50 time <= 1.20 × control and median throughput >= 0.80 × control. Percentiles from small fixed large-object batches are diagnostics, not a production p99/SLO claim.



The first cumulative-overwrite run is retained in .tmp/modernization/native.json and native.log. It was not accepted:

10 MiB GET measured 6.372 → 10.289 ms at concurrency 1 and 8.365 → 11.321 ms at concurrency 4, over budget.
Concurrent 1 GiB candidate PUTs eventually hit the client’s 60-second timeout.
PostgreSQL logged frequent checkpoints, heavy checkpoint sync, vacuum and approximately 39 GiB chunk relations in each database. The workload accumulated overwritten files while the default 1 GiB WAL budget introduced checkpoint phase differences; planner statistics also differed between the databases.
A subsequent GET check on the unchanged binaries measured 10.963 → 9.762 ms, demonstrating that the original read difference was not stable. The initial query plans were not captured, so this is not a definitive single-cause diagnosis.

The controlled rerun explicitly analyzes read fixtures, uses fresh buckets for each PUT batch, matches checkpoints outside timed work, and uses a 16 GiB WAL budget / 30-minute checkpoint timeout on the benchmark instance only. This does not change production durability or silently tune a user’s database.



The controlled matrix completed all 400 runs without request errors or timeouts. Thirty-nine of forty short-run cases passed directly. deploy/bench/compare.py drives that existing load generator; it is not a new load engine or conformance framework. It requires disposable endpoints/databases. --postgres-before / --postgres-after enable explicit ANALYZE/checkpoint preparation, and --isolate-writes creates/drops a fresh bucket per PUT run.
The measured run records and client benchmark output are also retained in benchmarks/modernization-2026-10.json, without database credentials. It includes the rejected short-run gate and its explicit steady-state replacement, not just favorable aggregate numbers.

  --before http://127.0.0.1:19114 --after http://127.0.0.1:19124 \

just ci matches the GitHub gate set. Docker-backed suites share setup helpers, use isolated binaries/logs and keep explicit PostgreSQL port mappings stable across restart. title: Modernization implementation and performance comparison
text:
Shared parent metadata for range-only caching. Logged, schema-local records cache size, origin validator and headers, but never represent a body. Validation uses the database clock and excludes time spent waiting for HEAD. TTL/retention, mutation fences, flush/drop and read-only consumption are covered.
One-round-trip cache shadow resolution. Write-back ownership/tombstones take precedence over shared read cache in one PostgreSQL query. Missing or partially initialized cache namespaces retain independent-lookup fallback.
Renewable, publication-fenced fill ownership. Owner-token renewal uses the database clock. Publication locks/checks live ownership and the origin version; an expired, cancelled or superseded owner cannot publish. Waiters do not cancel the owner and have explicit, fetch-budget-aware fallback limits.
Shared disk spool byte admission. Fills, foreground writes and pending uploads share a configurable 8 GiB payload budget. Unknown-length growth is nonblocking to avoid partial-reservation deadlock. Cleanup is idempotent; known-size copies retain file-copy fast paths. Exhaustion is retryable before acknowledgment; acknowledged pending bodies remain logged in PostgreSQL.
Outbox wake hints. Successful durable publication wakes a local worker instead of always waiting for the idle poll. The buffered hint is lossy and carries no job authority; database claims and one-second cross-gateway/crash fallback polling remain unchanged.
PostgreSQL 18 publication SQL. Inline and chunked entry points share one mutation. RETURNING old.file_id, old.parts supplies garbage ownership without an unconditional pre-read. TTL, CAS, multipart metadata cleanup, origin fences and body/outbox atomicity remain transactional.
Cache retirement safety. External origin changes retire only the observed write-cache generation. Old fill ownership and read-cache fences are removed atomically, preventing stale-fill resurrection without hiding the new origin. Newer publications and authoritative delete tombstones remain protected.
Compatibility and diagnostics. Missing keys are distinct from missing buckets, restoring static-index fallback. Namespace stats have the correct result shape. Partial payloads do not advertise whole-object checksums. Warm range hits are reported accurately. Helm scratch resources and spool metrics are aligned, and durability/pooling/quota documentation is qualified.

Preserved: unconditional multipart write-back, including small multipart bodies. The end-to-end test now waits for asynchronous origin persistence rather than incorrectly requiring the origin file to exist before acknowledgment. Session key locks remain around remote writes; a local token check alone cannot stop a stale remote upload.

Same host: AMD Ryzen 7 7700X, Linux/amd64, Go 1.27.3.
Same PostgreSQL 18 instance for both disposable databases, 1 GiB shared_buffers, synchronous_commit=on, and worker AIO. No UNLOGGED storage.
Separate control/candidate processes and databases; identical client and fixture bytes. Request order alternates before/after across five repetitions.
Actual Snappy Parquet fixtures generated with DuckDB 2.0, with 122,880-row groups: 10,490,851; 67,128,878; 268,489,564; and 1,073,940,706 bytes. The largest is approximately 1 GiB, 0.019% above that exact byte boundary.
HEAD, GET, footer ranges and PUT at concurrency 1 and 4. S3 signing is omitted in the gateway load generator because signatures are intentionally ignored; both binaries use that same client. Transport experiments above still sign.
Relevant per-case gates: candidate median p50 time <= 1.20 × control and median throughput >= 0.80 × control. Percentiles from small fixed large-object batches are diagnostics, not a production p99/SLO claim.



The first cumulative-overwrite run is retained in .tmp/modernization/native.json and native.log. It was not accepted:

10 MiB GET measured 6.372 → 10.289 ms at concurrency 1 and 8.365 → 11.321 ms at concurrency 4, over budget.
Concurrent 1 GiB candidate PUTs eventually hit the client’s 60-second timeout.
PostgreSQL logged frequent checkpoints, heavy checkpoint sync, vacuum and approximately 39 GiB chunk relations in each database. The workload accumulated overwritten files while the default 1 GiB WAL budget introduced checkpoint phase differences; planner statistics also differed between the databases.
A subsequent GET check on the unchanged binaries measured 10.963 → 9.762 ms, demonstrating that the original read difference was not stable. The initial query plans were not captured, so this is not a definitive single-cause diagnosis.

The controlled rerun explicitly analyzes read fixtures, uses fresh buckets for each PUT batch, matches checkpoints outside timed work, and uses a 16 GiB WAL budget / 30-minute checkpoint timeout on the benchmark instance only. This does not change production durability or silently tune a user’s database.



The controlled matrix completed all 400 runs without request errors or timeouts. Thirty-nine of forty short-run cases passed directly. Concurrent 10 MiB GET still showed +26.2% p50 in its seven-request batches, so it was not waived: five paired 1,000-request steady-state runs per binary followed. Median p50 was 11.304 → 11.240 ms (-0.6%), median throughput 326.416 → 328.873 requests/s (+0.8%), with zero errors. Both databases used matching bitmap heap/index scan plans. title: Modernization implementation and performance comparison
text: The full vulnerability check found pre-existing GO-2026-6617 in golang.org/x/net v0.59.0. Production now uses the fixed v0.60.0; no AWS or MinIO dependency was added to the gateway module. A same-database follow-up compared the pre-patch candidate with the final binary: 4 KiB HEAD 0.106 → 0.109 ms, concurrent ~10 MiB GET 10.567 → 10.791 ms, ~1 GiB GET 939.534 → 946.253 ms, and concurrent ~1 GiB footer ranges 0.284 → 0.287 ms. All were within 3%, without errors. The primary matrix above predates only this HTTP/2 dependency security patch and local outbox wake hints (which do not run on native read paths); the representative final-binary check is recorded in .tmp/modernization/security-http-smoke.json.

title: Modernization implementation and performance comparison
text:
test/loadgen now supports fixed S3 request counts, unsigned comparisons, Parquet payload files and range offsets. It checks body-copy errors rather than counting a truncated response as success.
deploy/bench/compare.py drives that existing load generator; it is not a new load engine or conformance framework. It requires disposable endpoints/databases. --postgres-before / --postgres-after enable explicit ANALYZE/checkpoint preparation, and --isolate-writes creates/drops a fresh bucket per PUT run.
The measured run records and client benchmark output are also retained in benchmarks/modernization-2026-10.json, without database credentials. It includes the rejected short-run gate and its explicit steady-state replacement, not just favorable aggregate numbers.
Example, after building control/candidate binaries and the common load generator:
python3 deploy/bench/compare.py \
  --before http://127.0.0.1:19114 --after http://127.0.0.1:19124 \
  --loadgen .tmp/modernization/loadgen \
  --payload .tmp/modernization/parquet-10MiB.parquet \
  --payload .tmp/modernization/parquet-64MiB.parquet \
  --payload .tmp/modernization/parquet-256MiB.parquet \
  --payload .tmp/modernization/parquet-1024MiB.parquet \
  --postgres-before "$BENCH_BEFORE_URL" --postgres-after "$BENCH_AFTER_URL" \
  --isolate-writes --repeats 5 --out .tmp/modernization/native-isolated.json
Use --seed-endpoint with --ops range,head for a range-only origin-cache comparison. Seed directly at the origin, not through the proxy: a proxy PUT or full GET would warm the write-back/whole-body cache and invalidate that experiment.
Validation: unit/race tests, PostgreSQL integration with the race detector, the pinned 36-test s3t allow-list, codec/range fuzzing, Helm lint/render, hk check --all --profile ci including vulnerability checks, and the full Docker end-to-end contract including boto3, RESP, OJS, cache tier, DuckDB and DuckLake. New regression tests cover owner renewal/loss, stale inline/COPY publication, read-only range hits, metadata TTL/flush/logging, scratch cleanup/admission, same-ETag newer-write protection and external-origin refresh fencing.
Real AWS/Aurora performance, actual replica promotion and production tail latency remain unverified. Logged state and local commit durability are not a promise of lossless promotion of an asynchronous replica.

This pass also changes ownership and shared implementations:

One native and one origin S3 adapter implement read/write/multipart capabilities, with one backend-selection policy. In particular, origin part copies cannot accidentally take the native fast-copy path.

Six ordinary stream operations now use the store’s existing transaction lifecycle. Maintenance transactions that deliberately roll back no-op or missing-schema paths remain explicit.
Both pool policies share failed-open cleanup. Writable and read-only startup use the same layout validation.

The 13,230-line docs/benchmarks/modernization-2026-10.json file is benchmark evidence, not Go code. Commit-level insertion totals that include it are not a code-size measure. Relocation was separately checked for declaration identity after the intentional refactors. Four added regression tests cover backend selection, tier replacement/fallback, lock cleanup (including panicking validation) and transaction rollback. The origin HTTP integration test also exercises multipart part-copy routing through the unified adapter.



The final pass removes ordinary comments from first-party Go code. Only compiler directives (//go:build, //go:embed) and vendored license headers remain. Readability now comes from names, capability-sized interfaces and sectioned implementations.
Specific simplifications:

pgx.Batch now sends job rows and global index rows in one round trip instead of two statements per job.
RESP EXISTS groups cache keys into one query while preserving duplicate-key semantics and s3:// bucket reads.
Origin registry lookups use an atomic refresh clock and reader lock; tier construction and closure happen outside the reader lock.
Streamed bodies return their first pooled chunk correctly and share one next-chunk/error path between Read and WriteTo.
One HTTP-origin request builder applies configured headers and trace propagation consistently to reads, writes and deletes.
Namespace relation-size SQL and chunk-layout checks have one definition each.
CRC-64/NVME uses slicing-by-8 tables and is verified against a bitwise reference.
Standard library helpers replace local itoa, lower, manual hex/ETag validation, manual ISO-8601 assembly and one-off sorted-map loops.
The S3 client now lives in internal/s3client; the misleading nested module and replace chain are gone. Loadgen and the client share one SigV4 signer, and the plain-HTTP origin shares the same pooled transport policy.
S3 route handlers return errors; one mapper converts store/origin failures into S3 codes. 145 scattered writeError branches collapsed into that path.
Store *Ref suffixes are gone, upload/part/completion variants use one method with options, and withSchema centralises missing-schema reads.
S3, OJS and RESP metrics share internal/telemetry; parameter structs replace the longest positional call sites; time-driven tests use testing/synctest.

title: Guide validation
text:
Guide index · Research ledger
just guides is the disposable executable specification for the named snippets on these pages. It uses test/data_plane.py and deploy/bench/stack.sh, the same SQL/HTTP/origin fixtures as the existing analytical and recovery gates—not a new load engine or conformance framework. The required just contract runs it too.
Verification markers bind tests to the actual SQL, JSON, shell and Python shown in the guides. The report records document/snippet/tool hashes, actual versions, query plans, positive and negative outcomes. Missing/unexecuted markers fail the gate. Endpoint/port/demo database substitution and intentional failure injections are test fixture parameters, not alternative examples.









Area
Executable check




PostgreSQL
Million-row application fixture; same 20 results before/after index, chosen index/buffers captured; transaction-local budgets revert.


Mixed-load procedure
Custom pgbench canary and existing test/loadgen run against the same cluster; raw transaction logs/error counts retained. Two-second smoke only, no SLO or speedup claim.


Extraction
Actual PostgreSQL scanner → Parquet → pgvs3; another client verifies counts/sums/payload; conditional manifest rejects a repeated create.


DuckLake
Candidate configuration syntax; fixed-64 2D Hilbert (lake.hilbert64) and fixed-32 hash (bucket(32, customer_id)) partitioning + SORTED BY, wide-column skip_stats_columns + byte-bounded row groups, batch merge_adjacent_files + rewrite_data_files; catalog reopen through B; inline tiny insert produces no object until flush.


Freshness/cache
Direct source mutations do not change the old extract; direct origin mutation stays stale inside TTL, then revalidates; shared full/range hits cause no extra origin reads.


Staging
Block origin writes, ACK logged pending body, read on B, inspect pending SQL/metrics, unblock and compare origin bytes.


Jobs
Rollback leaves no intent/job; lost enqueue response reconciles; mismatched ID payload refuses success; redelivery after SQL effect suppresses duplicates and rejects old lease token.


Scheduling/retention
Due work/retry fetch without forcing maintenance; terminal pruning allows ID reuse, while an application receipt still suppresses the effect.


Streams
Oversized snapshot batch returns 413 without partial pagination; repeat receive returns the active batch; ACK advances it.


Operations
PostgreSQL 18 diagnostic queries, optional statement statistics, CLI/probes/metric names and guarded demo cleanup.






Base pgvs3 75802d0, layout v25; Linux amd64, PostgreSQL/pgbench 18.6, DuckDB 2.0.0. Actual loaded extension versions/hashes are in the report: DuckLake 417a9117f5 (catalog format 1.1), httpfs 77392a7207, PostgreSQL scanner c0f5a3c0c4. Normal signed/official extensions are used; no production Go, schema SQL or dependencies were changed.
$ just guides
guides: 35 bound snippets, 12 scenario checks passed
guides ok (35s); artifacts: .tmp/verify/guides.rVqHQl

$ just docs
Output created: _site/index.html

$ python3 test/documentation.py
{'documents': 24, 'local_links': 199, 'snippets': 35, 'svgs': 5}

$ mise exec python -- python -m unittest discover -s deploy/bench -p '*_test.py'
Ran 24 tests
OK








Observation
Verified result
Not established by it




OLTP access path
Identical 20 IDs; plan root buffer visits 12,436 → 23; candidate uses orders_customer_recent. SET LOCAL restores work_mem=4MB and max_parallel_workers_per_gather=2.
Universal index benefit or production p99. Buffers are plan observations, not a throughput ratio.


Extraction
1,000,000 rows, 23,217,273-byte Parquet; ID/cents/payload aggregates match on B. Source UPDATE/DELETE does not alter the old export. Repeated manifest create is 412.
CDC, cross-system transactions or a bounded age after an undetected failed refresh.


Same-cluster canary
Control and mixed logged SQL transactions, zero failed/skipped; concurrent object GETs, zero errors.
Performance acceptance: two-second runs are explicitly performance_gates_evaluated:false. Raw logs remain; the count difference is not a tuning conclusion.


DuckLake layout, skewed-hotspot 24-bit Hilbert sort & hash-32 compaction
Persisted candidate options read back; actual ZSTD row groups of 122,880 and 16,960 rows. 90%-skewed NYC hotspot across 2026/2027 sorted by 24-bit hierarchical hilbert_id (lake.hilbert64 catalog macro) merges two batches into one ZSTD file, rewrites deleted slice, suppresses min_value/max_value in ducklake_file_column_stats for wide_payload, and returns 3240 | 256 | 72 (including the 32-bucket hash table) on A and B. Tiny insert is catalog-only until flush.
That 256 MB file target or this layout is fastest for every query shape.


Cache/staging
Warm whole/range reads on B add zero origin reads; v1 remains inside TTL, then v2 revalidates. Pending bytes are non-expiring/readable, cleanup refuses them, and origin drain preserves bytes/ETag.
A generic SWR policy, independent capacity or lossless async promotion.


Jobs
Rollback/no job, lost enqueue reconciliation, mismatched envelope refusal, effect-before-ACK redelivery and stale-token 409. Receipt/effect count stays one even after retained ID removal/reuse.
Permanent uniqueness or exactly-once external work. Retention age is advanced only on one owned fixture row.


Streams
Ceiling 413, same active batch on repeat, ACK then empty receive.
Pagination, job leases on batches or a hard retention/disk cap.



Canonical report: .tmp/verify/guides.rVqHQl/guides.json, SHA-256 8f63be5765a85f21108db9948e7c6c654dcc3429b05c46f24ae6b812fa737b71 (superseding .tmp/verify/guides.YWTtwr/guides.json, SHA-256 45d1c5f70f09c227da6300be5f4b7a09db7a5d337cf2ee469722461852af1123, .tmp/verify/guides.Roi71e/guides.json, SHA-256 fd4f7d697b8f8f5f85afc2d7a057983326b3e958df0d99f1d489f22c78b0ed8b, .tmp/verify/guides.YSR72E/guides.json, SHA-256 cc57880f7f178d0f7b8ea2111964c06b2dc67aacd18b98b43ac4422046099339, .tmp/verify/guides.c8g6AD/guides.json, SHA-256 4f5fd634f3755b6eec59524de47c86873b32d610c713f72398b4d39b35d7b6cd, .tmp/verify/guides.VLXXPz/guides.json, SHA-256 333b97c06044baac9fa7f5dc904d9fb9c44191ab61dea1d3e8a51b70b8871ad7, and the 34-snippet .tmp/verify/guides.sUjCDv/guides.json, SHA-256 bdf47490d977c7cbc14c69309b617d06fc5d5a5d6ad0b7abe543f713bf517788, which remain retained). It contains the checks, plans, capacity snapshot, actual versions and document/ snippet/tool/binary hashes. All recorded document/tool hashes were compared with the delivered sources. This validation page is excluded from document hashes to avoid a self-referential report-hash cycle. Reports/transcripts/data stay ignored; GitHub’s existing failure upload includes the guide JSON and canary logs.
The complete just ci also passed: format/modernizer/import/tidy/vet/staticcheck/ vulnerability checks, race Go tests, 24 Python tooling tests, uncached race integration, four fuzz targets, Helm/kind, the contract (including these guides and pinned ObjFS recovery), physical-replica/promotion/pending-restore fault checks, interop and s3t. ShellCheck and Python compilation were checked separately. This is a local gate result, not a claim that a hosted CI run or cloud deployment passed.
The frozen-source CI run retained integration (44 s), Helm/kind (72 s), contract (50 s), fault (91 s), interop (16 s) and s3t (13 s) artifacts. Its embedded guide report, .tmp/verify/contract.E4QASf/guides.json (SHA-256 76a9f5cf74317b49cc1c38e928da81313537ec97a127072611f06a94ffd709ce), and the updated 35-snippet standalone run .tmp/verify/guides.rVqHQl/guides.json both completed with matching source hashes. Full CI transcript: .tmp/guidance-20261031/ci-frozen.log, SHA-256 32c0e44297bde13dac56934b321f8521625a1292b9ba626c49b079bb5a8fc0bf.



44/44 primary source URLs returned HTTP 200. Archived URL/date/body hashes are in .tmp/guidance-20261031/sources/fetch-44.json, SHA-256 55cb4a10d55ec6acfc826e723b648d599e465fe2c18145dbaeac9abb0593a989 (retaining the earlier 32-page fetch.json and 33-page fetch-final.json); the archived body hashes were checked too. These are research snapshots, not vendor binaries or vendor performance tests.

.tmp/verify/guides.OFzcOK: diagnostic query failed on ambiguous relname. Fixed the shown query to t.relname; the failed report/log remain.
.tmp/verify/guides.7mk8au: harness assumed serve --help exited zero. The existing CLI exits two; the harness now checks its real status/output instead of changing runtime behavior. Failed evidence remains.
.tmp/verify/guides.GPIO9D: expected count for events_hash32 after deleting id < 4096 was written as 72 instead of 71 (4096 = 8 × 500 + 96, removing 9 of the 80 rows for customer_id = 42). Fixed the documented expected value and assertion; failed evidence remains.
.tmp/verify/guides.BYo7Gd: a CTE-based CREATE MACRO lake.spread16 worked in a local DuckDB catalog but failed binder resolution when serialized into a PostgreSQL DuckLake catalog (ducklake:postgres:). Replaced it with the pure-scalar list_extract macro lake.hilbert64 applied at 4 hierarchical levels (24-bit = \(4,096 \times 4,096\) grid); failed evidence remains.
Later successful 32-snippet trials and the expanded 34-snippet canary trial remain alongside the canonical run; none replaces or overwrites a failure.




These are correctness/syntax/failure-window checks, not performance acceptance. The existing 10 MiB–1 GiB paired/capacity runners and published measurement ledgers remain authoritative for their tested workloads. No performance test of PlanetScale, ClickHouse, River or Spice.ai, managed-provider deployment, arbitrary network partition, production SLO, full CDC pipeline, parallel application relay, permanent deduplication or exactly-once external effect is claimed.
Physical standby/promotion and pending-body logical restore belong to just fault; physical archive/PITR and recovery of external effects still require an operator drill. Link/fence/Python/JSON checks run in standard-library CI tests; external page status is dated research evidence, not an always-online CI dependency.

Warm whole/range reads on B add zero origin reads; v1 remains inside TTL, then v2 revalidates. Pending bytes are non-expiring/readable, cleanup refuses them, and origin drain preserves bytes/ETag.
A generic SWR policy, independent capacity or lossless async promotion.


Jobs
Rollback/no job, lost enqueue reconciliation, mismatched envelope refusal, effect-before-ACK redelivery and stale-token 409. Receipt/effect count stays one even after retained ID removal/reuse.
Permanent uniqueness or exactly-once external work. Retention age is advanced only on one owned fixture row.


Streams
Ceiling 413, same active batch on repeat, ACK then empty receive.
Pagination, job leases on batches or a hard retention/disk cap.

title: Protect OLTP while adding pgvs3
text:
Guide index · Next: analytical snapshots
Goal: keep short SQL transactions responsive while object ingest, cache fills, refreshes and jobs share the cluster. First fix expensive application queries; pgvs3 cannot compensate for a missing index or an oversized connection fleet. The experiment below is executable; fleet sizing and SLO thresholds require measurement in your deployment. Research basis.


For each gateway, reserve up to pool-max + min(pool-max, 64) connections (main + chunk pools). Count maximum replicas during a rollout, application pools, DuckLake catalogs, DuckDB PostgreSQL scanner pools, operators and HA tools. Keep PostgreSQL’s reserved connection slots out of the usable application budget.
Example arithmetic, not a recommended fleet: four gateways at pool-max=16 can use 128 connections. One surge gateway makes that 160; 40 application, 16 extraction/catalog and 20 operational slots bring the envelope to 236. That is already tight on a server with max_connections=256 and reserved slots. Scaling an HPA without this calculation can remove the headroom needed to recover.

Gateway runtime requires direct or session-compatible PostgreSQL connections. Maintenance and ordered origin writes hold session advisory locks. Transaction pooling breaks that contract even if prepared statements work or SETs move into server configuration. PgBouncer may still suit application SQL that does not depend on session state; validate that application separately.
Bound extract/refresh jobs in their own client pool. An extraction can open multiple PostgreSQL connections; threads=4 is not a cluster connection quota.
Start with current gateway admission defaults; inspect waits before raising them. S3 admission allows 32 active and 64 waiting per gateway for at most one second. Waiting is not a durable queue. fill-concurrency=8 and disk-spool admission are additional, distinct bounds.




Use psql "$PGVS3_URL" against the disposable quick-start database. This creates one million deterministic orders; it deliberately refuses an existing schema. The same data is used by the analytics guide. Allow roughly a few hundred MiB of database/WAL headroom, not just the eventual Parquet size.

CREATE SCHEMA guide_app;
CREATE TABLE guide_app.orders (
    id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    amount_cents INTEGER NOT NULL,
    payload TEXT NOT NULL,
    paid BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT false,
    fulfillment_count INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0
);
INSERT INTO guide_app.orders (id, customer_id, created_at, amount_cents, payload)
SELECT g, (g % 10000)::INTEGER,
       TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-10-01 00:00:00+00' + g * INTERVAL '1 second',
       (g % 10000)::INTEGER, md5(g::TEXT)
FROM generate_series(0, 999999) AS g;
ANALYZE guide_app.orders;
Run the query before and after creating the index. ANALYZE in EXPLAIN executes the query; do not casually profile production mutations this way.

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, WAL, SETTINGS, TIMING OFF, FORMAT JSON)
SELECT id, created_at, amount_cents
FROM guide_app.orders
WHERE customer_id = 42
  AND created_at >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-10-01 00:00:00+00'
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 20;

CREATE INDEX orders_customer_recent
ON guide_app.orders (customer_id, created_at DESC, id DESC)
INCLUDE (amount_cents);
ANALYZE guide_app.orders;
Expected: the same 20 IDs, from 990042 down to 800042 in steps of 10,000. The candidate normally uses orders_customer_recent, visits far fewer buffers and avoids sorting a broad scan. Compare actual rows, loops, buffers and whole application latency, not planner cost units. An index-only scan can still fetch heap pages until vacuum updates the visibility map. The retained test plan is evidence for this data distribution, not proof for yours.
This ordinary index build is for the demo. On a live application table, plan a CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY outside a transaction, budget disk/WAL and inspect pg_index.indisvalid after failure. Remove an invalid build deliberately before retrying. Do not add indexes to pgvs3’s generated relations or disable scans globally: its metadata and chunk pools intentionally use different plans.



When a PostgreSQL table grows toward a billion rows or carries wide attributes (TEXT, JSONB, BYTEA, embeddings), physical tuple layout dominates buffer-hit ratios and vacuum cost:

Separate hot narrow state from wide payloads (TOAST boundary): PostgreSQL pages are 8 KiB and TOAST compresses or moves attributes out-of-line once a tuple crosses roughly 2 KiB (TOAST_TUPLE_THRESHOLD). Unchanged out-of-line TOAST values are not rewritten on UPDATE, but SELECT *, wide inline attributes or frequent updates to wide JSONB columns still dirty heap/TOAST pages and amplify WAL. Keep frequently updated status/counters and B-tree filter keys in a narrow table, split rarely read wide columns into a 1:1 companion table by primary key, and store multi-MiB blobs or batch extracts in pgvs3 buckets.
Prefer fixed 32–64 partitions (HASH or empirical Hilbert/Morton quantiles) over time-growing DDL: Time-partitioned tables require ongoing cron jobs to create future partitions and risk insert failures when a partition is missing. Unless your primary goal is dropping whole expired time windows (DETACH PARTITION / DROP TABLE), use 32 or 64 fixed partitions created once at initialization:

By ID or tenant: PARTITION BY HASH (tenant_id) (or id) with MODULUS 32 (or 64). At 1 billion rows across 64 partitions, each child table holds ~15.6M rows—keeping B-trees shallow in shared_buffers and letting autovacuum workers clean partitions in parallel across orders of magnitude of growth.
By 2D space under density skew: Never partition a skewed spatial table by 64 equal-area geographic grid cells (1 urban cell will get 80% of the rows while 45 ocean cells sit empty). Instead, compute a 32/64-bit 1D Hilbert or Morton (curve_id) integer, sample 31 or 63 empirical quantile cutpoints (percentile_disc), and use PARTITION BY RANGE (curve_id) so every child table holds ~1/32 or ~1/64 of the rows regardless of hotspot density.
Reserve rolling time RANGE partitions strictly for tables where bulk TTL deletion via DROP TABLE is mandatory.

Match the index type to physical correlation: Use composite B-trees (with INCLUDE covering columns) for selective point/prefix lookups, BRIN (timestamptz_minmax_ops or box_inclusion_ops) when rows are physically appended in time/space order and you want a tiny lossy block-range index, or GiST/SP-GiST when selective 2D spatial lookups must run directly in OLTP. Remember that unique/primary-key constraints on a partitioned PostgreSQL table must include all partition-key columns (and cannot use expression partition keys).




Prefer per-transaction changes over a cluster-wide memory increase. In a separate psql session, this demonstrates scope, not a universally safe budget:

BEGIN READ ONLY;
SET LOCAL statement_timeout = '30s';
SET LOCAL lock_timeout = '1s';
SET LOCAL work_mem = '16MB';
SET LOCAL max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 0;
SELECT count(*), sum(amount_cents) FROM guide_app.orders;
COMMIT;
Expected: 1000000 | 4999500000. SET LOCAL ends at transaction completion; it does not change gateway pools or another application’s session. Capture settings before/after when testing overrides. A PostgreSQL timeout aborts the transaction: roll back and retry the whole transaction only if its effects are safe to replay. A lost commit response is ambiguous; reconcile by business key.
work_mem is per sort/hash operation, not reserved once per connection. Hash operations can multiply it by hash_mem_multiplier; parallel workers and concurrent queries multiply demand again. Keep room for shared buffers, the OS, backend overhead, maintenance, gateway RSS and DuckDB/native-extension caches. shared_buffers=25% is upstream’s starting heuristic for a dedicated server, not a prescription for a container that also runs DuckDB. Do not solve spills by blindly raising global work_mem or removing sync/WAL durability.











Pressure
First move
Verify before increasing limits




Application SQL queues for connections
Reduce competing pools/refresh concurrency
Pool wait, active/idle sessions, rollout ceiling.


OLTP waits on storage or WAL
Throttle fills, exports and object writes
pg_stat_io, pg_stat_wal, checkpoint rates, application p95/p99 and errors.


Query spills but host has headroom
Inspect plan; scope memory to that transaction
Temp bytes and end-to-end latency under concurrency, not one isolated run.


Autovacuum falls behind
Find old snapshots/slots and table churn
Dead-tuple trend, last autovacuum, XID age, primary and standby feedback.


Read replicas lag or cancel scans
Shorten/scatter extracts or serve allowed reads elsewhere
Replay barrier/freshness; enabling feedback can shift cost into primary bloat.



Separate application/catalog databases improve ownership and recovery planning, not physical isolation. If the application SLO still fails at bounded load, move analytical bytes/refresh compute to another cluster or an external origin. Keeping one service fewer is not worth unpredictable OLTP.



Run just guides for the exact fixture, both plans, result equivalence and scoped settings checks. For real acceptance, replay your application transactions and object workload against the same primary/cluster and capture both latency/ error distributions. just load creates its own isolated clusters; running it beside an unrelated application database does not test their shared-cluster contention. Retain the control, sample counts, caches, data layout and failures. See measurement and diagnosis.


After the analytical export, save this as probe.sql. It is a small read/write canary, not your application’s representative workload. The logically unchanged UPDATE still creates tuple/WAL work; use only the demo:

\set order_id random(0, 999999)
BEGIN;
SELECT amount_cents FROM guide_app.orders WHERE id = :order_id;
UPDATE guide_app.orders SET fulfillment_count = fulfillment_count WHERE id = :order_id;
COMMIT;
Run a control with PostgreSQL 18 pgbench (do not use -i, which initializes and can destroy standard pgbench tables):
pgbench "$PGVS3_URL" -n -M prepared -c 2 -j 2 -T 30 -l \
  --log-prefix control -f probe.sql
Download the owned snapshot as orders.parquet and build the existing load generator with mise exec go -- go build -o loadgen ./test/loadgen. In a second terminal run it against the gateway backed by that same primary:

loadgen -endpoint "$PGVS3_ENDPOINT" -bucket guide-analytics -unsigned \
  -op get -payload-file orders.parquet -prefix guide-read-probe \
  -count 2 -workers 2 -duration "${PGVS3_GUIDE_DURATION:-30s}"
While it runs, repeat pgbench with --log-prefix mixed. Prefill creates two objects under the named demo prefix; it is not a cold-origin test or a read-only operation. Check the loadgen JSON’s errors, not just its exit status. pgbench stdout reports averages; per-transaction logs store elapsed microseconds in column three. Count failed/skipped rows separately before calculating tails. For realistic arrivals, use your observed rate (-R) and count schedule lag and skips rather than hiding overload behind closed-loop throughput.
Alternate control/mixed order across several longer repetitions, then change one admission/pool/layout setting. Require the application SLO and each relevant object-path budget. The guide gate uses two-second runs solely to verify the canary, concurrency, log format and zero errors; it claims no p99 isolation or winning configuration from that smoke. Logs stay with the report; remove the owned probe objects as part of the final demo bucket cleanup.
To undo just this demo index: DROP INDEX guide_app.orders_customer_recent;. Keep guide_app while following analytics/jobs. To end the manual walkthrough, follow owned-data cleanup; never drop an unfamiliar schema to make a recipe pass.

title: Reliable jobs, application outboxes and streams
text:
Guide index · Before: demo application · Next: operations
Goal: bridge a committed application change to OJS without pretending HTTP participates in its SQL transaction. Expect retries; make effects idempotent. If you need enqueue/completion inside the caller’s SQL transaction, a library with an explicit transaction API (for example River) is a better fit than writing pgvs3’s internal tables. Research and differences.



Transactional SQL Outbox, OJS Lease Token State Machine and 3-Segment TRUNCATE Stream Rotation












Need
Use
Boundary




Competing workers, leases, priority and retries
OJS jobs
Each HTTP lifecycle operation commits independently.


Independent fan-out/replay cursors
OJS streams
Snapshot-delimited batches; effects and batch ACK are separate.


Atomic application change + publish intent
Application-owned SQL outbox
Relay later to HTTP; not a distributed transaction.


Atomic application SQL effect + HTTP ACK
Not supplied
Commit a deduplication receipt with the effect, then ACK.



OJS args must be a JSON array, e.g. [{"order_id":42}], not an object; meta, if present, is an object. A caller UUID identifies a stored job, not a permanent unique-work key. A duplicate ID in its original queue returns 409 conflict; it does not compare payloads or return the original job as successful insertion. Jobs can be removed by retention (24h default for terminal jobs), expiry or namespace deletion. After removal, an old ID can be inserted again. The manifest correctly advertises unique_jobs:false. Keep the ID and queue immutable: reusing an ID in a different queue can surface a global job-index storage error instead of 409. Do not use a changed queue as a retry strategy or treat an arbitrary error as successful insertion.



In the disposable guide_app schema from the PostgreSQL guide:

CREATE TABLE guide_app.outbox (
    event_id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    job JSONB NOT NULL CHECK (job ? 'id' AND job->>'id' = event_id::TEXT),
    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    published_at TIMESTAMPTZ
);
CREATE INDEX outbox_unsent ON guide_app.outbox (created_at, event_id)
    WHERE published_at IS NULL;
CREATE TABLE guide_app.receipts (
    event_id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    order_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES guide_app.orders(id)
);
The UUID below is a fixed demo event. Real producers create a stable event ID once per business transition and persist it, rather than generating one on every HTTP retry. Keep its envelope immutable.

BEGIN;
UPDATE guide_app.orders SET paid = true WHERE id = 42;
INSERT INTO guide_app.outbox (event_id, job) VALUES (
    '018f0000-0000-7000-8000-000000000042',
    '{"id":"018f0000-0000-7000-8000-000000000042","type":"order.fulfill","args":[{"version":1,"order_id":42}],"queue":"guide-jobs"}'
);
COMMIT;
Expected: paid order + unsent outbox row, but no OJS job yet. Replacing COMMIT with ROLLBACK leaves neither business change nor intent. The test does both. The following is a runnable single-relay demonstration, using Python’s standard library and psql. Save as relay.py, set PGVS3_URL and PGVS3_ENDPOINT to the disposable writer endpoints, then run python3 relay.py. The test uses the same code. It holds no SQL transaction/lock across HTTP.

import json
import os
import subprocess
import uuid
from urllib.error import HTTPError
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen

def sql(statement):
    return subprocess.check_output([
        os.environ.get("PSQL", "psql"), os.environ["PGVS3_URL"],
        "-XAt", "-v", "ON_ERROR_STOP=1", "-c", statement
    ], text=True, timeout=30).strip()

def call(path, job=None):
    request = Request(os.environ["PGVS3_ENDPOINT"] + "/ojs/v1" + path,
                      data=None if job is None else json.dumps(job).encode(),
                      headers={"Content-Type": "application/openjobspec+json"})
    with urlopen(request, timeout=10) as response:
        return json.load(response)

raw = sql("SELECT job FROM guide_app.outbox WHERE published_at IS NULL "
          "ORDER BY created_at, event_id LIMIT 1")
if raw:
    expected = json.loads(raw)
    event_id = str(uuid.UUID(expected["id"]))
    try:
        actual = call("/jobs", expected)["job"]
    except HTTPError as error:
        if error.code != 409:
            raise
        actual = call("/jobs/" + event_id)["job"]
    for field in ("id", "type", "args", "queue"):
        if actual[field] != expected[field]:
            raise RuntimeError("job ID collision or changed envelope: " + field)
    sql("UPDATE guide_app.outbox SET published_at=now() "
        "WHERE event_id='" + event_id + "'::uuid AND published_at IS NULL")
    print(json.dumps({"published": event_id, "observed_state": actual["state"]}))
A network error leaves the row unsent. Retry this program with a bounded backoff and jitter: a prior committed POST becomes 409, then GET + envelope comparison reconciles it. Do not treat every 409 as success; a different payload/queue must stop and alert. Read this reconciliation from the primary, not a lagging replica. If GET races retention and returns 404, leave unsent and retry/reconcile; do not invent a new UUID. published_at means transport accepted, not business effect completed—monitor cancelled/discarded jobs separately.
This deliberately uses one relay. For parallel relays add short SQL claim leases, owner tokens, bounded retry scheduling and dead/error inspection in your application outbox; do not hold FOR UPDATE locks during network calls or copy this loop to hundreds of processes. Persist all relevant immutable fields and include them in reconciliation if extending the envelope (including options or metadata). Retain/reconcile intents and worker receipts for your replay/restore horizon, independently of OJS job retention.



Fetch on a writable endpoint:

{"queues":["guide-jobs"],"count":1,"worker_id":"guide-worker","visibility_timeout_ms":30000}
Send that JSON to POST /ojs/v1/workers/fetch. Validate the returned type, argument version, order ID and stable event ID against your application intent. For this demo, the effect SQL is:

BEGIN;
WITH first_delivery AS (
    INSERT INTO guide_app.receipts (event_id, order_id)
    VALUES ('018f0000-0000-7000-8000-000000000042', 42)
    ON CONFLICT (event_id) DO NOTHING
    RETURNING order_id
)
UPDATE guide_app.orders AS o
SET fulfillment_count = fulfillment_count + 1
FROM first_delivery AS d WHERE o.id = d.order_id;
COMMIT;
Expected: running it twice leaves fulfillment_count=1 and one receipt. The receipt and effect commit together. It protects this demonstrated SQL effect, not an email/payment/HTTP call outside the transaction; use that downstream system’s idempotency key and reconciliation as well. Validate payload identity before accepting a receipt collision. Do not expire receipts before jobs can be replayed, retried or restored from an older backup.
Then POST /ojs/v1/workers/ack with the returned job ID and current lease_token, e.g. {"job_id":"…","lease_token":"…","result":{"applied":true}}. If the process dies after SQL commit but before ACK, redelivery sees the receipt and suppresses a second effect. If a lease expires/reclaims, the old token gets 409 stale_lease; that is not permission to overwrite the newer delivery. Heartbeat well before the visibility deadline, or stop work and reconcile when ownership is lost. timeout_ms is job metadata, not a worker process killer.




Due scheduled/retryable jobs and expired non-exhausted active leases are claimed lazily by fetch; no minute-long maintenance wait is required. Expired jobs are excluded from claims; maintenance removes expired/terminal rows and marks exhausted expired leases discarded. Queue-state counts can lag those transitions until claim/maintenance; they are not a freshness clock.
Long polling is at most two seconds for an existing empty queue. Fetch accepts at most 64 queues and 100 jobs; requests and batches have a 1 MiB body bound. Fetch claims queues in the supplied order, not one global cross-queue priority order. Avoid a hot first queue starving later queues; use dedicated workers or rotate bounded subscriptions.
Fetch no more than can start/heartbeat safely. Measure enqueue/claim/ACK tails, oldest ready work, retries, abandoned leases and autovacuum, not merely jobs/sec. queue-concurrency is server request admission, not worker concurrency or an application SQL resource reservation.
Use bounded atomic batches (POST /jobs/batch, at most 100) for independent jobs when useful; it is not atomic with application SQL. Retryable nack follows the configured backoff/attempt limit; cancellation/discard is not success.
No workflows, cron, queue pause/resume, permanent uniqueness or job-level DLQ management is supplied. Streams have a separate retry/DLQ API.




Save/run this Python snippet with PGVS3_ENDPOINT set to a writable gateway. It creates only guide-events; processing here means inspecting IDs, not an external business effect:

import os
from urllib.error import HTTPError
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen

def post(path, body):
    request = Request(os.environ["PGVS3_ENDPOINT"] + "/ojs/v1" + path,
                      data=json.dumps(body).encode(),
                      headers={"Content-Type": "application/openjobspec+json"})
    with urlopen(request, timeout=10) as response:
        return json.load(response)

post("/queues/guide-events/consumers", {"consumer": "audit", "from_tick": 0})
post("/queues/guide-events/messages/batch", {"messages": [
    {"type": "order.paid", "payload": {"id": 42}},
    {"type": "order.paid", "payload": {"id": 43}}
]})
try:
    post("/queues/guide-events/receive", {"consumer": "audit", "max": 1})
except HTTPError as error:
    if error.code != 413:
        raise
else:
    raise RuntimeError("expected batch_too_large, not a partial page")
batch = post("/queues/guide-events/receive", {"consumer": "audit", "max": 100})
again = post("/queues/guide-events/receive", {"consumer": "audit", "max": 100})
assert batch["batch_id"] == again["batch_id"] and batch["count"] == 2
post("/streams/ack", {"queue": "guide-events", "batch_id": batch["batch_id"]})

Snapshot ticks prevent the late-commit sequence gap; they do not make the application’s SQL + HTTP append atomic. On an ambiguous append, do not assume a caller message ID deduplicates insertion. Deduplicate downstream by your stable business event key. Fan-out consumers advance independently; cooperative members must eventually ACK contiguous batches. A failed member is not an OJS job lease; plan recovery of its outstanding batch explicitly.
Retention is a minimum, not a disk cap: a slow consumer/active batch pins segments beyond it. Inspect /queues/{q}/consumers, /info and /dlq; do not unsubscribe a slow consumer merely to reclaim space without accepting lost replay history. Full stream model.

Keep reports and investigate failures before retrying cleanup; remove only owned demo data.

Need
Use
Boundary




Competing workers, leases, priority and retries
OJS jobs
Each HTTP lifecycle operation commits independently.


Independent fan-out/replay cursors
OJS streams
Snapshot-delimited batches; effects and batch ACK are separate.

Application-owned SQL outbox

Not supplied

OJS args must be a JSON array, e.g. [{"order_id":42}], not an object; meta, if present, is an object. A caller UUID identifies a stored job, not a permanent unique-work key. Jobs can be removed by retention (24h default for terminal jobs), expiry or namespace deletion. After removal, an old ID can be inserted again. The manifest correctly advertises unique_jobs:false. Keep the ID and queue immutable: reusing an ID in a different queue can surface a global job-index storage error instead of 409. Do not use a changed queue as a retry strategy or treat an arbitrary error as successful insertion.

title: Share object bytes without confusing freshness or authority
text:
Guide index · Before: analytics · Next: jobs
Goal: remove repeated origin byte transfers across workers while keeping the copy of record and allowed staleness explicit. pgvs3 is an object-byte cache and durable write stage, not an automatic query-result cache or refresh engine. Research basis.



Shared Origin Cache, Coalesced Cold Fills and Ack-First Write-Back Outbox












Workload
Start with
Do not assume




Immutable Parquet, repeatedly queried
Versioned keys; shared whole/range cache
A cache hit avoids DuckDB decoding or aggregation.


Mutable origin key
Explicit validation TTL within your stale budget
Direct origin changes invalidate PostgreSQL immediately.


Latency-sensitive large writes
Durable write-back only if readers use pgvs3 until drain
ACK means origin copy exists or an asynchronous standby can be promoted losslessly.


Origin-only downstream readers
Synchronous writes, or gate discovery on verified drain
Publishing a manifest last makes asynchronously staged data atomic at the origin.


Application result caching via RESP
Application-owned versioned key + TTL/invalidation
pgvs3 knows which SQL rows make a result stale.



Prefer immutable dataset keys. For a hot set that fits only partly in PostgreSQL, measure selective ranges before filling entire GiB objects. Fills consume logged PostgreSQL bytes, indexes, WAL and replay capacity; they are not free reads.



Use a disposable S3-compatible origin on 127.0.0.1:18014 and a writable pgvs3 gateway on :8014. Both are private. The origin must support versioned conditional mutations for production write use. just guides supplies an independent PostgreSQL-backed S3 origin, two gateways and an instrumented proxy; it does not need cloud credentials.
For this local demo, set PGVS3_ORIGIN_ENDPOINT=http://127.0.0.1:18014 and create only the named test object:

curl -fsS -X PUT "$PGVS3_ORIGIN_ENDPOINT/upstream"
curl -fsS -X PUT --data-binary 'version-one' \
  "$PGVS3_ORIGIN_ENDPOINT/upstream/guide-edge/version.txt"
Save as origin.json (real origin credentials are outbound secrets, unlike dummy credentials sent by clients to pgvs3):

{
  "type": "s3",
  "config": {
    "bucket": "upstream",
    "endpoint": "http://127.0.0.1:18014",
    "access_key": "test",
    "secret_key": "test",
    "bucket_lookup_type": "path"
  }
}
Attach it to a dedicated bucket/cache namespace; this also creates the per-bucket catalog row. The long TTL makes the stale case observable, not a recommendation for mutable production keys:

pgvs3 origin --url "$PGVS3_URL" --bucket guide-edge \
  --cache-namespace guide-origin --cache-ttl 1h \
  --range-cache-chunk 1048576 set origin.json
Allow up to the bounded one-second configuration refresh. Read once on A, then run the same command on B by setting PGVS3_ENDPOINT to its address:

curl -fsS -D - "$PGVS3_ENDPOINT/guide-edge/version.txt"
Expected: version-one; the warmed B request has X-Cache: HIT and causes no origin GET/HEAD. HTTP headers alone are not request-count proof: the harness counts origin requests independently and disables DuckDB client file/metadata caches for the Parquet shared-hit checks.
Change the object directly at the origin, not through pgvs3:

curl -fsS -X PUT --data-binary 'version-two' \
  "$PGVS3_ORIGIN_ENDPOINT/upstream/guide-edge/version.txt"
The warmed cache still returns version-one within its TTL. For the demo, switch to validation on every request:

pgvs3 origin --url "$PGVS3_URL" --bucket guide-edge \
  --cache-namespace guide-origin --cache-ttl 0s \
  --range-cache-chunk 1048576 set origin.json
After configuration discovery, the next read returns version-two; it now requires origin metadata I/O even when the body has not changed. Zero TTL is not zero retention or free strict consistency across systems/replicas. Restore your saved origin configuration to undo the experiment. Do not clear the origin on a live bucket as an invalidation trick: that changes routing and authority, not merely freshness.



Large (>8 MiB) cold ranges pass through unless range caching is enabled. A 1 MiB aligned chunk is a candidate: it can help nearby column/footer reads but overfetch isolated tiny ranges. Smaller chunks trade overfetch for more rows/requests; larger ones can evict useful working set. Measure:

origin requests and bytes, time to first byte and full query p95/p99;
full-object versus selective queries, 10/100/1,024 MiB files and concurrency;
warm B/standby reads with client caches off, not just a repeated query in A;
PostgreSQL relation/WAL growth, pool waits and OLTP latency during cold fills.

Shared lease ownership coalesces cold fills but has a bounded waiter timeout and pass-through fallback. It is not a promise of exactly one origin request through every failure. Standby gateways consume replayed hits but never fill; misses can still load the origin. Readiness does not mean a dataset is warm or fresh.



By default, unconditional PUT/COPY above 8 MiB and unconditional multipart completion at any size commit the body and outbox in PostgreSQL before ACK. Small/conditional writes are synchronous. Pending bodies have no expiry; committed idle retention starts after handoff. Test the large path by making the origin unavailable for writes, uploading a Parquet file, reading it through B, then restoring the origin and verifying identical bytes there. just analytics and the guide gate exercise this exact sequence.
Observe both sides of the handoff:

SELECT namespace, count(*) AS rows, coalesce(sum(size), 0) AS bytes,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE dead) AS dead,
       max(now() - created_at) AS oldest
FROM s3p.pending_uploads
GROUP BY namespace;
pgvs3 pending --url "$PGVS3_URL" list adds attempt/error details. Size backlog headroom as ingress bytes/sec × credible outage duration, plus live cache, unpublished/retired files, physical overhead and WAL. For example, 50 MiB/s for 20 minutes is about 58.6 GiB of payload alone. This is arithmetic, not a measured storage multiplier. If drain throughput cannot exceed sustained ingress, the backlog will never catch up. Throttle writers before disk exhaustion.
On origin precondition conflict, do not assume the pending version won; reconcile the origin/application generation. Dead rows need repair and explicit retry, not silent deletion. Never truncate s3w_, delete pending bodies, reset tokens or shorten their expiry to reclaim space. A cache flush is not recovery and cannot discard acknowledged data.




Warm entries inside TTL can be served without origin I/O. Expired entries and misses can require the origin; pgvs3 is not a general stale-while-revalidate or serve-stale-on-error policy engine. Test your desired outage behavior.
Write-through DELETE leaves a 30-minute tombstone. Direct origin recreation may stay hidden until it expires; recreation through pgvs3 replaces it.
In s3c_, origin fills are rebuildable but standalone RESP values are not. Reserve distinct namespaces for distinct ownership/retention policies.
Scratch spools are temporary, with a per-process payload budget. Keep disk headroom for logs/overhead as well; failed byte admission remains fail-fast.
Use owned-data cleanup only after pending work is drained and the test origin is no longer serving readers. Never turn a pending namespace into a “disposable cache” by renaming it.

title: Differential on the PostgreSQL object data plane
text:
DuckDB Differential is an experimental client option, not a new pgvs3 storage backend or a replacement for DuckLake. The standard disposable benchmark includes it with just differential. Logged layout v25, shared fills, replicas and existing clients remain. The accompanying bounded S3 admission queue is a separate gateway improvement, not a Differential storage optimization.


Differential runs stock native DuckDB storage over a local repository: SQLite metadata plus append-only payload/journal segments. It exports content-addressed 256 KiB chunks in packs of up to 8 MiB. With a native pgvs3 bucket, these S3 objects are logged PostgreSQL rows, just like DuckLake’s Parquet objects.








Profile
What returns from a write
Remote visibility




DuckLake + PostgreSQL catalog + pgvs3 objects
Object upload and catalog commit
Other attached DuckLake clients can discover the committed catalog state


Differential, ordinary commit
Native local sync in its repository
Not a PostgreSQL-backed commit merely because DATA_PATH is S3


Differential snapshot export
Local commit plus synchronous differential_create_snapshot
A new plain head attachment reads that exported snapshot


Differential SHIP_WAL 'sync'
Local sync plus remote epoch publication
Recoverable shipped state; plain head attachments still read the last exported snapshot, not necessarily the latest commit



The benchmark compares the first, third and fourth rows. It retains ordinary statement time separately and never credits a local-only return as a remotely durable acknowledgement. Additional snapshot publication for the sync-WAL profile is measured separately. A commit-level FOLLOW reader is an upstream option, but its polling/transaction semantics are not benchmarked here.
The native catalog can make small DDL/transactions cheaper than a PostgreSQL DuckLake catalog. That hypothesis does not establish faster fresh attachment, remote scans, lower total storage, or equivalent operational capabilities. The exported packs are native DuckDB storage, not Parquet files for other engines. Producing interoperable Parquet remains an explicit export operation; the existing DuckLake/Parquet path is not removed. Native DuckDB buffers and the writer’s repository must not be mistaken for shared pgvs3 caching. Gateways remain stateless; the additional repository belongs to the DuckDB client.



just setup
just differential-setup
just differential --differential-mib 10,100 --passes 3
# Include the large cohort, or run it separately to bound storage churn:
just differential --differential-mib 1024 --passes 3
Equivalent benchmark entry point: just bench differential .... A quick functional smoke is:
just differential --differential-mib 1 --passes 1 \
  --differential-ddl-iterations 1 --differential-small-commits 2
The opt-in setup pins Differential v1.1.0, source commit 43203569f46b3a7f0c3a88fa8b4c34a50052ceb0, for DuckDB 2.0.0. Automatic provisioning supports the upstream Linux amd64/arm64 and macOS arm64 artifacts. It verifies the complete archive SHA-256 before extracting only the extension, records the extension hash, and refuses to overwrite a different cached binary. Only Linux amd64 is exercised in this repository’s recorded run.
These are upstream CI artifacts, not permanent release assets. Workflow 40585660508 artifacts currently expire 2027-01-25. Preserve the verified .tmp/deps/differential/ cache or use a source build; do not silently substitute the latest artifact. Community installation is not assumed to be available.
To supply an explicitly built extension:

  --differential-mib 10 --passes 3

git -C .tmp/differential-source checkout --detach 43203569f46b3a7f0c3a88fa8b4c34a50052ceb0
git -C .tmp/differential-source submodule update --init --recursive
cd .tmp/differential-source
# With CMake/Ninja and the upstream prerequisites:
make vcpkg
export VCPKG_TOOLCHAIN_PATH="$PWD/build/vcpkg/scripts/buildsystems/vcpkg.cmake" GEN=ninja
make release
# Artifact: build/release/extension/differential/differential.duckdb_extension
The source-build fallback is documented, not exercised by the pgvs3 measurements. No agent plugin, patched DuckDB, FUSE service or daemon is installed. Unsigned extension loading is enabled only in the experimental DuckDB processes; there is no global DuckDB setting change. Credentials use temporary TYPE s3 secrets, never attach options or persisted secrets. Client processes disable EC2 metadata discovery so an unavailable metadata service cannot dominate attachment.



deploy/bench/differential.py is a part of the existing DuckDB runner, not a separate infrastructure harness. deploy/bench/stack.sh owns the disposable PostgreSQL 18 container and two gateways; capacity.py supplies its storage/WAL observations. Work is sequential, with profile order rotated between repetitions. It does not rerun or replace the existing direct-gateway performance matrices.

Identical deterministic Snappy Parquet inputs target 10 MiB, 100 MiB and 1 GiB; reports retain actual sizes, generation SQL and hashes. Each cohort has fresh namespaces and a fresh client repository. DuckLake data inlining is off.
DDL on empty tables, schema evolution on the loaded table, bulk loading, 32-row small commits, a 1% string update, 50% deletion and a full table drop are measured individually. --differential-ddl-iterations and --differential-small-commits default to five; --passes defaults to three.
Reader processes use gateway B, a fresh repository and no writer-local files. Each scan/range reader is separate. External file caching, Parquet metadata caching and Differential’s remote disk cache are off; memory is 2 GB with four execution threads per client. HTTP client pool capacity and the Differential SDK request cap are both 16, below the gateway’s default 32-request admission limit. Retried 5xx responses invalidate a timed sample; they cannot inflate a claimed client speedup. The repeated query can still use native DuckDB buffer pages and is labeled same_client_repeat, not another cold read.
Fresh attachment, schema discovery and first query are separate, with their sum also reported. A faster query after an expensive native attachment is not automatically a faster fresh-client operation. Process startup and extension setup are outside that sum (client_setup_seconds is retained separately). Neither server buffers nor OS caches are flushed; this is not a cold-disk or WAN benchmark.
Results are checked against an independent local-input reference using row count, key sum, string length and a 128-bit sum of row hashes. Schema, updates, deletions, range filters and post-cleanup reads must match. A sentinel table verifies fresh access even after the data table is dropped.
Actual gateway request/response-byte deltas cover both httpfs and the Differential C++ SDK. DuckDB’s HTTP log alone would miss the SDK. PostgreSQL catalog traffic is not S3 traffic and is not counted as such.
Capacity snapshots include object bytes, allocated bucket/catalog relations, cluster WAL positions/retention, local repository/spill bytes and allocated filesystem blocks. Server WAL includes other work on the isolated cluster; ordinary vacuum does not guarantee relation shrinkage. Inventories do not measure RSS, shared extension/input files or filesystem metadata overhead.
DuckLake’s explicit delete_threshold => 0.5 makes its file rewrite eligible after half the rows are deleted. Its default 0.95 threshold would leave those files unchanged. Rewrite time and new/retired objects are measured, not treated as free compaction. Differential’s metadata compaction is not an equivalent table rewrite; that distinction is part of the storage comparison.

Each path reports its own latency ratio and 20% budget result against DuckLake. This is an alternative-client evaluation, not a gateway regression pass. Budget misses remain visible and do not remove the existing path or silently change the preferred setup. A completed experiment means its stated checks ran, not that every optional profile passed a replacement/adoption gate.
Known client limits remain failures, not zero-latency samples. The release cannot synchronously ship an epoch larger than 256 MiB; the 1 GiB fixture’s bulk CTAS hits that limit. Its error says the commit is durable locally but was not shipped. The runner retains that failed remote acknowledgement, marks the corresponding profile unavailable, and does not retry it by batching or weakening durability. It finishes other profiles and writes complete: true with explicit failures and all_profiles_completed: false; the command still exits nonzero. Do not blindly retry a failed bulk INSERT: local state may already have committed.
All reports live in the unique printed .tmp/verify/bench.*/ directory, including per-worker jobs/results/logs and incremental differential/progress.json. --out must be fresh. Failures and partial reports are retained. Management workers reject paths/provider roots outside their owned run; namespace teardown happens after, never instead of, the measured reclamation stages.




Release reader attachments and expire eligible old snapshots, keeping current branch heads. Snapshot, branch and WAL-chain roots still retain data.
Differential local GC removes unreferenced mappings/payload; active journals and retained readers can delay physical segment reclamation. A separate fresh process measures cleanup after the writer exits.
differential_compact performs SQLite incremental vacuum. Its page/byte result is local metadata reclamation—not a native table rewrite, remote-pack compaction, or PostgreSQL vacuum.
Remote GC first condemns unreachable objects, then deletes eligible condemned objects after a grace period. Indexes/descriptors sharing live packs can remain. The newest shipped chain and its base are roots as well as public snapshots.
Deleted pgvs3 objects retire body ownership; pgvs3 reaping and PostgreSQL vacuum then make their physical space reusable. These timings/footprints are separate.

The disposable GC drill deliberately uses a one-second grace, with waits between phases. That is not an operational retention recommendation. The current DuckDB file can still map free blocks; dropping SQL data need not immediately shrink exported payload. The benchmark records the actual result rather than attributing all observed reclamation to differential_compact.



The release-client proof exercises SDK multipart uploads/SHA-256 metadata, conditional publication, ranged pack reads and a writer exiting with os._exit without detach or shutdown checkpoint. Another repository recovers every shipped acknowledgement, continues with the same identity through the other gateway, and recovers again after remote GC. Explicit branch-head takeover is needed to resume snapshot publication/numbering after identity-preserving recovery.
This is not an HA controller or a global writer fence. A deliberately restarted old repository acknowledged another sync-WAL commit and produced a newer chain; a subsequent fresh recovery no longer contained the recovered writer’s later marker. Conflicting snapshot publication was rejected, which did not prevent the WAL-state replacement. The negative probe is retained separately from the valid one-writer recovery proof; it is not a successful safety claim.
Fence the old DuckDB writer and its repository before failover; do not merely switch gateways or take over branch heads. Do not restart that stale repository as another writer. PostgreSQL’s object durability does not arbitrate the native client’s independent histories. Multi-host/shared writers, followers, merge semantics, arbitrary partitions, power loss, physical backup/PITR coordination and origin-backed Differential locations remain outside this evaluation.
Upstream’s release status still reports v1_complete=false; loading successfully is not full Linux or power-loss qualification. Retain DuckLake and the existing PostgreSQL roles unless the measured workload and operating constraints justify an explicit client choice.
