CPU profiles (15s each, Go pprof):

4 KiB GET: getObject 53% cumulative; metaRef 33%; pgx query 22%; socket writes 34%. A dedicated inline-object read path was prototyped and benchmarked. It did not improve throughput (62.4k vs 63.1k req/s at 64 workers), so it was reverted. Query/transport latency, not metadata field decoding, dominates this path.
4 KiB PUT: putObject 44%; putInlineRef 33%; pgx query 22%; socket writes 19%; MD5/SHA ~5.1%; GC ~7%. Preallocating the inline body from Content-Length removed the io.ReadAll growth/copy path and improved the 16-worker PUT result from 24.2k to 26.7k req/s. Reusing the inline buffer from a bounded 64 KiB pool then improved a fresh three-sample mean from 26.3k to 27.3k req/s at 16 workers and 32.2k to 33.3k at 64 workers; the 64-worker p99 fell from about 7.9 ms to 7.3 ms.
64 MiB GET: syscalls 70%; streamRows 59%; pgx row decoding 44%; appendRow 14%; socket writes 33%. A direct-decode experiment skipped the decoded-row → response-buffer copy for unclipped full-object reads, but the result was flat to slightly worse (6.59 vs 6.83 GiB/s at 8 workers), so it was reverted. Large reads remain syscall- and transport-bound.
64 MiB PUT: the framer now writes full rows directly from the incoming buffer and retains only the trailing partial row, removing a full-write copy into pending. An 8-worker three-sample mean improved from 19.8 to 21.0 req/s (1.24 to 1.31 GiB/s); p50 fell from ~399 to ~379 ms and p99 from ~467 to ~436 ms. Parallel MD5/SHA changed throughput by at most about 2% and raised CPU; probes that skipped hashing or compression changed it by less than 1%. Neither path is the next target.
Warm cache 4 KiB GET: the warm-hit path was doing two metadata lookups (MetaHeader for the cache decision, then GetBody for the body). Reusing the first metadata row for the body read raised 1/16/64-worker throughput from 7.2k/33.9k/49.7k to 9.4k/39.0k/62.9k req/s, matching native inline GET. The canonical cache row above predates this change.
Query execution: the default pgx cache_statement path remains fastest. Switching the whole connection to cache_describe, exec, or simple_protocol reduced 4 KiB GET/PUT throughput by roughly 18–30% at 16 workers, so no query-mode change is retained.

The ownership-aware large-PUT row feed was also built and rejected. It was correct, but the segment/reader path measured about 20.0 req/s versus 21.3 req/s for direct framing: removing the copy did not repay the extra per-row bookkeeping. Large PUT is left at direct framing. A GOGC=200/400 experiment initially looked much faster, but the gain disappeared when the load generator was pinned to its own GOGC=100; the gateway GC target is not a retained change.
The next measured slice is the native 4 KiB PUT query/bind path. The current profile is about 22% pgx query/bind, 19% socket writes, and 5% hashing. The first experiment is a narrow unconditional bucket inline-write path with fewer bound parameters and less server-side branching, benchmarked at 16 and 64 workers against the current 33.3k req/s. It will be kept only if it beats that result. Small GET is at its query/transport ceiling, warm cache GET matches native, and large reads are at the syscall ceiling.

title: Benchmarks
text:
The exploratory matrix uses 5-second tests. 4 KiB tests use 2,000 keys; 8 MiB and 64 MiB tests use 16 and 8 objects; ListObjectsV2 lists 1,000 keys per page from a 2,000-key bucket. Gateways hold no in-process cache; metadata and ≤64 KiB objects are served directly from PostgreSQL shared_buffers.


Save a control binary before making changes, then run the current tree against it:
mkdir -p .tmp
mise exec go -- go build -o .tmp/pgvs3-before ./cmd/pgvs3
# Make the change, then:
just load --before-bin .tmp/pgvs3-before --profile native \
  --payload /path/to/10m.parquet --payload /path/to/100m.parquet \
  --ops head,get,range,put --workers 1,4 --repeats 5
just load --before-bin .tmp/pgvs3-before --profile origin --cache-state cold \
  --payload /path/to/10m.parquet --ops get,range --workers 1,4 \
  --range-size 65536 --repeats 5
--after-bin selects a saved candidate instead of building the current tree. --out selects a fresh output path; existing outputs are never overwritten. Otherwise artifacts and paired.json remain in the unique printed .tmp/verify/ directory. --no-small omits the default 4 KiB case. --requests overrides the size/state-aware per-sample budget; all counts and raw samples are recorded.
compare.py is the only paired driver and still uses test/loadgen, not a second load engine. It alternates binary order, hashes frozen binaries and payloads, checks object/range sizes and bytes, checks persisted origin directory/namespace/ TTL/range settings, and rejects unexpected cache paths. Cold filesystem-origin fixtures use distinct keys with no prior cache bodies or metadata, and validate the completed fills. Loadgen’s opt-in -unique-reads shares one read sequence across workers; its default workload is unchanged. Cold here means cold gateway cache, not cleared operating-system page cache.
Each case fails independently above +20% median p50 or below -20% median request rate, or on any request/fixture error. A valid report has complete: true; partial reports retain complete: false. failed_gates names regressions rather than hiding them in an aggregate. Range labels distinguish aligned chunks, whole-object cache ranges and pass-through. The exploratory matrix remains available without --before-bin, reports saturation errors instead of treating them as acceptance, and writes actual NDJSON. PGVS3_BENCH_DURATION shortens that matrix for fixture smoke tests only; use repeated paired runs for acceptance.



Use disposable isolated clusters only. Resource mode deletes its fixture keys, advances their committed-cache expiry deadlines, reaps and vacuums after each case. It refuses pending bodies at cleanup and never advances a pending body’s expiry.
Generate reproducible inputs with the existing DuckDB tool, without a gateway:
mise exec uv -- uv run --quiet --no-project --with duckdb==2.0.0 \
  python deploy/bench/duck_bench.py --parts fixtures --out .tmp/capacity/fixtures.json
This produces approximately 10/100/1,024 MiB Snappy Parquet and exact-size binary fixtures under .tmp/capacity/payloads/. Actual sizes, generation SQL, seeds and SHA-256 hashes are recorded. Binary fixtures repeat a seeded 1 MiB block: they are incompressible at pgvs3’s 8,120-byte block size, not unique random streams across the entire file. --fixture-mib selects smaller smoke inputs; existing files are never overwritten.
just load --capacity --after-bin .tmp/pgvs3-candidate --profile origin \
  --payload .tmp/capacity/payloads/parquet-100MiB.parquet --no-small \
  --ops get,range,put,overwrite --workers 1,4 --range-size 65536 \
  --replication async --checkpoint-writes --repeats 5

--capacity uses one candidate endpoint/cluster and the existing loadgen to capture resource costs. It sets mode: capacity, performance_gates_evaluated: false and failed_gates: null; completion means the fixtures/observations passed, not a before/after performance claim. Use ordinary uninstrumented paired runs for the regression gate. Separate clusters on one host still contend for the same physical disk.
--resources enables snapshots and observations on separate primary clusters. --replication async|sync adds a real physical standby per side and enables resources. sync selects one named synchronous standby; it does not mean remote_apply. Recovery state, system identifiers and replay positions are validated. Standbys use hot_standby_feedback=on; feedback/snapshots can hold back primary vacuum. No production replication policy is changed.
overwrite uses loadgen’s opt-in -overwrite: each worker reuses one prefilled key, retaining retired files for the lifecycle measurement. Ordinary PUT keeps its distinct-key behavior. Use --cache-state cold --ops get,range for empty origin-cache fills; otherwise reads are explicitly warmed and verified.
--checkpoint-writes prepares publication/cold-fill samples with a primary checkpoint, replay barrier and standby restartpoint outside timed work. The duration is recorded, not hidden as free work. Use a one-request sample budget for 1 GiB resource cohorts and retain several paired repetitions; larger bursts are a separate sustained-churn experiment, not a peak-throughput comparison.
--isolate-origin-put is a separate paired PUT-only filesystem fixture. After drain and byte verification it deletes only that sample’s origin keys; before the next sample it truncates the otherwise empty owned cache tables. It refuses pending bodies, incomplete multipart uploads or unrelated keys and cannot be combined with resource mode. This isolates fresh publication ACKs; it is not a retention/reaping or sustained-upload-throughput measurement.
Each raw run records pre-run, post-loadgen and post-drain snapshots: logical object-row bytes, heap/index/total relation bytes, pending state, WAL insertion positions, checkpoint statistics, gateway metrics and standby replay. The post-loadgen snapshot is not the exact instant of the last HTTP ACK. Acknowledgement latency remains loadgen’s per-request measurement; after-loadgen drain is reported separately, not hidden inside ACK throughput.
Lifecycle snapshots show delete, injected committed-row expiry, reaping and vacuum separately. Ordinary vacuum makes space reusable but need not shrink relation files. The logical count includes expired rows until reaped. Cleanup verifies the reaper actually drained rather than merely losing the maintenance-leader race, records reaping/vacuum time, and uses the explicit --maintenance-timeout deadline (default ten minutes).
WAL bytes are isolated-cluster LSN advancement, including headers/padding, checkpoint/full-page-image and background work—not a per-table WAL counter. Observer pg_settings describe its psql session and cluster defaults, not the gateway’s connection-local SET policy.
Gateway gauges use a 100 ms poll interval plus probe time, so their observed peaks are lower bounds. Cross-node WAL position gaps include probe skew; they are not simultaneous end-to-end lag measurements. pgvs3_spool_peak_bytes is exact reserved-payload high water since that gateway started, not a resettable per-case peak. Pool counter deltas also include metrics observations. Replay catch-up time includes SQL/polling overhead.
Resource collection can perturb short measurements. Keep the same observations on both sides, retain raw records, and use uninstrumented paired runs to resolve performance-gate failures. Do not silently discard a failed resource comparison.

The paired driver defaults to a five-minute S3 request timeout for large fixtures; --request-timeout changes it. Standalone loadgen keeps its one-minute default and exposes -timeout. A client deadline failure remains an error, not a retry or a successful sample; loadgen stdout/stderr are retained in the failure.
resource_schema: 1 and complete: true identify finished observations. Only a paired report with performance_gates_evaluated: true and empty failed_gates also establishes its measured regression gate. Full configuration and binary/ payload hashes remain in the report. See data-plane-results.md for recorded results and deployment-sizing limits.

CPU profiles (15s each, Go pprof):

4 KiB GET: getObject 53% cumulative; metaRef 33%; pgx query 22%; socket writes 34%. A dedicated inline-object read path was prototyped and benchmarked. It did not improve throughput (62.4k vs 63.1k req/s at 64 workers), so it was reverted. Query/transport latency, not metadata field decoding, dominates this path.
4 KiB PUT: putObject 44%; putInlineRef 33%; pgx query 22%; socket writes 19%; MD5/SHA ~5.1%; GC ~7%. Preallocating the inline body from Content-Length removed the io.ReadAll growth/copy path and improved the 16-worker PUT result from 24.2k to 26.7k req/s. Reusing the inline buffer from a bounded 64 KiB pool then improved a fresh three-sample mean from 26.3k to 27.3k req/s at 16 workers and 32.2k to 33.3k at 64 workers; the 64-worker p99 fell from about 7.9 ms to 7.3 ms.
64 MiB GET: syscalls 70%; streamRows 59%; pgx row decoding 44%; appendRow 14%; socket writes 33%. A direct-decode experiment skipped the decoded-row → response-buffer copy for unclipped full-object reads, but the result was flat to slightly worse (6.59 vs 6.83 GiB/s at 8 workers), so it was reverted. Large reads remain syscall- and transport-bound.
64 MiB PUT: the framer now writes full rows directly from the incoming buffer and retains only the trailing partial row, removing a full-write copy into pending. An 8-worker three-sample mean improved from 19.8 to 21.0 req/s (1.24 to 1.31 GiB/s); p50 fell from ~399 to ~379 ms and p99 from ~467 to ~436 ms. Parallel MD5/SHA changed throughput by at most about 2% and raised CPU; probes that skipped hashing or compression changed it by less than 1%. Neither path is the next target.
Warm cache 4 KiB GET: the warm-hit path was doing two metadata lookups (MetaHeader for the cache decision, then GetBody for the body). Reusing the first metadata row for the body read raised 1/16/64-worker throughput from 7.2k/33.9k/49.7k to 9.4k/39.0k/62.9k req/s, matching native inline GET. The canonical cache row above predates this change.
Query execution: the default pgx cache_statement path remains fastest. Switching the whole connection to cache_describe, exec, or simple_protocol reduced 4 KiB GET/PUT throughput by roughly 18–30% at 16 workers, so no query-mode change is retained.

The ownership-aware large-PUT row feed was also built and rejected. It was correct, but the segment/reader path measured about 20.0 req/s versus 21.3 req/s for direct framing: removing the copy did not repay the extra per-row bookkeeping. Large PUT is left at direct framing. A GOGC=200/400 experiment initially looked much faster, but the gain disappeared when the load generator was pinned to its own GOGC=100; the gateway GC target is not a retained change.
The next measured slice is the native 4 KiB PUT query/bind path. The current profile is about 22% pgx query/bind, 19% socket writes, and 5% hashing. The first experiment is a narrow unconditional bucket inline-write path with fewer bound parameters and less server-side branching, benchmarked at 16 and 64 workers against the current 33.3k req/s. It will be kept only if it beats that result. Small GET is at its query/transport ceiling, warm cache GET matches native, and large reads are at the syscall ceiling.

Warm reads were about 52x faster on 10 MiB, 47x on 100 MiB and 44x on 1 GiB. Cold fills were 25%–28% slower than direct origin because the complete body is now written to the WAL-logged shared read cache. Write-back acknowledgement was about 5x faster than the constrained origin PUT. That is the cost of making fills visible to read-only replicas; warm reads themselves are unchanged.



Compared the pre-refactor 766720e binary with the reorganized cache layer on the same local PostgreSQL 18.6 primary (synchronous_commit=on, 128 MiB shared_buffers) and constrained S3 origin described above. No layout, chunk codec, SQL ingest or PostgreSQL body-streaming code changed. Production Go source in internal/objcache decreased from 3,556 to 3,131 lines (12%), without removing providers or protocol features. Fixtures were incompressible byte payloads, not a DuckDB query benchmark.
The full sweep used three samples for each cold fill and write-back acknowledgement; 21/11/7 warm reads for 10 MiB/100 MiB/1 GiB; 12 requests with four concurrent readers per size; 21 HEADs; five cold aligned-range requests; and 31 warm 64 KiB range requests. The outbox was drained between writes and the cache truncated between cold samples. Medians are wall-clock HTTP request times, including body transfer.

title: Object data-plane proof and capacity evidence
text:
Date: 2026-10-29. Control: 07e8731; layout v25 on both sides.
This pass implements the three priorities in roadmap.md: prove the PostgreSQL operating model, maintain one analytical scenario and measure the byte-store trade-off. It does not add a protocol or replace the storage engine. schema.sql is byte-identical; acknowledged bodies and shared fills remain logged.


just fault extends the existing disposable Docker harness with a PostgreSQL 18.6 primary, two physical standbys and an independent S3 origin fixture. pg_is_in_recovery(), streaming state and replay LSNs are asserted, not inferred from a gateway’s --read-only flag.

Native Parquet, 80 MiB sequential reads, multipart snapshot reads, whole-object cache hits, aligned blocks/parent metadata and two pending bodies are read from the real standby after replay. Bytes, metadata and public ETags match; shared hits generate no origin requests. Mutations remain rejected on the read-only gateway.
synchronous_commit=on plus one named synchronous standby defines the eligible promotion target. The old primary/writable fleet is fenced. An in-flight COPY publishes no partial object; the promoted writer preserves the acknowledged native, single-write-back and multipart data.
A second standby’s receiver is deliberately disconnected before a marker is acknowledged. Promoting that ineligible, unreplayed copy loses the marker while retaining its earlier baseline. This is the expected asynchronous durability boundary, not an accepted promise of lossless arbitrary promotion.
A consistent whole-database pg_dump/pg_restore carries native bytes, pending bodies, metadata and outbox state together. Reads and doctor succeed before resuming uploads. The pending restore uses a fresh isolated recovery-origin bucket; this is not a restore of an entire external origin or a PITR exercise.
After fencing the old fleet, the fixture injects lease expiry to bound the test. New writes replace old pending tokens; upload drain preserves the newer bytes, and delete tombstones prevent resurrection in the exercised workflow. Session locks are not fencing across two independently writable PostgreSQL timelines.

The initial restore drill found a real liveness gap: persisted origin tiers were opened only by S3 traffic. Registry.Start now owns a cancellable one-second refresh, joined by Close, so an idle restored gateway resumes pending work. The request catalog check, tier borrowing and read-only no-fill/no-flush rules remain. No HA controller or exactly-once PostgreSQL/origin commit is implied.



just analytics runs the README’s actual DuckDB/DuckLake SQL on disposable gateways; just contract reuses it. The 19,438,062-byte Parquet object has one million rows, the expected aggregates and valid footer ranges. Native and origin-backed queries run through another gateway with client caches disabled. The S3 origin fixture counts calls, proving shared whole/range hits rather than mistaking a client-local cache for shared storage.
The scenario also reads a PostgreSQL-only pending body while origin writes fail, then verifies the origin copy and stable ETag after drain. DuckLake tables reopen through another gateway in each role. Data inlining is disabled for that example so the table exercises object files; catalog/object commits remain separate.



The existing test/loadgen remains the only paired load engine. Resource mode adds observations and lifecycle checks, not another benchmark framework:

Separate primary clusters prevent before/after WAL accounting from mixing. Each optional real standby is checked against its primary’s system identifier.
Reproducible Snappy Parquet and seeded block-incompressible inputs target 10 MiB, 100 MiB and 1 GiB. Actual sizes, SQL/seeds and hashes are retained.
Snapshots record logical object-row bytes, heap/index/total relation footprint, WAL positions, pending state, checkpoints, pool metrics and replay positions. Delete, fixture-only committed expiry, reaping and vacuum are separate stages.
ACK latency is loadgen’s request measurement. Post-loadgen observations and remaining outbox drain are separate; they are not the exact instant of the last ACK or a claim of steady-state origin upload throughput.

The initial paired resource trial accumulated nine roughly 1 GiB objects per side, triggered heavy checkpoint/reclamation pressure and exceeded the original 120-second cleanup deadline. Its incomplete report is retained. The 18 fully completed cohorts were not repeated; the unfinished cases use smaller sample budgets and explicit checkpoint preparation. Another large seed hit the old one-minute client deadline under that pressure; it is retained as a failed setup, not a request sample or data-plane speedup.
The large apparent before/after timing swings in those resource trials are not credible application improvements: the supposedly isolated clusters share a physical disk. The driver now separates single-endpoint --capacity observations from uninstrumented paired performance gates, while reusing the same fixtures and loadgen. Capacity-only reports explicitly say no performance gate was evaluated. Cleanup records its duration, verifies actual reaper drain and has an explicit deadline. Request deadlines are configurable rather than silently retrying.
pgvs3_spool_peak_bytes adds exact reserved-payload high water since gateway startup. Sampled gateway gauge peaks remain lower bounds; cross-node WAL gaps include probe skew, and replay barrier times include SQL/polling overhead. WAL is whole isolated-cluster LSN advancement, including headers/padding, checkpoints and background work. Warm/cold describes gateway state, not cleared OS caches. See the full method.



Host: Ryzen 7 7700X, 16 threads, 61 GiB RAM; rootful Docker/overlayfs on the local host. Primaries use 1 GiB shared buffers, pool 32 and a 4 GiB WAL target; physical standbys use 1 GiB shared buffers and hot_standby_feedback=on. The target is a single PostgreSQL data plane, not disk isolation from other processes.
The ledger covers 60 size/path cohorts with three observations per candidate: native GET/range/PUT/overwrite, warm-origin equivalents and cold whole/range fills for six inputs. Eighteen completed native cohorts were retained from the first partial run; four large-write cohorts completed separately, and the remaining 38 use the explicit single-endpoint capacity mode. Their timing values are observations, not evidence that the application became faster.

The uninstrumented comparisons cover 56 paths, workers 1/4, both fixture types, native/warm/cold origin reads, metadata/ranges and native/write-back PUTs. There are 396 raw sample runs, including all six failed original cases. Every selected path has a passing qualified comparison within the 20% budget; the largest accepted p50 increase is 18.6%, and the largest rate reduction is 15.6%. No request errors were accepted as samples.
This is not a claim that the first sweep passed:

A seven-request native 100 MiB PUT trial missed p50 while its median rate differed by only 3%. Five paired 15-request repetitions on a fresh fixture passed (230.476 → 226.180 ms). The original tail-heavy runs remain retained.
Three origin 100 MiB PUT cases failed in the accumulated write/churn sweep. Five paired bounded cohorts with checkpoint preparation passed independently; their timings were not averaged into the originals.
The cold binary 100 MiB range/four-reader case followed a disk-heavy whole-fill cohort and failed. A fresh five-pair, 100-request cold-range comparison passed (9.433 → 9.411 ms). Its original samples are also retained.
A 1 GiB Parquet origin PUT failed in the retained-data comparison. Explicit PUT isolation drains/verifies/deletes the sample and resets only the empty owned cache between repetitions. Five pairs passed (3,149.927 → 3,160.448 ms). This qualifies the publication-ACK path, not sustained origin throughput.

The source store/COPY/read queries and layout are unchanged. The measured runtime changes are idle origin-registry refresh and spool-reservation telemetry. Large favorable swings under storage pressure are not presented as improvements. The measurement archive retains original failures, per-case followups, actual inputs/configuration and binary hashes.



The complete just ci passed: formatting/modernizer/import/tidy/vet/staticcheck and vulnerability checks; race-enabled Go tests; 11 standard-library Python tooling tests; uncached race integration (44 s); four fuzz targets; Helm lint and kind (76 s); contract including the maintained analytical scenario (28 s); the expanded physical-replica/fault/restore gate (92 s); interop including restic (16 s); and s3t (17 s including setup). ShellCheck and local documentation links were checked separately. Failure artifacts include the evidence JSON.



These are PostgreSQL 18.6/DuckDB 2.0.0 loopback fixtures, not AWS/Aurora results. The resource origin is a filesystem fixture; the analytical/fault scenarios use the S3 driver against an independent gateway. Neither substitutes for a remote service’s latency, TLS/authentication, cost or durability validation.
The promotion test explicitly fences the old fleet; arbitrary partitions and ambiguous in-flight origin mutations still need operational reconciliation. Physical backup/PITR tooling, production tails, large sustained working sets and co-location interference remain deployment-specific proof obligations. A 32 TiB relation ceiling is not a measured production dataset size.

title: Differential evaluation and S3 burst admission
text:
Date: 2026-10-31. PostgreSQL 18.6, DuckDB 2.0.0, layout v25.
Keep DuckLake and the existing storage roles as the default. Differential is now an opt-in, pinned comparison in the standard setup. Small native DDL can be cheaper, but that does not establish a universally better PostgreSQL-backed DuckDB configuration. In particular, the release’s synchronous-WAL bulk limit and writer-fencing boundary prevent a blanket replacement recommendation.
The accompanying S3 admission fix is independent: short request bursts now queue within bounds instead of immediately triggering client retry backoff.


See differential.md for provisioning, exact contracts and the measurement method. Inputs are deterministic Snappy Parquet, approximately 10 MiB, 100 MiB and 1 GiB. The three profiles are:

DuckLake’s PostgreSQL catalog plus native pgvs3 object bytes, with data inlining disabled.
Differential ordinary statements plus synchronous snapshot export before the measured remote acknowledgement.
Differential SHIP_WAL 'sync', with separately timed snapshot visibility.

These compare remote durability under the stated single-writer/primary policy, not identical reader-refresh semantics. A plain Differential head reader sees the last exported snapshot, not every shipped commit. Fresh-reader results include attachment, schema discovery and first query; process/extension setup is separate. Warm repeats can use native DuckDB buffers and must not be called shared-cache or PostgreSQL speedups.
The final matrix completed 24 cohorts: three repetitions of every profile at 10/100 MiB, and of DuckLake/snapshot export at 1 GiB. title: Publish analytical snapshots, not repeated OLTP scans
text:
Guide index · Before: demo source tables · Next: cache
Goal: extract a deliberate source snapshot once, then run repeated scans on Parquet/DuckLake with a measured freshness budget. PostgreSQL remains the OLTP system; DuckDB executes the analytical SQL; pgvs3 stores or caches the object bytes. This is application-managed materialization, not built-in CDC. Research basis.



DuckLake Fixed Hash Buckets, 24-Bit Hierarchical Hilbert Curve and Density-Adaptive Row Groups







Need
Choice
Cost or limit not to overlook




Portable immutable extracts; simplest publication
Parquet + application manifest
You own refresh, schema evolution, deletes and manifest/reader retention.


Catalog snapshots, table DDL and multi-file lifecycle
DuckLake + PostgreSQL catalog + pgvs3
Catalog/object commits are separate; maintain files, snapshots and PostgreSQL.


Experiment with native DuckDB small commits
Differential
Local repository, external writer fencing and a retained large sync-WAL failure. Not the default.


Native format over SlateDB
ObjFS
Extra memory, write/retention costs and SQL read-only clients that still PUT retention checkpoints. Not a standby endpoint client.



Choose native objects or origin-backed staging independently of the file format. Object cache hits reduce remote I/O, not decoding, joins or aggregation. For repeated join-heavy queries, a local DuckDB materialization can help, but its refresh, extra storage, RSS and restart/recovery are separate costs; pgvs3 does not manage that accelerator.
The locally qualified DuckLake workflow is one coordinated writer per dataset prefix/catalog and many readers. That is not an upstream single-writer limit: DuckLake’s PostgreSQL catalog supports multi-client concurrency with conflict handling. Concurrent-writer/failover policies need their own qualification; a shared bucket is neither a global writer lock nor a transaction coordinator.



Prerequisites: DuckDB 2.0.0, httpfs/postgres extensions, the disposable guide_app.orders fixture and the quick-start gateway. Create a fresh native bucket with curl -fsS -X PUT "$PGVS3_ENDPOINT/guide-analytics". Use a source read-only role in real deployments; the local credentials below are demo-only.
In a new DuckDB session (the test substitutes only host/port/database):

INSTALL httpfs; LOAD httpfs;
INSTALL postgres; LOAD postgres;
CREATE SECRET (TYPE s3, KEY_ID 'test', SECRET 'test', REGION 'us-east-1',
    ENDPOINT '127.0.0.1:8014', URL_STYLE 'path', USE_SSL false);
CREATE SECRET (TYPE POSTGRES, HOST '127.0.0.1', PORT 5432,
    DATABASE 'pgvs3_bench', USER 'postgres', PASSWORD 'postgres');
SET threads = 4;
SET memory_limit = '1GB';
SET pg_pool_max_connections = 4;
SET pg_statement_timeout_millis = 30000;
ATTACH '' AS source (TYPE postgres, READ_ONLY, SCHEMA 'guide_app',
    ISOLATION_LEVEL 'REPEATABLE READ');
The bounded client settings illustrate syntax, not optimal throughput. Configure a local disk temp_directory and its capacity for larger-than-memory operators. The PostgreSQL scanner’s connections count separately from pgvs3’s pools. Use temporary DuckDB secrets or your deployment’s secret injection; do not put production passwords in URLs, SQL transcripts or persistent secret files.

BEGIN;
COPY (
    SELECT id, customer_id, created_at, amount_cents, payload
    FROM source.guide_app.orders
    ORDER BY id
) TO 's3://guide-analytics/orders/snapshot-v1.parquet'
  (FORMAT PARQUET, COMPRESSION ZSTD, ROW_GROUP_SIZE 122880);
COMMIT;
Use a new immutable key per generation. REPEATABLE READ keeps source reads inside this extraction transaction consistent, but a long snapshot can retain old PostgreSQL tuples. Bound duration and refresh concurrency. Close/commit promptly; do not keep the source transaction open while dashboards query files. An S3 publication is not rolled back by a later DuckDB/source transaction error. Failed exports can leave unpublished files: retain them for investigation, then clean them only after the reader/publication safety window.



In a fresh DuckDB client pointing at gateway B/the read service, run:

SELECT count(*) AS rows, sum(id) AS id_sum, sum(amount_cents) AS cents
FROM read_parquet('s3://guide-analytics/orders/snapshot-v1.parquet');
Expected: 1000000 | 499999500000 | 4999500000. Also validate schema, business invariants and projected string columns; a metadata-only count(*) is not proof that every data page is readable. The guide test hashes the transferred body and checks the payload length sum (32000000) with client caches disabled.
Only after validation, publish a small discovery object. This example is for a native pgvs3 bucket and creates the pointer only if absent:

curl -fsS -X PUT "$PGVS3_ENDPOINT/guide-analytics/current.json" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -H 'If-None-Match: *' \
  --data-binary '{"generation":"v1","files":["orders/snapshot-v1.parquet"],"rows":1000000,"id_sum":499999500000}'
Expected: 200; another create returns 412, not a silent overwrite. Readers read one manifest generation and pin its listed keys for the query. Advance a pointer with the previous quoted ETag in If-Match; on 412, reread and reconcile instead of blindly retrying. Never remove files used by retained manifests or active readers. A production manifest should also record schema version, source snapshot/window, completion time, integrity checks and freshness.
Objects and pointer are separate publications, not a multi-key transaction. With an origin-backed bucket, a new object can still be pending in PostgreSQL when a synchronous pointer reaches the origin. Do not expose that pointer to origin-only readers until all referenced bodies are verified at the origin. Monitor outbox drain or use synchronous staging for that delivery contract.











Stage
Record
Failure policy




Source extraction
Snapshot/window and source version/watermark
Fail the generation, retain previous known-good manifest.


Publication
Validated file set and pointer generation
Reconcile ambiguous PUTs by key/validator; never advertise partial data.


Origin staging
Pending bytes/oldest age, remote validation
Alert on drain lag; preserve PostgreSQL-only bodies.


Query serving
Manifest/catalog generation, replica lag, result-cache age if any
Reject too-old data or explicitly serve labeled stale data; do not silently query OLTP on every miss.



These delays can stack. A five-minute refresh plus cache/result TTL and replica lag is not a five-minute freshness guarantee. A failed refresh has no finite bound unless you detect it and enforce a maximum served age. Test updates, deletes, late commits, clock skew and schema changes before incremental refresh. max(id) or max(updated_at) alone can miss late-committing rows; overlap alone does not solve deletes. For continuous source mutations use a separately operated CDC pipeline with replica identity, keys, deduplication, deletes and slot/WAL retention designed explicitly. pgvs3 supplies none of that automatically.



In a separate DuckDB session, create the same temporary S3 secret first. This uses the quick-start ducklake_catalog database, not the application one. The following is a syntax-validated candidate, not a measured winning preset:

INSTALL ducklake; INSTALL postgres; LOAD ducklake; LOAD postgres;
CREATE SECRET (TYPE POSTGRES, HOST '127.0.0.1', PORT 5432,
    DATABASE 'ducklake_catalog', USER 'postgres', PASSWORD 'postgres');
ATTACH 'ducklake:postgres:' AS lake
    (DATA_PATH 's3://guide-analytics/ducklake/', METADATA_SCHEMA 'guide_lake');
CALL lake.set_option('parquet_compression', 'zstd');
CALL lake.set_option('parquet_row_group_size', 122880);
CALL lake.set_option('target_file_size', '256MB');
CALL lake.set_option('data_inlining_row_limit', 10);
CREATE TABLE lake.orders AS
    SELECT * FROM read_parquet('s3://guide-analytics/orders/snapshot-v1.parquet');
FROM lake.options();
Compare projected full scans and selective filters at 10/100/1,024 MiB with just bench tuning. Row groups are rows, file targets are bytes; neither is a hard exact physical file size. Larger groups improve scan/compression efficiency; smaller ones can improve pruning but cost metadata/requests. Sorting by useful filters matters more than blindly choosing 8,192-row groups. DuckDB 2.0 Parquet uses async I/O: inspect async_threads, read-ahead and HTTP pool capacity as well as execution threads; keep aggregate client pressure within gateway admission.
Inlining is another choice, not an invisible benchmark advantage:

CREATE TABLE lake.inline_probe (i INTEGER);
INSERT INTO lake.inline_probe VALUES (42);
SELECT * FROM lake.inline_probe;
CALL ducklake_flush_inlined_data('lake', table_name => 'inline_probe');
Expected: 42 before and after flushing. The tiny insert initially lives in the catalog, not an object; flushing creates a Parquet file. Benchmark pure object writes with inlining disabled and label that choice. Retain it when it helps your actual small-commit workload. Persistent set_option settings affect future writes; undo by restoring the saved scoped values, not merely RESETting an unrelated session option.



When scaling DuckLake and Parquet on pgvs3 to billion-row collections, wide columns, spatiotemporal relations, or batch-write / fast-read workloads, physical layout determines whether queries scan kilobytes or terabytes.



Use the narrowest native types (BIGINT, INTEGER, SMALLINT, TIMESTAMPTZ, DOUBLE): Never store numeric IDs or timestamps as VARCHAR. DuckDB bitpacks integers on disk, but in-memory execution vectors, hash tables and sort buffers allocate according to the declared SQL type. Narrow types cut RAM, spill I/O and join CPU.
Prefer ordered integers, timestamps or UUIDv7 over random UUIDv4: DuckDB and DuckLake rely on file- and row-group-level zone maps (min/max bounds). Random UUIDv4 values span [0000…, ffff…] in every row group, making zone-map pruning useless. Monotonic integers or timestamps (or UUIDv7 paired with a timestamp filter) keep row-group bounds disjoint.
Encode low-cardinality strings as ENUM or integer-keyed dimension tables: Parquet dictionary-encodes strings on disk, but repeated joins and GROUP BY on integer keys execute faster and use less hash memory.
Omit PRIMARY KEY / UNIQUE constraints on analytical tables: In native DuckDB tables, constraints build ART indexes that slow bulk loads by 2–4×, consume non-evictable buffer memory, and are not used by joins or aggregations. Enforce uniqueness in the OLTP source or batch deduplication step instead.












Bottleneck on wide tables
Mechanism
Concrete fix




Row-group memory explosion
parquet_row_group_size defaults to 122880 rows. At 8 KiB/row across wide columns, one row group is ~960 MiB uncompressed in writer RAM.
Set parquet_row_group_size_bytes (e.g. '32MB' to '128MB') or reduce parquet_row_group_size (e.g. 16384–32768) on wide tables.


PostgreSQL catalog bloat
DuckLake records per-file, per-column min/max stats in ducklake_file_column_stats. Hundreds of wide VARCHAR/JSON/blob columns across thousands of files bloat the catalog.
Call lake.set_option('skip_stats_columns', ['wide_col', ...], table_name => '...') so min/max bounds are only stored for filter/join columns.


Unnecessary byte transfers
SELECT * fetches and decompresses every column chunk in matching row groups.
Project only required columns. For top-K or selective lookups needing wide payloads, filter/rank on narrow keys first, then join back by key (late materialization).


Compaction rewrite cost
Updating or compacting a table rewrites wide blobs alongside narrow metrics.
Split immutable multi-KiB/MiB blobs into a companion table (joined by id) or store large blobs as direct pgvs3 objects referenced by key/ETag.






Time-growing partitions (year/month/day) add operational friction: partition counts grow without bound over multi-year histories, backfills across years scatter thousands of small files, and PostgreSQL OLTP tables need cron jobs to pre-create future partitions. For most collections, 32 to 64 fixed partitions paired with SORTED BY handle two to three orders of magnitude of growth (e.g., 10 MiB to 10 GiB per partition, or 640 MiB to 640 GiB total) with zero ongoing partition maintenance:

How a fixed partition count scales across orders of magnitude: When a fixed partition is small (e.g., 10 MiB), ducklake_merge_adjacent_files compacts it into one sorted Parquet file. When the table grows 100× (e.g., 1 GiB per partition), DuckLake automatically splits that partition into multiple sorted target_file_size (256MB–512MB) files with non-overlapping min/max zone maps on the SORTED BY keys. You get file-level and row-group-level pruning on time and space without ever adding new partition keys.
Strategy A — Fixed 32–64 Hash Buckets (bucket(32, id) + SORTED BY (ts, id)): Use when queries filter by tenant_id, customer_id, device_id or id:
CREATE TABLE lake.events_by_customer (
    customer_id INTEGER, id BIGINT, ts TIMESTAMPTZ, amount_cents INTEGER
)
PARTITIONED BY (bucket(32, customer_id))
SORTED BY (ts, id);
DuckLake hashes customer_id into 32 fixed Murmur3 buckets (0..31). Equality and IN filters on customer_id prune 31/32 of the partitions immediately, and SORTED BY (ts, id) prunes files and row groups by time within each bucket.
Strategy B — High-Resolution 2D Hilbert / Morton SORTED BY (curve_id, ts) (Density-Adaptive Spatial Pruning): What happens when spatial density is heavily skewed (e.g., 90% of points in NYC/Tokyo and 10% across oceans/rural areas)?

The equal-area partition trap: If you partition by 64 equal-area coarse grid cells (PARTITIONED BY (coarse_cell)), 1 urban partition gets 90% of all bytes while 50 sparse partitions create tiny <1 MiB files on every insert. And if your spatial key is too coarse (e.g. \(64 \times 64\)), millions of urban rows share the exact same cell ID and cannot prune inside the city.
Why high-resolution SORTED BY (curve_id, ts) is automatically density-adaptive: Map coordinates to a high-resolution 1D space-filling integer—such as a 32-bit or 64-bit Hilbert or Morton (Z-order) key across a \(65,536 \times 65,536\) (\(4.3 \times 10^9\)-cell) grid—and use SORTED BY (curve_id, ts) without equal-area spatial PARTITIONED BY. Because Parquet row groups (122,880 rows or parquet_row_group_size_bytes) and DuckLake files (target_file_size = '256MB') slice the sorted stream by row/byte count (empirical quantiles) rather than geographic area:

Sparse rural/ocean regions automatically pack into one row group/file (zero tiny-file waste).
Dense urban hotspots automatically split into many row groups and files, each covering a tiny neighborhood with razor-sharp min(lat)..max(lat) and min(lon)..max(lon) zone maps!

When you also want 32–64 fixed PARTITIONED BY buckets on skewed spatial data: Either partition by an orthogonal entity key (PARTITIONED BY (bucket(32, tenant_id))

SORTED BY (curve_id, ts)), or partition curve_id by empirical quantiles (31 or 63 cutpoints from quantile_disc(curve_id, ...)) so every bucket holds \(\approx 1/32\) or \(1/64\) of the rows.


When to still use time partitions (epoch_day / epoch_month): Only when your dominant operation is dropping whole expired time windows by partition or strictly isolating each day’s ingest files from older history.




When you can batch writes (minutes/hours) to maximize read speed:

Ingest in batches and sort + compress heavily: Accumulate batches rather than committing tiny files. Either insert pre-sorted batches (SORTED BY (...) with parquet_compression = 'zstd' and parquet_compression_level = 9 to 19), or set sort_on_insert = false during fast micro-batch ingest and let the batch compaction step sort the merged output.

Run this executable skewed-hotspot 24-bit hierarchical Hilbert sort + fixed-32 hash + wide-column + batch-compaction recipe in the same DuckLake session:

CREATE MACRO lake.hilbert64(rx, ry) AS (
    list_extract([
         0,  1, 14, 15, 16, 19, 20, 21,
         3,  2, 13, 12, 17, 18, 23, 22,
         4,  7,  8, 11, 30, 29, 24, 25,
         5,  6,  9, 10, 31, 28, 27, 26,
        58, 57, 54, 53, 32, 35, 36, 37,
        59, 56, 55, 52, 33, 34, 39, 38,
        60, 61, 50, 51, 46, 45, 40, 41,
        63, 62, 49, 48, 47, 44, 43, 42
    ], ((rx::INTEGER & 7) * 8 + (ry::INTEGER & 7)) + 1)::BIGINT
);

CREATE TABLE lake.spatiotemporal (
    id BIGINT,
    customer_id INTEGER,
    ts TIMESTAMPTZ,
    lat DOUBLE,
    lon DOUBLE,
    hilbert_id BIGINT,
    wide_payload VARCHAR
)
SORTED BY (hilbert_id, ts);

CALL lake.set_option('skip_stats_columns', ['wide_payload'], table_name => 'spatiotemporal');
CALL lake.set_option('parquet_row_group_size_bytes', '1MB', table_name => 'spatiotemporal');
CALL lake.set_option('parquet_compression', 'zstd', table_name => 'spatiotemporal');
CALL lake.set_option('parquet_compression_level', 9, table_name => 'spatiotemporal');

INSERT INTO lake.spatiotemporal
WITH grid AS (
    SELECT i AS id, (i % 500)::INTEGER AS customer_id,
           TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-10-01 00:00:00+00' + i * INTERVAL '1 minute' AS ts,
           CASE WHEN i % 10 < 9 THEN 40.70 + (i % 1000) * 0.0001 ELSE 25.0 + (i % 10000) * 0.0025 END AS lat,
           CASE WHEN i % 10 < 9 THEN -74.02 + ((i // 1000) % 100) * 0.0001 ELSE -125.0 + ((i // 1000) % 100) * 0.055 END AS lon,
           repeat(md5(i::VARCHAR), 8) AS wide_payload
    FROM range(20000) AS t(i)
),
quantized AS (
    SELECT *,
           ((lat - 25.0) / 25.0 * 4095)::INTEGER AS gx,
           ((lon + 125.0) / 55.0 * 4095)::INTEGER AS gy
    FROM grid
)
SELECT id, customer_id, ts, lat, lon,
       (lake.hilbert64(gx >> 9, gy >> 9) << 18)
       | (lake.hilbert64(gx >> 6, gy >> 6) << 12)
       | (lake.hilbert64(gx >> 3, gy >> 3) << 6)
       | lake.hilbert64(gx, gy) AS hilbert_id,
       wide_payload
FROM quantized;

INSERT INTO lake.spatiotemporal
WITH grid AS (
    SELECT i + 20000 AS id, (i % 500)::INTEGER AS customer_id,
           TIMESTAMPTZ '2027-03-01 00:00:00+00' + i * INTERVAL '1 minute' AS ts,
           CASE WHEN i % 10 < 9 THEN 40.70 + (i % 1000) * 0.0001 ELSE 25.0 + (i % 10000) * 0.0025 END AS lat,
           CASE WHEN i % 10 < 9 THEN -74.02 + ((i // 1000) % 100) * 0.0001 ELSE -125.0 + ((i // 1000) % 100) * 0.055 END AS lon,
           repeat(md5((i + 20000)::VARCHAR), 8) AS wide_payload
    FROM range(20000) AS t(i)
),
quantized AS (
    SELECT *,
           ((lat - 25.0) / 25.0 * 4095)::INTEGER AS gx,
           ((lon + 125.0) / 55.0 * 4095)::INTEGER AS gy
    FROM grid
)
SELECT id, customer_id, ts, lat, lon,
       (lake.hilbert64(gx >> 9, gy >> 9) << 18)
       | (lake.hilbert64(gx >> 6, gy >> 6) << 12)
       | (lake.hilbert64(gx >> 3, gy >> 3) << 6)
       | lake.hilbert64(gx, gy) AS hilbert_id,
       wide_payload
FROM quantized;

CALL ducklake_merge_adjacent_files('lake', 'spatiotemporal');
DELETE FROM lake.spatiotemporal WHERE id < 4000;
CALL ducklake_rewrite_data_files('lake', 'spatiotemporal', delete_threshold => 0.05);

CREATE TABLE lake.events_hash32 (
    customer_id INTEGER, id BIGINT, ts TIMESTAMPTZ
)
PARTITIONED BY (bucket(32, customer_id))
SORTED BY (ts, id);

INSERT INTO lake.events_hash32
SELECT customer_id, id, ts FROM lake.spatiotemporal;

WITH matched AS (
    SELECT id, hilbert_id
    FROM lake.spatiotemporal
    WHERE (hilbert_id >> 18) = lake.hilbert64(5, 7)
      AND lat BETWEEN 40.7100 AND 40.7199
      AND lon BETWEEN -74.0200 AND -74.0100
      AND ts >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-10-01 00:00:00+00'
)
SELECT count(*) AS rows,
       max(length(s.wide_payload)) AS payload_bytes,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM lake.events_hash32 WHERE customer_id = 42) AS customer_rows
FROM matched AS m
JOIN lake.spatiotemporal AS s USING (id);
Expected: 3240 | 256 | 72. Even though 90% of the 40,000 rows are concentrated inside a tiny 0.10° × 0.01° NYC hotspot across 2026 and 2027, sorting by the 24-bit hierarchical hilbert_id (4 levels of lake.hilbert64 across a \(4,096 \times 4,096 = 16.7\text{M}\)-cell grid) subdivides the dense hotspot into tight 1 MB row groups without creating empty ocean files, merges the two batches into one sorted ZSTD file, rewrites the deleted slice, suppresses min_value/max_value catalog stats on wide_payload, and verifies the 32-bucket hash table (72 rows).
DuckLake maintenance (merge/rewrite, expire snapshots, clean old/orphan files), pgvs3 reaping and PostgreSQL vacuum are three distinct stages. DROP TABLE is not remote space reclamation. Use the installed extension’s maintenance reference and a retention window longer than active readers/writers and recovery needs; zero-age cleanup examples from benchmarks are not a production policy. Coordinate catalog, data database and any external origin backups.




just guides executes these snippets, reopens the catalog through another gateway, demonstrates inlining/flush and proves a later source change does not update the existing extract. Recorded scope. For tuning acceptance use the paired runner, not these functional timings. Keep the demo data for jobs, then use owned-data cleanup.

title: Publish analytical snapshots, not repeated OLTP scans
text:
Need
Choice
Cost or limit not to overlook




Portable immutable extracts; simplest publication
Parquet + application manifest
You own refresh, schema evolution, deletes and manifest/reader retention.


Catalog snapshots, table DDL and multi-file lifecycle
DuckLake + PostgreSQL catalog + pgvs3
Catalog/object commits are separate; maintain files, snapshots and PostgreSQL.


Experiment with native DuckDB small commits
Differential
Local repository, external writer fencing and a retained large sync-WAL failure. Not the default.


Native format over SlateDB
ObjFS
Extra memory, write/retention costs and SQL read-only clients that still PUT retention checkpoints. Not a standby endpoint client.



Choose native objects or origin-backed staging independently of the file format. Object cache hits reduce remote I/O, not decoding, joins or aggregation. For repeated join-heavy queries, a local DuckDB materialization can help, but its refresh, extra storage, RSS and restart/recovery are separate costs; pgvs3 does not manage that accelerator.
The locally qualified DuckLake workflow is one coordinated writer per dataset prefix/catalog and many readers. That is not an upstream single-writer limit: DuckLake’s PostgreSQL catalog supports multi-client concurrency with conflict handling. Concurrent-writer/failover policies need their own qualification; a shared bucket is neither a global writer lock nor a transaction coordinator.

title: Publish analytical snapshots, not repeated OLTP scans
Publish analytical snapshots, not repeated OLTP scans
text:
In a fresh DuckDB client pointing at gateway B/the read service, run:

SELECT count(*) AS rows, sum(id) AS id_sum, sum(amount_cents) AS cents
FROM read_parquet('s3://guide-analytics/orders/snapshot-v1.parquet');
Expected: 1000000 | 499999500000 | 4999500000. Also validate schema, business invariants and projected string columns; a metadata-only count(*) is not proof that every data page is readable. The guide test hashes the transferred body and checks the payload length sum (32000000) with client caches disabled.
Only after validation, publish a small discovery object. This example is for a native pgvs3 bucket and creates the pointer only if absent:

curl -fsS -X PUT "$PGVS3_ENDPOINT/guide-analytics/current.json" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -H 'If-None-Match: *' \
  --data-binary '{"generation":"v1","files":["orders/snapshot-v1.parquet"],"rows":1000000,"id_sum":499999500000}'
Expected: 200; another create returns 412, not a silent overwrite. Readers read one manifest generation and pin its listed keys for the query. Advance a pointer with the previous quoted ETag in If-Match; on 412, reread and reconcile instead of blindly retrying. Never remove files used by retained manifests or active readers. A production manifest should also record schema version, source snapshot/window, completion time, integrity checks and freshness.
Objects and pointer are separate publications, not a multi-key transaction. With an origin-backed bucket, a new object can still be pending in PostgreSQL when a synchronous pointer reaches the origin. Do not expose that pointer to origin-only readers until all referenced bodies are verified at the origin. Monitor outbox drain or use synchronous staging for that delivery contract.

title: Publish analytical snapshots, not repeated OLTP scans
text:
Stage
Record
Failure policy




Source extraction
Snapshot/window and source version/watermark
Fail the generation, retain previous known-good manifest.


Publication
Validated file set and pointer generation
Reconcile ambiguous PUTs by key/validator; never advertise partial data.


Origin staging
Pending bytes/oldest age, remote validation
Alert on drain lag; preserve PostgreSQL-only bodies.


Query serving
Manifest/catalog generation, replica lag, result-cache age if any
Reject too-old data or explicitly serve labeled stale data; do not silently query OLTP on every miss.



These delays can stack. A five-minute refresh plus cache/result TTL and replica lag is not a five-minute freshness guarantee. A failed refresh has no finite bound unless you detect it and enforce a maximum served age. Test updates, deletes, late commits, clock skew and schema changes before incremental refresh. max(id) or max(updated_at) alone can miss late-committing rows; overlap alone does not solve deletes. For continuous source mutations use a separately operated CDC pipeline with replica identity, keys, deduplication, deletes and slot/WAL retention designed explicitly. pgvs3 supplies none of that automatically.

       (lake.hilbert64(gx >> 9, gy >> 9) << 18)
       | (lake.hilbert64(gx >> 6, gy >> 6) << 12)
       | (lake.hilbert64(gx >> 3, gy >> 3) << 6)
       | lake.hilbert64(gx, gy) AS hilbert_id,
       wide_payload
FROM quantized;

INSERT INTO lake.spatiotemporal
WITH grid AS (
    SELECT i + 20000 AS id, (i % 500)::INTEGER AS customer_id,
           TIMESTAMPTZ '2027-03-01 00:00:00+00' + i * INTERVAL '1 minute' AS ts,
           CASE WHEN i % 10 < 9 THEN 40.70 + (i % 1000) * 0.0001 ELSE 25.0 + (i % 10000) * 0.0025 END AS lat,
           CASE WHEN i % 10 < 9 THEN -74.02 + ((i // 1000) % 100) * 0.0001 ELSE -125.0 + ((i // 1000) % 100) * 0.055 END AS lon,
           repeat(md5((i + 20000)::VARCHAR), 8) AS wide_payload
    FROM range(20000) AS t(i)
),
quantized AS (
    SELECT *,
           ((lat - 25.0) / 25.0 * 4095)::INTEGER AS gx,
           ((lon + 125.0) / 55.0 * 4095)::INTEGER AS gy
    FROM grid
)
SELECT id, customer_id, ts, lat, lon,
       (lake.hilbert64(gx >> 9, gy >> 9) << 18)
       | (lake.hilbert64(gx >> 6, gy >> 6) << 12)
       | (lake.hilbert64(gx >> 3, gy >> 3) << 6)
       | lake.hilbert64(gx, gy) AS hilbert_id,
       wide_payload
FROM quantized;

CALL ducklake_merge_adjacent_files('lake', 'spatiotemporal');
DELETE FROM lake.spatiotemporal WHERE id < 4000;
CALL ducklake_rewrite_data_files('lake', 'spatiotemporal', delete_threshold => 0.05);

CREATE TABLE lake.events_hash32 (
    customer_id INTEGER, id BIGINT, ts TIMESTAMPTZ
)
PARTITIONED BY (bucket(32, customer_id))
SORTED BY (ts, id);

INSERT INTO lake.events_hash32
SELECT customer_id, id, ts FROM lake.spatiotemporal;

WITH matched AS (
    SELECT id, hilbert_id
    FROM lake.spatiotemporal
    WHERE (hilbert_id >> 18) = lake.hilbert64(5, 7)
      AND lat BETWEEN 40.7100 AND 40.7199
      AND lon BETWEEN -74.0200 AND -74.0100
      AND ts >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-10-01 00:00:00+00'
)
SELECT count(*) AS rows,
       max(length(s.wide_payload)) AS payload_bytes,
       (SELECT count(*) FROM lake.events_hash32 WHERE customer_id = 42) AS customer_rows
FROM matched AS m
JOIN lake.spatiotemporal AS s USING (id);
Expected: 3240 | 256 | 72. Even though 90% of the 40,000 rows are concentrated inside a tiny 0.10° × 0.01° NYC hotspot across 2026 and 2027, sorting by the 24-bit hierarchical hilbert_id (4 levels of lake.hilbert64 across a \(4,096 \times 4,096 = 16.7\text{M}\)-cell grid) subdivides the dense hotspot into tight 1 MB row groups without creating empty ocean files, merges the two batches into one sorted ZSTD file, rewrites the deleted slice, suppresses min_value/max_value catalog stats on wide_payload, and verifies the 32-bucket hash table (72 rows).
DuckLake maintenance (merge/rewrite, expire snapshots, clean old/orphan files), pgvs3 reaping and PostgreSQL vacuum are three distinct stages. DROP TABLE is not remote space reclamation. Use the installed extension’s maintenance reference and a retention window longer than active readers/writers and recovery needs; zero-age cleanup examples from benchmarks are not a production policy. Coordinate catalog, data database and any external origin backups.

title: Publish analytical snapshots, not repeated OLTP scans
text: just guides executes these snippets, reopens the catalog through another gateway, demonstrates inlining/flush and proves a later source change does not update the existing extract. Recorded scope. For tuning acceptance use the paired runner, not these functional timings. Keep the demo data for jobs, then use owned-data cleanup.

title: Workload guides
text:
Keep OLTP in PostgreSQL SQL. Use pgvs3 for object bytes, shared object caching, durable origin staging and bounded companion queues. It does not make arbitrary application SQL faster, implement CDC or turn PostgreSQL into a distributed columnar engine. Start with the path that removes your bottleneck, not with every interface enabled.



pgvs3 Data-Plane Architecture and Authority Flow




What is the primary access and mutation contract?
├── Point reads/writes, strict ACID constraints, <10 ms OLTP p99
│   └── Keep in PostgreSQL SQL (docs/guides/postgres.md)
│       ├── Wide columns (>2 KiB TOAST / blobs)?
│       │   └── Split hot narrow row from cold payload table, or store multi-MiB blobs in pgvs3
│       ├── Need 32–64 zero-maintenance partitions across 10M–1B+ rows?
│       │   └── Fixed HASH(id/tenant_id), or 32–64 quantile RANGE bounds on 1D Hilbert/Morton curve_id (avoids hotspot skew)
│       └── Only use time RANGE partitions if you must DROP/DETACH whole expired months
├── Analytical scans, aggregations, or billion-row history (minutes-to-hours freshness)
│   └── Extract to Parquet / DuckLake on pgvs3 (docs/guides/analytics.md)
│       ├── Single-table/snapshot export? ──► Immutable Parquet + conditional manifest
│       ├── Entity / tenant / ID filters? ──► Fixed PARTITIONED BY (bucket(32..64, id)) + SORTED BY (ts, id)
│       ├── 2D/spatiotemporal filters (including skewed hotspots)?
│       │   └── High-res 32/64-bit Hilbert/Morton SORTED BY (curve_id, ts) (row groups & target_file_size auto-split dense hotspots by row/byte quantiles!)
│       ├── Billion rows + wide columns? ──► Byte-bounded row groups, skip_stats_columns, late materialization
│       └── Willing to pay slow/batch writes for peak read speed?
│           └── Batch sorted ZSTD writes + merge/rewrite compaction (or sealed ObjFS/DuckDB for heavy joins)
├── Shared S3/HTTP acceleration or durable write-back staging across workers
│   └── Origin-backed pgvs3 cache/stage (docs/guides/cache.md)
└── Asynchronous background work or fan-out from committed SQL changes
    └── Application SQL outbox + OJS jobs/streams (docs/guides/jobs.md)



I need to…
Start here
Success means




Protect transaction latency while adding analytics/cache/jobs
Protect OLTP
Measured application tails, connection waits, WAL and vacuum remain inside your budget.


Model schemas, wide columns, spatiotemporal partitions or batch-for-read DuckLake
Publish analytical snapshots
Tight file/row-group pruning, bounded writer RAM and catalog stats, and explicit freshness/compaction cost.


Reuse S3/HTTP bytes across clients and gateways
Cache and staging
Another gateway serves the same bytes without an origin fetch; TTL and pending-write authority are understood.


Reliably hand committed application work to HTTP workers
Jobs, outboxes and streams
Rollbacks enqueue nothing; retries and worker crashes do not duplicate the demonstrated SQL effect.


Diagnose latency, capacity or recovery trouble
Observe and recover
Identify the constrained resource, preserve acknowledged data and verify recovery before routing traffic.



For setup use the quick start. For flags/API and topology details use operations, not a copied deployment preset. Sources records the research behind these decisions; validation separates executable evidence from deployment advice.



Every optimization moves cost between four hardware budgets. Name which resource you are spending and which one you are saving before changing a schema or knob:










Design choice
Memory (RAM)
Disk & PostgreSQL WAL
Network / HTTP I/O
CPU




Restrictive types (BIGINT/INT/TIMESTAMPTZ vs VARCHAR/UUIDv4)
Shrinks DuckDB execution vectors and hash/sort state; avoids non-evictable ART index buffers when omitting PKs.
Smaller Parquet pages, smaller PG indexes, tighter zone maps.
Fewer bytes transferred per column chunk.
Faster vectorized comparisons, hashing and bit-unpacking.


Wide-column projection + late materialization + skip_stats_columns
Avoids buffering wide strings/blobs during filtering, grouping and sorting.
Keeps ducklake_file_column_stats small in the PG catalog; avoids TOAST churn.
Transfers only narrow filter/key column chunks; wide chunks fetched only for matched rows.
Skips ZSTD decompression and string decoding on unreferenced columns.


Byte-bounded row groups (parquet_row_group_size_bytes) on wide tables
Prevents 122,880 × wide_row from buffering hundreds of MiB per writer thread.
Slightly more row-group metadata headers; finer pruning granularity.
Smaller byte-range fetches for selective queries.
More row-group footer checks; lower spill risk.


Fixed 32–64 partitions (bucket(32..64, id) or 64-cell Hilbert prefix) + SORTED BY
Sorting/compaction buffers a batch in writer RAM (or spills to temp_directory); bounded catalog metadata.
Zero DDL cron maintenance; fixed bucket count prevents small-file explosions across years while target_file_size splits growing buckets cleanly.
Prunes to 1..k of 32–64 buckets, then skips non-overlapping row-group byte ranges on the sort key.
Pays sort CPU once on batch write/merge to save scan CPU on every read.


Batch write-for-read (SORTED BY, high zstd, merge/rewrite)
Higher batch writer/compactor RAM; lower reader buffer footprint.
Rewrites small/deleted files (extra PG WAL + reaper work during batch window); smaller steady-state footprint.
Minimum GET requests and byte transfer; zero delete-file merge-on-read fetches.
Heavy batch sort + ZSTD compression CPU; minimal query decompression/filter CPU.


pgvs3 shared origin cache (s3c_) & range caching
Uses PG shared_buffers + OS page cache (and gateway spool ≤8 MiB in RAM).
Cold fills write logged PG chunks rows and WAL; consumes vacuum/reap capacity.
Eliminates repeated upstream S3 GETs across gateways and standbys.
Zstd block check on fill; low CPU on warm PG bitmap heap scans.














Layer
Who computes/owns it?
Freshness and durability boundary




Application SQL rows
PostgreSQL/application
SQL transaction; indexes/plans matter. pgvs3 does not intercept these queries.


Native objects
pgvs3 + PostgreSQL
One object’s committed publication; logged bytes. No transaction spanning an application’s SQL and an HTTP PUT.


Shared origin-byte cache
pgvs3 s3c_ rows
TTL/version revalidation, not SQL-result invalidation. Fills write PostgreSQL WAL.


Pending origin writes
pgvs3 s3w_ + outbox
Acknowledged bytes may exist only in PostgreSQL until origin handoff. Not disposable or TTL-expiring.


Analytical materialization
DuckDB/DuckLake/application
Extract/catalog snapshot and its refresh schedule. pgvs3 transports bytes, not source-table changes.


Jobs / stream deliveries
OJS / application workers
Leases or acknowledged batches; effects and HTTP acknowledgements are separate commits. Expect redelivery.



DuckDB buffers, Parquet metadata caches and native-extension caches are client-private, not pgvs3 shared-cache hits. A SQL results cache is yet another layer: pgvs3 has no automatic one. If storing application results via RESP, the application must define keys, invalidation, TTL, stale serving and sensitive-data scope; co-location does not supply them.



Write down before changing settings:

Correct answer: source of record, allowed staleness, delete/update handling, idempotency key, RPO/RTO and which replica may serve the read.
Budget: application p95/p99 and error rate, object ACK latency and drain rate, refresh lag, queue age, disk/WAL/scratch headroom and connection ceiling.
Experiment: control and candidate, identical 10 MiB–1 GiB files/queries, cold/warm definitions, concurrent OLTP and retained failures. Change one axis.
Acceptance: report each affected path independently. The project’s 20% regression budget is not permission to breach a stricter application SLO. Roll back the setting or move the workload off-cluster if that SLO fails.

More gateways increase client handling capacity, not PostgreSQL CPU, WAL, disk or autovacuum isolation. Separate schemas, databases, roles and pools are ownership/admission boundaries, not resource reservations. Use another cluster or external analytical storage when a shared cluster cannot meet both budgets.



just setup
just guides
Requires Docker, the mise toolchain and access to the official DuckDB extension repository. This reuses the existing disposable two-gateway/origin harness, runs named snippets from these pages and retains guides.json, query plans and failure evidence under the printed .tmp/verify/guides.*/ directory. It creates only fixture-owned data; it is not a load test or cloud qualification.
For a manual walkthrough, start the quick-start gateway, use a disposable database, and have pgvs3, psql and curl on PATH plus a DuckDB 2.0 session. In the client terminal set:
export PGVS3_URL='postgres://postgres:postgres@127.0.0.1:5432/pgvs3_bench?sslmode=disable'
export PGVS3_ENDPOINT='http://127.0.0.1:8014'
Then follow PostgreSQL → analytics → jobs. These examples reserve guide_app, guide-analytics, guide-jobs and guide-events; stop if those names already contain your data. Recipe SQL mutations are to application-owned demo tables, not pgvs3 internals. The test alone advances one owned terminal job’s age to exercise normal retention without a day-long wait. Cache experiments use a separately owned test origin.

No public endpoint or tenant boundary. The listener never authenticates, authorizes or terminates TLS. Anyone who can reach it can read or destroy all namespaces. Keep it private; dummy S3 credentials are not access control.





Native versus origin-backed costs and replica proof.
Per-path benchmark acceptance and capacity capture.
DuckLake, Differential and ObjFS trade-offs.
Authority, acknowledgements and multi-worker invariants.

The quality bar here is inspectable: prerequisites, state ownership, runnable recipes, expected results, negative cases, measurement, recovery and safe cleanup. The named reference projects inform that bar; no unmeasured vendor-performance or universal-replacement claim is implied.

title: Measure, diagnose and recover
text:
Guide index · Topology/flag reference
Goal: find the constrained layer before turning a knob, and recover the complete acknowledgement boundary rather than only its metadata. The SQL below is checked on PostgreSQL 18. Use a monitoring role (pg_monitor/appropriate statistics privileges) to inspect other sessions; owning pgvs3 data does not require superuser or these optional monitoring extensions. Research basis.


Save versions, settings, fixture hashes, concurrency, client caches, role, replication policy and the old binary/configuration before a trial. Record:







Path
Measure separately




Application OLTP
Whole transaction p50/p95/p99, errors, pool wait, rows/buffers and WAL.


Object reads
HEAD, whole GET, footer/range, cold fill, warm shared hit and client-private repeat.


Object writes
ACK time, bytes/sec, outbox drain/oldest age and replica replay.


Materialization
Extract/load + validate + publish + maintenance, refresh lag, query time, extra files/RSS.


Jobs/streams
Enqueue, claim, SQL effect, ACK, redelivery/retry, queue age, pinned retention.



Use the existing paired runner for changes to gateway performance and just load --capacity --replication async for resource observations. Retain every affected path and failed trial; compare with the 20% per-path budget and your stricter application SLO. Do not average a regression away with a faster unrelated query. just guides verifies semantics/syntax, not a production speedup, maximum dataset size or vendor comparison.
An X-Cache: HIT means shared object bytes, not cached query results. A fresh DuckDB connection can still share instance-private state with another connection; use a new process when that distinction matters. Disable both enable_external_file_cache and parquet_metadata_cache when attributing shared hits, count origin traffic independently, and label OS/PostgreSQL caches that were not evicted. Never drop production OS caches to make a chart “cold”.






curl -fsS "$PGVS3_ENDPOINT/healthz"
curl -fsS "$PGVS3_ENDPOINT/readyz"
pgvs3 doctor --url "$PGVS3_URL"
pgvs3 stat --url "$PGVS3_URL" --json
Liveness does not touch PostgreSQL. Readiness checks connectivity/layout, not writer role, warmth, freshness, disk headroom or absence of pending writes. Inspect SQL role explicitly:

SELECT pg_is_in_recovery(), current_setting('transaction_read_only');
SELECT name, setting, unit, source
FROM pg_settings
WHERE name IN ('server_version', 'max_connections', 'superuser_reserved_connections',
    'reserved_connections', 'shared_buffers', 'work_mem', 'hash_mem_multiplier',
    'max_parallel_workers_per_gather', 'io_method', 'effective_io_concurrency',
    'max_wal_size', 'synchronous_commit', 'synchronous_standby_names')
ORDER BY name;
pg_settings describes this SQL session. A monitoring connection does not show the per-connection policy of gateway pools or DuckDB’s scanner. For example, gateway chunk reads disable the statement timeout, and the main/chunk planner settings differ. Do not copy gateway planner controls into application SQL.
Scrape /metrics: correlate S3 admission waiting/rejected counters, main/chunk pool acquired/max connections and empty-acquire waits with request duration and errors. More client HTTP connections are not more PostgreSQL capacity. For pool contention, the ratio of the rates of pgvs3_pg_pool_empty_acquire_wait_seconds_total to pgvs3_pg_pool_empty_acquire_count_total is mean wait per contended acquire, not p99. Observe the chunk-pool equivalents too. Guard division by zero and counter resets in your monitoring system.




SELECT pid, usename, application_name, state, wait_event_type, wait_event,
       now() - xact_start AS xact_age, backend_xmin,
       pg_blocking_pids(pid) AS blockers, left(query, 160) AS query
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE datname = current_database() AND pid <> pg_backend_pid()
ORDER BY xact_start NULLS LAST
LIMIT 30;








Signal
Investigate first
Avoid




Lock/blocker PIDs
Owner transaction, DDL, ordered per-key origin writes
Killing every connection or retrying mutations without reconciliation.


IO, checkpoints or WAL pressure
Fills/ingest, storage saturation, archive/slot lag
Raising all concurrency limits together.


ClientWrite
Slow reader/network/backpressure; snapshots stay open longer
Assuming PostgreSQL CPU is the bottleneck.


Long idle transaction / old xmin
Leaked session, long extract, standby feedback
Shortening reaper grace or disabling vacuum to hide the symptom.



Use query text carefully; it can contain business data/secrets. Collect only what is needed, restrict access and redact before sharing diagnostics.



pg_stat_statements is optional: add it to shared_preload_libraries with your normal change/restart procedure, then CREATE EXTENSION pg_stat_statements in the diagnostic database. Do not replace an existing preload list. The disposable guide fixture preloads it; normal pgvs3 operation requires no extension.

SELECT queryid, calls, round(total_exec_time::NUMERIC, 2) AS total_ms,
       round(mean_exec_time::NUMERIC, 2) AS mean_ms, rows,
       shared_blks_hit, shared_blks_read, temp_blks_written, wal_bytes,
       left(query, 180) AS query
FROM pg_stat_statements
WHERE dbid = (SELECT oid FROM pg_database WHERE datname = current_database())
ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC LIMIT 10;
SELECT stats_reset FROM pg_stat_statements_info;
These are cumulative successful-statement aggregates since collection/reset, not latency percentiles or a history of failed requests. Compare deltas over a known interval; do not reset a shared production collector for your experiment. Collect application tails separately. track_io_timing adds timing detail but can add overhead; assess it rather than interpreting disabled zero timings as zero I/O cost. High shared-buffer hit ratio alone does not prove good queries.

SELECT schemaname, t.relname, n_live_tup, n_dead_tup,
       last_autovacuum, last_autoanalyze,
       age(c.relfrozenxid) AS xid_age, pg_total_relation_size(relid) AS bytes
FROM pg_stat_user_tables AS t JOIN pg_class AS c ON c.oid = t.relid
WHERE schemaname = 'guide_app' OR schemaname = 's3p'
   OR left(schemaname, 4) IN ('s3b_', 's3c_', 's3w_', 's3q_')
ORDER BY bytes DESC LIMIT 30;
SELECT * FROM pg_stat_wal;
SELECT * FROM pg_stat_checkpointer;
SELECT * FROM pg_stat_io WHERE backend_type = 'client backend';

Combine them with host RSS, disk latency/IOPS, filesystem free bytes and queue depth. pg_stat_checkpointer, not older pg_stat_bgwriter checkpoint columns, is the PostgreSQL 18 checkpoint view. Logical object length, allocated relation bytes, WAL retained on disk and local gateway scratch are different quantities.



Use pending-write SQL plus pgvs3_pending_uploads_{bytes,oldest_seconds,dead}. Set an oldest-age threshold from your handoff/freshness SLO, page on nonzero dead rows and forecast disk exhaustion from growth. The pending gauges are database-wide and repeated on every gateway: do not sum them across identical fleets as if each owned the rows. Pool/admission/spool gauges, in contrast, are per process. Scrape failures or missing metrics are not zero backlog.
On the primary:

SELECT application_name, state, sync_state, sent_lsn, write_lsn, flush_lsn, replay_lsn
FROM pg_stat_replication;
SELECT slot_name, slot_type, active, restart_lsn,
       pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn) AS retained_bytes
FROM pg_replication_slots;
An empty replication view on the demo single node is expected, not HA proof. max_wal_size is not a hard disk cap: slots/archiving can retain more. Resolve an abandoned slot with its owning consumer/rebuild plan; never delete pg_wal files. hot_standby_feedback can reduce standby cancels while retaining primary bloat. Measure both, not just replica query latency.












Incident
Preserve / fence first
Verify before returning traffic




Gateway crash
Database is authoritative; remove dead worker
Another worker reads known key/ETag and resumes pending drain. Local spool loss is not body loss after ACK.


Origin unavailable
Keep s3w_ + pending rows; throttle before space exhaustion
Same bytes readable via pgvs3; drain and origin version/integrity after repair. Never flush pending bodies.


Ambiguous PUT / enqueue / ACK
Preserve stable key/event ID; no unconditional new identity
GET/HEAD/validator or job/receipt reconciliation on the primary. A disconnect is not proof of rollback.


PostgreSQL primary lost
Fence old primary and writable fleet with the HA mechanism
Eligible promotion under the configured durability policy, writer routing, layout, known native/pending data, new writes and resumed drain.


Restore / PITR
Restore into isolated endpoints; initially read-only, outbox not allowed to hit live origin
Catalog + native bytes + pending bodies/control + application intents/receipts; validate external effects/origin separately.


Disk filling
Stop/reduce new load, retain acknowledged state
Identify payload/WAL/retired/history/slot costs; expand or deliberately reclaim unneeded data. VACUUM FULL needs extra disk and exclusive locks.



synchronous_commit=on gives local WAL durability and waits for configured synchronous standbys when present; it does not make an arbitrary asynchronous replica a lossless promotion target. flush_lsn and replay_lsn are different: remote durability is not immediate read visibility. For read-after-write on a chosen physical standby, record a post-ACK primary WAL barrier and wait until that standby has replayed it, with a bounded deadline. Verify common cluster/ timeline history; comparing LSN numbers across unrelated/promoted timelines is not a fencing or consistency protocol. Route freshness-critical reads to the primary if the contract is not established.
The bounded just fault drill proves physical-standby native/shared/pending reads, synchronous promotion, a deliberate asynchronous loss counterexample and consistent pending-body logical restore. It is not a physical archive/PITR tool qualification or an automatic HA controller. Evidence.




Record RPO/RTO, backup ID, timeline/target, versions/layout, origin mapping, active DuckLake writers/compaction/cleanup and replay/receipt retention.
Restore a complete database/cluster into an isolated network. For production, use tested physical base backups + continuous WAL/managed PITR; a replica is not a backup. A logical pg_dump is not input to WAL replay.
Restore pgvs3 bodies/control rows together. A dump of one s3w_ schema omits s3p.pending_uploads; a metadata-only restore can orphan acknowledged bodies. Coordinate application/catalog recovery too. Pause DuckLake writes and cleanup for manual multi-component backups; retain every referenced object version.
Start read-only gateways first; run doctor, verify known full/range object hashes/ETags and pending-body readability, and reopen a known DuckLake snapshot. Confirm no outbox worker has contacted the live origin.
Clone/remap the recovery origin before enabling writable workers. Reconcile origin conflicts and external effects that cannot be rolled back with SQL. Confirm queue receipts prevent duplicate effects over the chosen replay horizon.
Only after checks, switch traffic via the HA/routing mechanism. Test a fresh write, observed replay, drain and backlog alarms. Record achieved RPO/RTO and any lost/duplicated business effects; do not declare success from /readyz alone.

Native pgvs3 has no S3 versioning/replication/Object Lock. Upstream lake backup recipes relying on those features require a suitable external origin, not a setting in pgvs3. Physical PITR, provider HA, network partitions, production tail-latency budgets and exact alert thresholds remain deployment validation.



just guides owns disposable containers and removes them on exit, retaining reports. For the manual demo only, stop its extractors/relay/workers/readers, verify no other data uses the reserved names and wait for pending rows to drain. Then the following removes all demo namespace data; it is not a maintenance recipe for a live dataset:

set -eu
test "$("${PSQL:-psql}" "$PGVS3_URL" -XAt -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 \
  -c "SELECT count(*) FROM s3p.pending_uploads WHERE namespace='guide-origin'")" = 0
pgvs3 origin --url "$PGVS3_URL" --bucket guide-edge clear
pgvs3 drop --url "$PGVS3_URL" --kind cache --force guide-origin
pgvs3 drop --url "$PGVS3_URL" --force guide-edge
pgvs3 drop --url "$PGVS3_URL" --force guide-analytics
pgvs3 drop --url "$PGVS3_URL" --kind queue --force guide-jobs
pgvs3 drop --url "$PGVS3_URL" --kind queue --force guide-events
)

Measure separately




Application OLTP
